Part One, Section One of the Verses and Songs of the Various Patriarchs of the Chan School.
Recorded by Shi Zisheng of Wulao Peak Gāthās of the Buddhas and Patriarchs:
Vipaśyin Buddha
The body arises from within the signless (wherein all phenomena are established upon the foundation of non-abiding), just like various forms produced by illusion; moment by moment, it is an illusion.
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are illusions. The human mind and consciousness are originally non-existent. Offenses and blessings are all empty and have no place of abiding.
(They are like water-moons and mirror-images.)

The arising of all wholesome karmas by Śikhin Buddha is fundamentally an illusion (the Patriarchal Buddhas cannot show their heads). The creation of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion (afflictions and deluded karma are liberated in their own place).
The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind (manifesting activity and function according to nature and conditions). These illusions produce that which has no root and no real nature.
(The samādhi of language is both vertical and horizontal; it unfolds and supports without moving a single hair’s breadth.

Vipaśyin Buddha borrowed the four great elements to form a body (blending into a single unity: the crane is white and the crow is black; earth, water, fire, and wind). The mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects.

The mind is neither defiled nor pure; defilement and purity are the mind itself. If the external objects before one do not exist, the mind likewise does not exist—like gathering firewood or selecting vegetables.
Transgressions and blessings are like illusions, arising and then ceasing—where words are cut off and responses accord with the moment.

Kāśyapa Buddha seeing that the body has no reality is the Buddha’s seeing; realizing that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s realization (what kind of bowl did he get?). All sages nowadays speak of this as a dream and an illusion.

Having realized that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty (its essence and function are suchness, pervading the entire dharma-realm), how can such a person differ from the Buddha (in their blue, yellow, red, and white,
they encompass and cover all spiritual capacities)?

Kanakamuni Buddha did not perceive a physical body, yet he knew he was a Buddha (to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha as the true Triple Gem). If there were truly such knowledge, it would be distinct from a Buddha (spiritual wisdom is uncreated;

it is precisely and entirely so). The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty (the nature of sin is itself the true nature; arising and ceasing have no basis). Thus, they are serene and have no fear.
Birth and death (the gate of self-enjoyment through the seven inversions and eight delusions).

Kāśyapa Buddha, the nature of all sentient beings is pure (all relying on the self-nature *dharmakāya*, pure in every thought-moment). From the beginning, there has been no birth and nothing to be extinguished (beyond words).
The Way is severed (like a valley containing sound). This very body and mind are born of illusion (the four elements and five aggregates are themselves the Dharma-body).
Within this illusory transformation there is neither sin nor merit (for they manifest through the absence of mental activity).

The Buddha Śākyamuni is an illusory transformation, without cause and without birth (the myriad phenomena, as vast as they are, have from the very beginning been moment-to-moment free of dependence). All are thus naturally seen (phenomenon after phenomenon does not interfere with one another;

they function while being without function). All dharmas are none other than self-transformed births (unfolding and rolling up, granting and seizing, killing and enlivening according to the occasion). Illusory transformations are without birth.
Fearless (in the face of what is contrary or favorable, responding directly to the capacity of the occasion [with straightforward rules], one emerges with valor; what is there to fear?).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahākāśyapa: "I possess the treasury of the pure, true Dharma-eye.
I entrust it to you. You should listen attentively. He spoke in verse:
The Dharma is fundamentally without Dharma (the numinous, awakened true mind is complete in each and every one). Without Dharma, all dharmas are also Dharma (the non-cognizing prajñā).

Now, when I transmit the state of no-dharma (the teaching of the Dharma is without attainment), how could dharma after dharma ever have been a dharma (what can seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing take as an object)?
The First Patriarch Mahākāśyapa said:

"The Dharma of dharmas is the original nature of dharmas (attained without cultivation, with every thought in accord). There is no dharma and no non-dharma (the essence of the single truth is neither right nor wrong; even 'non-dharma' does not exist)."

Why, within a single dharma (the one path to the gate of nirvāṇa), would there be both what is dharma and what is non-dharma? (How could the gate of the one path be divided into existence and non-existence? [The "use" has no inherent substance; where there is no substance, there is no obstruction.)
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, originally possessed the Dharma (attaining the ground through the teacher). Having transmitted it, he said there was no Dharma (not obtained from another).

Each has realized for themselves (eating when hungry, drinking when thirsty, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down). Having realized this, there is not even "no-Dharma" (what can be called mountains, rivers, and the great earth?).

The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin, taught that neither dharma nor mind exists (the ground of the reality-limit). Where there is no mind, there is also no dharma (the dual extinction of mind and objects).
When he spoke of these mental dharmas (speaking of the three times as one), these dharmas were not mental dharmas (he never uttered a single word; what need is there for lips and teeth?).

The mind of the Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, is the primordial mind from the very beginning (remaining undiminished while dwelling within the six realms of existence, and remaining undiminished while abiding among the four types of noble ones). This original mind is not a substantial dharma (comprehending that there are no external objects; all things are but mind alone).

There is a dharma that possesses the fundamental mind (discussing the true mark without destroying conventional designations); it is neither mind nor the fundamental dharma (where ordinary and sage are as completely dissolved as ice melting and bricks crumbling).

The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Tīṭibha, attained mastery of the fundamental Dharma (in which all phenomena are unimpeded and every thought-moment is all-pervasive). There is neither dharma nor non-dharma (neither abiding nor a fundamental source).

Awakening is identical to non-awakening (delusion and awakening share the same source). One attains the mindless and the dharma-less (employing the wisdom of the unconditioned mind to respond appropriately to the capacities of sentient beings).

The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, had no mind that could be attained (for what can be attained by a mind that is no-mind?). What he spoke could not be called a dharma (speaking all day long yet without speaking).
If one realizes that the mind is no-mind (wherein sound and form are pure and true), only then does one understand the dharmas of the mind (calling everything by its name).

The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, had a mind identical to the realm of empty space (empty space is itself the mind). He manifested dharmas equal to empty space (dharmas are themselves empty space).

He realized the time of empty space (walking and sitting within empty space; all activities and movements are entirely empty space). There was neither "is" nor "is not" (supreme spiritual wisdom alone remains, unimpeded in responding to conditions).
The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, said:

"Space has neither interior nor exterior" (Space itself is the mind; as for the phenomena of the mind, what boundaries could they have? Space is likewise so). "The phenomena of the mind are also like this" (This verifies what was previously stated).

If one realizes emptiness, then form, emptiness, brightness, and darkness will not obstruct oneself; this is to penetrate the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), wherein the myriad phenomena emerge from True Suchness with unimpeded vigor.

The Ninth Patriarch, Vuddhamitra, held that the True Principle is fundamentally without dharma (function is identical to essence). By means of names, he manifested the True Principle (essence and function acting in tandem).
He received the "True-True Dharma" (to obtain it yet have no obtainment—merely obtaining in this way). It is neither true nor false (the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month).

The true body of the Tenth Patriarch, Master Xiè, is naturally and spontaneously real (pervading from antiquity to the present). Because it is real, its expression possesses principle (the Dharma-body preaches the Dharma-body).
Having realized the reality of reality (the Great Function manifests before one), there is neither practice nor cessation (one must not sit beneath Black Mountain; Prajñā is non-knowing).
The Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Punanayasa:

Delusion and enlightenment are like concealment and manifestation (killing or giving life according to the occasion). Brightness and darkness are not separate from one another (the whisk is itself the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body is itself the whisk). Now I transmit this dharma of concealment and manifestation (Do you see the concealed dharma?
Do you see the manifested dharma?). It is neither one nor two (It is not one: the lantern is the function, the pillar is the essence. It is not two: the lantern and the pillar [are one]).
"Shattered into a hundred pieces.

The twelfth patriarch, Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, appearing and disappearing is precisely this Dharma (when face-to-face you are presented with it, what do you see?). Brightness and darkness have never been two (ignorance is itself Buddha-nature). Now, I entrust this to you who have awakened.
To fully comprehend the Dharma (is not to fail the former sages). It is neither grasping nor abandoning (one cannot attain it by merely remaining in the middle).

The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, taught that the Dharma is neither hidden nor manifest (where the paths of ordinary and sage are cut off, and the forms of good and evil cease to exist). He spoke of this as the true limit of reality (liberation occurs right where seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing take place). To awaken to this—
The Dharma of Concealment and Manifestation (under these words, the myriad functions are penetrated). It is neither ignorance nor wisdom (worldly dharmas are themselves supramundane dharmas).

The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, named it the Dharma of Concealment and Manifestation (he did not stop there; he spoke of concealment and manifestation). Only then did he explain the principle of liberation (the seven perversions and eight inversions have never been moved by even a hair’s breadth). At this—

Since the Dharma is already unattested (one cannot further attest a dharma-body to another dharma-body), there is neither anger nor joy (when encountering the faults of the multitude, do not lose your constant deportment).

The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, originally spoke to the recipient of the Dharma-transmission (for things do not arise in isolation) regarding the principle of liberation (which is difficult for intellectual consciousness to pursue). In reality, there is nothing to be realized within the Dharma (the mountains are green and the waters are clear);
it has no end and no beginning (seeking the mind throughout the three periods of time, it cannot be found; this is why the transmission was received).

The Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra, realized that in the Dharma there is truly nothing to be realized (seeing and hearing are merely seeing and hearing; seeing and hearing are themselves unobtainable). He neither grasped nor rejected (the essence is itself the function).

The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent in form (to manifest various forms is precisely to see the essence of the Dharma). How could internal or external arise? (Sentient and insentient beings are one body—there is no distinction between heaven and earth; whatever is seen is without partiality.)
The Venerable Seventeenth Patriarch Saṃghanandin:

The ground of his mind was originally without birth (the myriad phenomena remain as they are, eternally quiescent); the causal ground arises from conditions (the three vehicles and five natures all arise from conditions);
causes and conditions do not obstruct one another (phenomena and principle, long and short, have no mutual hindrance); and the flowers and fruits are likewise so (as previously explained).

The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata, possessed various seeds within the ground of the mind (for it is from the arising of the mind that various images emerge). Through causes and conditions, he was able to sprout forth (sprouting from beneath the words of a spiritual friend).

Within conditions, there was no mutual obstruction (the myriad phenomena of the universe did not obstruct the eye of wisdom). Thus, in every birth, there was no birth (functioning while remaining without function).

The nineteenth patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, whose nature is fundamentally unborn (for nature is inherently pure), spoke of seeking a person (speaking of bodhi and nirvāṇa within the unborn nature).

Since there is nothing to be attained in the Dharma (there is not a single dharma transmitted to others), why harbor doubts where there are none to be resolved (what need is there to speak of enlightenment or non-enlightenment? All places are pure and liberated)?
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śākyamitra, said:
"To accord with non-arising upon hearing the words [of the Master]—nothing surpasses this. To be identical with the nature of the Dharma-realm (to traverse many kalpas in a single thought).

If one can understand in this way, one realizes what was previously explained. Having fully mastered both phenomena and principle, when someone asked Xuefeng, 'What is the student's own self? he replied, 'The entire universe is.'"
The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha:

"When bubbles and illusions are equally unimpeded (if one realizes all things are like illusions, what dharma could possibly obstruct?), why is there no awakening (to the fact that one puts on clothes, eats food, walks, stands, sits, and lies down)?"

The realization of the Dharma resides within this (for among all conditioned phenomena, none surpasses this). It is neither of the present nor of the past (what hindrance can there be between the present and the past, existence and non-existence, birth and cessation, or ordinary beings and sages)?
The Twenty-second Patriarch, Venerable Mañjarā:

"The mind turns according to the myriad objects; when meeting the long, it is long; when meeting the short, it is short. Where it turns is truly profound (entering this furnace, there is nothing that is not profound).
Recognizing one's nature as it follows the flow, one is neither joyful nor sorrowful (ignorance and inversion are originally pure)."

When the twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Helu, recognized the nature of mind (at this point, it is clearly understood), one may speak of the inconceivable (wherein speech unfolds and retracts with sovereign ease).

When it is fully realized, there is nothing to be attained (every phrase is inconceivable). Upon its attainment, one does not speak of knowing (Prajñā is non-knowing; yet there is nothing it does not know).

When the twenty-fourth patriarch, Venerable Siṃha, correctly expounded upon knowing and seeing (clearly and lucidly awakening), he said: "Knowing and seeing are both the mind (seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing are but the single true mind).
When the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing (the dharma of the mind is all dharmas). Knowing and seeing are right here and now (can you forcibly produce horns?)"

The twenty-fifth patriarch, the Venerable Śāṇavāsa, the Sage, spoke of knowing and seeing (to realize the Way upon hearing these words is to be a sage). Within the immediate situation, there is nothing that is not it (to pick it up and use it directly).
Now I have awakened to true nature (and am no longer deceived by others). There is neither the Way nor principle (what Dharma of the Buddha could possibly reach you?).

The True Nature of the Mind-Ground Treasury of the Twenty-sixth Patriarch, Bodhidharma (The true nature of the one mind encompasses all phenomena). Without head and without tail (Before, after, and in between—this mind cannot be named or delineated).

Responding to conditions to transform sentient beings (Like the bright autumn moon over the long river, he establishes teachings according to the capacity of the vessel). Expediently called "Wisdom" (Explaining *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* through expedient means—what is this?).
The Twenty-seventh Patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra:
The ground of the mind contains all seeds (all that exists emerges from the ground of the mind). Because of phenomena, and because of principle (worldly dharmas are themselves supramundane dharmas).

The fruit is fulfilled and Bodhi is perfected (the cause within the fruit; the fruit within the cause). The flower blooms and the world arises (when one flower opens, spring comes to the whole world—what do you call it?).
The Twenty-Eighth Patriarch, Bodhidharma:

"I have come to this land" (Master Bodhidharma came from the Western Heavens to the land of Tang). "To transmit the Dharma and save deluded minds" (nothing more than sitting facing a wall at Shaolin).

"One flower opens into five petals" (there is the Sixth Patriarch; who does not know that the flower has opened into five petals?). "The fruit ripens naturally" (from the flower comes the fruit; through the person, the mind is realized; realizing the non-...).
That which is attained).

The Second Patriarch, Grand Master Huìkě, originally had a ground for his conditions (one must first obtain the ground). Based on this ground, he planted the flowers of the Dharma (all phenomena arise from the ground of the mind). Originally, there was nothing at all.
The seeds (all dharmas have been quiescent from the very beginning) cannot produce flowers (because the mind is empty and still, its functioning is without differentiation).
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, said:

"Though the flower-seeds depend on the earth (phenomenal forms arise from the mind), from the earth the seeds produce flowers (within spiritual awakening, heaven and earth are clearly manifested). If there were no...
When a person plants seeds (the mind and its objects are suddenly forgotten; how can there be person or dharma?), the ground of flowers is entirely non-arising (seeing the Way everywhere).
The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoxin, said:

"The ground where flowers grow has arising" (seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing). Because of the ground, flowers arise and multiply (manifesting various forms within all things). Great conditions and nature...
(Conditioned arising is non-arising). When arising occurs, it is non-arising (the arising of every thought-moment which is itself non-arising).
The Great Master Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch, said:

"When sentient beings come, they plant seeds" (everyone possesses Buddha-nature). "Based on the cause, the fruit arises in turn" (there is no difference between cause and effect, or between ordinary beings and sages). Since that which is insentient has no [Buddha-nature]...
The seeds (penetrating sound and penetrating form) have neither nature nor birth (the nature of non-cognition pervades everywhere before one’s eyes).

The Great Master Huineng, the Sixth Patriarch, contains all seeds within his mind-ground (a single thought encompasses ten lands); when the rain falls universally, all sprout (when the Patriarch preaches the Dharma, sentient beings awaken). Sudden enlightenment is the flower.
Sentimentality has already ceased (sound and form are boundless; Prajñā is boundless). The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously accomplished (faithfully receive and practice).
Master Nanyue Huairang’s mind-ground contains all seeds;
when it meets with moisture, they all sprout. The flowers of samādhi are signless; what could be destroyed, and what could be formed?

The Great Master Ma of Jiangxi spoke of the mind-ground according to the occasion: "Bodhi is also simply peace; phenomena and principle are both unimpeded; that which arises is precisely non-arising."—The Third Patriarch’s Great Master’s *Inscription on Faith in Mind*.
The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will be transparently clear and bright.
A difference of a hair’s breadth creates a chasm between heaven and earth. If you wish for it to manifest before you, do not maintain notions of compliance or resistance;
for such conflict between the compliant and the resistant is a sickness of the mind. Failing to recognize the profound principle, one merely exerts oneself in vain by seeking stillness.
Perfectly identical to the great void, Without deficiency and without surplus. It is precisely because of grasping and rejecting That one does not match it.
Do not pursue conditioned objects; Do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of even-mindedness, All things are naturally exhausted.
Cessation returns to movement; Cessation itself further intensifies movement. If you merely stagnate at these two extremes, How can you know this single state?

If one path is not penetrated, effort is lost at both ends. To dismiss existence and pursue non-existence, or to follow emptiness while turning one's back on emptiness, involves excessive words and excessive deliberation;
these turn out to be inconsistent. When words are cut off and deliberation ceases, there is nowhere that penetration does not reach.
To find the essential meaning by returning to the root, yet to lose the source through following after illumination, is to momentarily revert to form—this surpasses the previous emptiness.
The transformations of the preceding emptiness all arise from delusive manifestations; do not seek the Truth, simply let go of views.
When the two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them; as soon as there is right and wrong, one becomes distracted and loses the mind.
Since duality arises from unity, do not even cling to that unity; when the One Mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.
No blame, no laws; no birth, no mind. The capacity can vanish along with the object; the object sinks as it pursues the capacity.
The object arises from the capacity, and the capacity arises from the object. If you wish to know these two segments, they are fundamentally one emptiness.
This one emptiness encompasses both; together they contain the myriad phenomena. Seeing neither the refined nor the coarse, how could there be partiality or factionalism?
The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and increasingly slow.
To grasp at it is to lose its measure and inevitably enter a deviant path. To let it be of itself, its essence has no coming or going;
following nature accords with the Way. In carefree wandering, there is an end to affliction; to bind one's thoughts is to deviate from the Truth. Sinking into dullness is not good.
Do not weary yourself with mental toil; what use is there for distinguishing between the distant and the near? If you wish to enter the One Vehicle, do not detest the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
When the six sense objects are not detested, one returns to the same state as perfect enlightenment. The wise act without contrivance (*anabhisaṃskāra*), while the foolish bind themselves.
The Dharma has no differentiation of dharmas; it is through delusion that one clings to them. To employ the mind by means of the mind—is this not a great error?
The deluded give rise to stillness and agitation; the awakened find neither good nor evil.
All dualistic extremes are falsely concocted by oneself, like dreams, illusions, or empty flowers—why labor to grasp them? Gain and loss, right and wrong: let them all be cast aside at once.
If the eye does not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord; if the mind does not diverge, the myriad dharmas are of one suchness.
The single suchness of the body is profound; In its stark stillness, it forgets all conditions. All phenomena are viewed as equal, Returning to and merging with the natural state.
That by which they are extinguished cannot be compared or likened; In stillness there is no movement, and in movement there is no stillness.
Since both are not established, how can there be one? Ultimately and exhaustively investigated, No fixed rules or patterns remain.
The mind is opened to equanimity, and all conditioned activities cease. Doubts are completely purified, and right faith becomes straight and upright.
Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. Empty and luminous, it illuminates itself without taxing the power of the mind.
It is not a place of discursive thought, difficult for the conscious intellect to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self.
It requires urgent resonance; it is simply called non-duality. Where there is no duality, all are identical, universally encompassing the wise of the ten directions.
All enter this school; the school is neither constricted nor extended. In a single thought-moment, ten thousand years exist or do not exist.
Before one's eyes throughout the ten directions, the smallest is identical to the great, as all boundaries are forgotten and severed.
The ultimate is great, while the relative is small; one does not see its boundaries or surface. Existence is itself non-existence, and non-existence is itself existence.
If it were not thus, there would be no need for guarding. One is all, and all is one.
If one can simply be thus, why worry about not reaching completion? The mind of faith is non-dual, and non-dual is the mind of faith.
The path of language is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present.
This is the Inscription on the Profound from Master Jia of Dongshan in Junzhou.

I humbly consider that with sounds beyond ordinary rhyme, one provisionally employs the profound chant to clarify the essential source. To enter deeply into the principle is to speak through non-action.

The purport of this assembly is that essence and function are indistinguishably fused, and the partial and the perfect intermingle. It is like the artisan Lun Pian who, having mastered his craft, wields his blade and brandishes his axe with such ease that they do not even graze the void;
thus, through mutual reversal and lateral reference, one relies on the bird-path to reach the vast emptiness and employs the mysterious way to encompass all.
Thus, although its essence is empty and quiescent, it does not conflict with the manifold movement of phenomena. Within the realm of existence, it is the absence of fixed phrases;

This is likened to a lotus in a furnace of red-hot embers (suddenly appearing where there was nothing; its subtlety lies in the state of its essence, which clarifies one's own nature).

Do not say that "no-mind" is the Way (if there is still this trace of a mark, sitting [in meditation] belongs to the realm of effort). Even "no-mind" is still separated by a further barrier (he has no such news;

The Patriarch’s intent, the Patriarch’s intent, is like space, yet it is not space (originally without arising or ceasing, nor coming or going; borrowing empty space as its essence and white clouds as its function—this is borrowing "function" to clarify "itself"). (It does not fall into the ranks of ordinary or sage; it transcends all existence and non-existence, standing far apart from the realm of perfect luminosity, solitary and independent beyond all things—a mysterious mechanism). Even the Three Sages have not yet reached it.

To clarify this principle (*The Three Sages are people who have reached the ultimate depth, yet they come back to practice on this side. If one goes in such a way for a single thought-moment, that is still directed toward effort;

Time is precisely the turning back to the point where the paths merge into a single essence. It is also said that through skillful means (*upāya*), one attains the wondrous; because the essence is profound, there is nothing to which one is obstructed.

The jade maiden gives birth to silkworms at night (where there is no silk, the Buddha-seed is never severed). Carrying a basket before the sun has risen (the essence follows what is after and the awakening precedes what is before; neither extreme is the middle way).

Picking fruit while the moon faces the window (observing at the moment of perfect fullness, not biased toward one side). Holding a fan for the cold sky in hand (not discarding such a time where being and non-being coexist). The body wears no shirt for the fifth month.

(Not concealing ugliness; not entering at the proper time). Gathering flowers to enter a foreign land (there is no place of resemblance; not entirely empty). To offer them to those among the Immortals (the most noble among all sages; their classes are not uniform).

I respectfully address those who study the profound mystery (do not pass the time in negligence; this matter must be penetrated). In practicing Chan, do not merely guard idleness (one must strictly avoid sitting in vain; it is enough to make one weep with grief).
The Inscription on Seated Meditation by Chan Master Mi (with a commentary and preface by Chan Master Dayang Ming’an).
I humbly observe that the models established by the former masters leave no aspect of phenomenon or principle unaddressed. All dharmas are empty and still; these are taken as one’s seat.

Meditation is not a matter of conceptual thought; the Way transcends coming and going. Sentient and insentient beings—neither are regarded. Though the provisional name "seat" is used to designate it, how could meditation [be such a thing]?

This clarifies the relationship between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). One should know that the arising of wisdom through seated meditation (*zuo chan sanmei*) encompasses them both entirely. Those who study the Chan lineage ought to understand the essence of sitting.
This is a brief commentary on the "Inscription on Meditation" (*Chan ming*), written by me following a request for instruction during a private interview. It follows below.

When coming, one does not enter the gate (there is no gate to enter). When departing, one does not leave the door (one departs without returning from whence one came). When sitting upright, one neither sits nor does not sit (there is no formal sitting).

When walking upright, one neither walks nor does not walk (the departure is not upright; the arrival is not auspicious). This is neither mind nor non-mind (both are without substance). It all depends on looking or not looking (there is no separate looking).

Returning to the root is not returning to the source (returning to the source is merely guarding what is held). Reverting to the origin leaves no path (the path for reverting to the origin does not pass through). If one chants:

The *Hujia Qu* (The Tune of the Hu Family; Kenbuquan; Zhibuqi). Every sound and every phrase do not touch [the surface] (every sound is unheard; the phrase remains hidden within the point). Whenever one recalls the "Snowy Verse" (there is a melody within the snow;

how can those who harmonize with it be distinguished?), The cold lamp does not require a candle (the cold lamp does not illuminate the candle; it stands still, and the snowy path is divided). As one sits, the stone shoots grow (in great sitting, there is no difference from arising);

What need is there to use an axe to hew them down? (When used, it does not function as a deliberate effort). To inform those who practice Zen (the words are subtle; one must clarify the essential meaning): Walk in the profound mystery (*xuan*).

Do not move your feet (one must strictly avoid facing the wind). You must not act in such a way (the whole body ultimately finds no place to rest). To act in such a way results in limitation (do not let phenomena and principle stagnate in what you grasp).
Let go of the weary grasping (grasping leads to nothing being attained). Casting off the hands, one is still bound (in vast openness, all objects of knowledge cease).

Step by step, nothing is brought forward (extending the hand does not meet the present; walking, there is no path to speak of). Shortening or extending, there is no interruption (step by step, there is no gap). It is not entirely contained within the seat.

The person (does not maintain full presence within the seat; ultimately, there is no characteristic of a seat). The great sun (the sun has no intentionality; its illumination does not pertain to the present).
The *Mingdao Song* (Verses on the Illumination of the Way) by Monk Luohan of Zhangzhou:
The ultimate Way is profound and vast; it cannot be proclaimed through words. If proclaimed through words, it is not the true pointer. Who would say that "this" exists?
It is present everywhere—how could it be likened to the "real" or the "void"? Should one attempt to distinguish between the real and the void, it is like a reflection appearing in a mirror.
Existence and non-existence are manifest, yet wherever they are, there is no injury. Without injury and without location, what can bind or obstruct?
Not relying on the achievement of effort, by what means could it be so? Whether it is "so" or "not so," both are but teeth and lips.
If one presents it in this way, the fundamental principle is buried; The principle is not something presented through thought, And cannot be seen or heard.
Seeing and hearing are not liberated; they are like the moon reflected in water. If one does not understand this, it becomes instead a superfluous dharma.
If even a single dharma has form, it clouds your eyes. When the eyes are obscured, the world appears jagged and vast.
My school is extraordinary: it is manifest and brilliant in the very presence of all. Both Buddhas and sentient beings alike receive its transformative power.
Do not lower your head; it is difficult to attain through mere deliberation. Break through the gateway of the face, and swiftly realize the joy that covers heaven and earth!
Cast off the roots and dust; yet, alas, they do not understand, and thus they vainly recite Master Zhigong’s "Song of the Twelve Hours" today.

At dawn, at the hour of Yin: within the frantic mechanism lies the person of the Way. Having endured suffering and hardship through countless kalpas, they fail to believe in the eternal holding of the wish-fulfilling jewel.
If one grasps at external objects, one enters the ford of delusion; even the slightest trace of it is but dust.
Do not dwell upon former appearances or characteristics; seeking out teachers externally is likewise not the truth.

The sun rises at the hour of Mao. In its functioning, there is no need for clever artifice. Even if divine light illuminates existence and non-existence, the mere movement of thought brings one into the harassment of demonic realms.
If you apply effort, you will never reach completion; day and night you will be twisted by others, self, and ego.
Do not arrange anything—just follow along as it is. When has affliction ever arisen in the mind-ground?
At the hour of eating, ignorance is fundamentally the body of Śākyamuni. Sitting or lying down, one does not know that the source is the Way;
thus one wanders aimlessly, suffering in vain. Recognizing sounds and forms, one seeks out the distant and the near—all such people are defiled by others.
If you wish to set your mind on seeking to become a Buddha, ask the empty sky to begin your departure from the dust of the world.

At the hour of Youzhong (9–11 a.m.), those who have not yet attained realization compete to seek it out. Even if you were to encounter the words of a truly transcendent patriarch, do not settle upon a conceptualized meaning within your mind.
Merely guarding the mysterious and devoid of words—yet if you cling to this, as before, it will still not be it.
If for a moment you spontaneously accept [the truth] and cease seeking, you will never again be driven by demonic realms throughout eternal kalpas.

At noon in the land of the South, there is a priceless jewel within the four great elements. One refuses to cast aside the mirage and the flowers in the sky, laboring in vain through intentional cultivation.
There has never been delusion; do not seek enlightenment. Let the morning sun rise and set as many times as it will;
within the body of form lies the formless body, and upon the road of ignorance lies the path of non-arising.

The sun has not yet reached its zenith. How could the mind-ground ever have attained the definitive meaning? The texts of other schools have their degrees of intimacy; there is no need for effort to seek this underlying intent.
It moves freely and unrestrainedly, utterly free from taboos. It dwells perpetually among humanity yet does not reside within the mundane world;
its functioning has always been amidst sound and form. Why do deluded men, failing to recognize it, strive with such schemes?
The hour of *shen* (the third watch). To study the Way, one must first not grow weary of the mundane dust. Phenomenal forms are originally but provisional accumulations;
where there is no shape, there is no need to further settle the "True. To strive for purity is merely to exhaust the spirit. Do not take deluded madness as your neighbor.
If you do not seek a place of non-abiding beneath these words, you are but a temporary so-called "renunciant."

The sun sets in the hour of You (5–7 p.m.). Illusory sounds and fragrances do not endure; even the exquisite delicacies of dhyāna-joy are not consumed, so who could further drink the wine of ignorance?
There is nothing to discard and nothing to preserve; vast and carefree, such a state has never existed before.
Even if one possesses great learning and mastery of past and present, this is merely wandering outside in folly and madness.

At dusk, during the hour of Xu, the wild child sets out to perform deeds and enters a dark room. Even if his mind were to penetrate infinite time, throughout kalpas how could it ever differ from this very day?
Should you attempt to deliberate upon it, you will instead become a mere whining chatterer; this only serves to make the heart as black as lacquer.
Day and night, the radiance of the sun and moon shines upon existence and non-existence, yet the deluded person calls this the *pāramitā*.

At the hour of Ren-ding (Hai), when one’s courageous diligence turns into indolence, and not even a hair’s breadth of the mind for cultivation arises, one remains eternally sovereign within the light of formlessness.
Transcending Śākyamuni and surpassing the patriarchs, yet if there is even a speck of dust in the mind, it will again become an obstruction.
One becomes dissolute, always like a person who is dazed and senseless. There is naturally someone of penetrating insight who loves such a person.
At midnight, when the mind abides in non-arising, that is itself birth-and-death. When has birth-and-death ever belonged to existence or non-existence?

When it is used, use it directly—do not rely on words and letters. The words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are merely external matters; recognize that at the very moment they arise, they are not [the truth].
If you search for them with deliberate intent, there is truly nothing at all. When the demons of birth-and-death come to test you, let them try as they will.
At the hour of Chou, when the cock crows, there is a single sphere of radiant light that has long been present. Seeking it within and without, one finds nothing at all;
yet its functioning within the realm of objects is entirely pervasive. It has no head to be seen, nor does it have hands. When the world perishes, it does not decay.
Listen to a word for those who have not yet realized it: who is it that opens their mouth right now?
Verses and Eulogies by Master Longya (with Preface). By Qi Ji of Nanyue. Preface:
Regarding the verses and eulogies transmitted within the Chan school, these extend from the twenty-eighth patriarch down to the sixth patriarch. After that, they were lost.
Later, many venerable elders from various regions also composed such works. This was primarily to chant and expound upon the profound essence of the mysteries.

Unless one possesses a study that transcends the conventional, these should not be evaluated through the lens of names and phrases. By the beginning of the Xiantong era, there were compositions by the two Great Masters Baizhang of Xinfeng and Baiya;
these circulated widely within the Zen groves. Although their form resembles poetry, their essential meaning is not that of poetry. [Those who] are deluded...
Upon seeing this, one might clap one's hands in approval. Recently, there was one who ascended the gate of Longya; he compiled the verses of the Master and requested a preface from me.
Longya’s successor was Xinfeng. Generally, whenever something is entrusted to an image or conveys a subtle excellence, it must contain the great intent.
It is like the dark-blue head of a horse or the embryo within a pearl oyster, radiating brilliance from beneath the waves;

yet upon holding it up and savoring its flavor, one only perceives the mind and thoughts becoming clear and tranquil, as if wandering through the vast void—all of which does not equal the manifestation of the written word.

Furthermore, it is said that when Confucius and Wenbo Xuezi exchanged a raised brow and a blink of the eye to demonstrate the Way, why should verbal expression have been an obstacle? Thus, I have composed this preface for it.
[End of] the Ear. There are ninety-five verses in total.
When one studies the Way, do not greedily seek after it. When all things are free of the mind, the Way accords with the head.
If you can realize the Way of no-mind through no-mind, once you have realized the Way of no-mind, then rest.
In studying the Way, one must first learn poverty; once one has learned poverty, the Way will become intimate.
When one realizes this state of being a poor man of the Way, the functioning of the Way is just like that of a poor person.
Having studied the Way, one receives the Teacher’s pointing-out and is thus set free. Within non-existence lies a path hidden among men;
even if one can expound a thousand sutras and treatises, a single phrase will be difficult to utter when the moment arrives.
In studying the Way, one must first establish oneself; ensure that the path of practice remains free from the dust of defilement. A true monk does not need to dwell in mountain caves;
wherever he goes, being without a fixed mind, he is already among men.
To study the Way, one must first have an awakening; it is like once competing in a swift dragon boat race.
Although it is the quiet ground of an old pavilion, only after winning it once does one finally rest.
To study the Way, one must first still the myriad activities of the mind; to use these activities to study the Way only gives rise to further doubt. This gate is vast and free from all obstructions;
though many may enter it, those who truly penetrate it are rare.
Once one attains the state of no-mind, the path of emotion is naturally stilled; when the six gates are at rest, the body need not toil. Those with whom one has affinity are not mere friends;
those for whom there is no further use are brothers in the shared brow.
Once one attains the mindless state, there is immediate vast emptiness; this is solely because the gate of the ancient patriarchs has been opened.
If, within this, one were to study according to the Three Vehicles, one would have no cause to encounter it for ten thousand kalpas.

The self-nature is suchness, spontaneously and eternally so; for this reason, my practice has ceased and I dwell by the Three Xiang Rivers. My twin brows have no further use, yet they are the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark;
where speech arises, there is no division, for my tongue is broad and long.
Since childhood, following a teacher to study the ancestral lineage; like bees entangled by idle flowers, they remain bound. A true monk does not falsely dwell beyond the clouds;
having attained [realization], he is without mind, and even form is empty.
Having attained the holy and transcended the mundane, he remains silent; the Sleeping Dragon forever fears the clarity of the azure pool.
If a person in this world could always remain thus, how could the great earth retain even his name?
Those who have attained the Way are no different from those who have not; with no sense of victory or defeat, one naturally rests the spirit.
Since ancient times, the virtuous ones have called me a "poor man of the Way," but within this gate, how many people can truly enter?

The emptiness of mind does not equal the peace of the emptiness of the Way; the Way and the emptiness of mind are of one and the same form. Those who investigate the mystery are not merely practitioners of the emptiness of the Way;
when they first encounter one another, it is not easy to discern them.
This life does not cease; when will it ever cease? Know that cessation occurs within this very life. The mind ceases only because of the absence of deluded thoughts;
when delusion is empty, the mind’s cessation is the time of rest.
The kalpa-fire once blew upon it with breathless force; yet it did not wither then, despite the lack of effort from its own power. Neither humans nor devas saw a cloud of dust arise;
their fears subsided, and each returned of their own accord.
The Way has no beginning, yet one studies the painting of dragons; originally, one has not yet grasped the traces of the brush-tip.
Once one has realized the true dragon, only then does one realize that all one’s efforts throughout life were in vain.
What is it that causes morning grief and evening sorrow? If one does not study in youth, one will feel shame in old age. It is not that the *li* pearl is begrudged by the black dragon;
rather, it is simply that people of this age do not know how to seek it.
Having realized the source of the mind, one is at peace everywhere; why need one face the forests and peaks all day long? When jade is burned in fire, it becomes even more lustrous;
when the lotus is in the water, its leaves grow ever drier.
Sweeping the floor, brewing tea, and handling the needle—there is nothing else remaining for the mind to dwell upon.
All who travel reach the mountain gate; my door has no gate, so seek it beyond.
Whether dwelling in city walls or in the mountains, having attained the Way, the mind is at ease wherever one is. It is truly like a small child returning to his parents;
as for clothing, one wears whatever is available to ward off the cold.
The six functions of the Way are like the eyebrows; only when their functioning is like the eyebrows can they be observed. When people perceive the Way, it is as if in silence;
human sentiment is entirely the sentiment of the Way, where all is at peace.
To attempt to study while following one's own emotions—how truly bitter! With doubt unsevered, delusion is hard to crush. Not yet having realized it, you must depart with your satchel;
once you have found leisure and are free from affairs, you may return.
The four winds blow and form things not in vain; how lovely are the green leaves hanging with pearls.
Though one may plant these mindless jewels, let others take them as they please.
The minds of worldly people cannot be subdued; they bring about calamity and sorrow, which accumulate until they reach the eyebrows.
Once the body realizes that the mind is without affairs, the eyebrows emit radiance of which one is unaware.
The monastic quarters are silent and still as I practice in summer; I close my door and keep people at a distance, yet I am aware of their wonder. My own house has its own shared tradition:
though none come from a thousand miles away, I am willing to accept him.
Gazing out the window, one does not realize that even an inch of time has passed. To practice with urgency is already too late;
by day, one merely passes the time attending to worldly affairs. How could the Way be realized within a garden?
Pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas have not yet exhausted emptiness; humans and devas come and go to seek the True Doctrine. How can they compare to the Buddha, the man free from doubt?
Sitting upright with no-mind, he is thus directly penetrating.
If one seeks the mark on the crown of the head, it is ultimately not to be seen; responding to conditions, it is like a valley that does not deviate from its direction.
This gate has no path to be found elsewhere; there is only the resting of the mind, which serves as the immediate encounter.

In these three matters, there is neither sorrow nor joy; the mind seeks only the Way. For now, I accompany the wandering clouds and waters, seeking no fame. Let others offer their myriad interpretations as they may;
my essence is naturally flawless and unstained by blue.

If you attempt to remove delusions with the mind, the delusions will be difficult to forget; if you do not realize the profound mystery, affairs will only grow more frantic. While you have not yet understood, you speak only of the Tathāgata’s secrets;
once awakened, you will know that nothing is concealed.

If a person has no mind to follow the ways of worldly sentiment, they will perceive that the path of ignorance is already enlightened. It is the person who can propagate the Way, and the Way that can manifest the person;
when the Way resides within the person, the person naturally finds peace.
All living beings share a single dust mote; the former sages practiced with diligence and early transcended the mundane. Since they were men of great capacity, so too am I;
who could prevent my spring from blooming when another’s does?
A difference of a hair’s breadth separates one by a thousand li; in a single kṣaṇa, awakening brings one level with the Patriarchs. The profound mystery must be realized within the profound;
the functioning of the Way is taught for the Way-practitioner to know.

Those who investigate the Way of the Mysteries must not be complacent. In the place of study, one must distinguish between black and white. Since time immemorial, the thousand sages have followed no divergent path;
yet the gates of wisdom that transcend conditions are manifold.
Formerly, Lady Wu studied the art of painting; she did not grasp the principles of Sengyao, nor was her work refined. She failed to paint horses successfully and even missed the mark with donkeys;
people of the time all laughed at her, deeming her lifelong efforts in vain.
With whitewashed walls and vermilion gates, how could affairs be many? With high walls and barred doors, one dwells as still as a mountain. Do not say that within city walls there are no men at rest;
if a person is without worldly intent, they are at ease wherever they are.
Frugal in expenditure and valuing plans to prolong one's days, mending clothes so as to avoid frequenting the human world—only those who are mindless in the Way act in this way;
yet it is truly difficult to attain such mindlessness.
The Way of Cold Moons and Frosty Heavens is solitary; a hall of Zen companions tends a cold brazier. Where the patched robe is worn through, ice penetrates the bones;
sitting deep into the night, there is not even charcoal left.

A myriad of elaborate arrangements are not as good as the ordinary; it does not startle others, yet it endures for a long time. When things proceed as usual, it is like the arrival of the autumn wind:
without intention, it cools people, and they cool themselves.
Knee-length trousers are mottled with the scars of fire; my entire body is shattered, yet I cannot be startled. Sitting alone in the mountain hut, I gaze upon the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
suddenly, all troubles vanish, and the human heart finds its fulfillment.
In a single room with a single bed, I dwell beyond the mundane world; with a single flask and a single bowl, I sustain my life.
Though there may be a path leading through the village before my door, how could I ever have known a single household?

What was not understood in former lives must now be understood; in this life, one shall deliver the bodies of all successive lifetimes. Those ancient Buddhas who were not yet awakened are the same as those today;
those who awaken today are themselves the ancients.
Eating wood and wearing grass, my heart is like the moon; throughout my life, there is neither thought nor limit.
If people of this age ask where I dwell, green waters and blue mountains are my home.
In the morning I see flowers blooming, the trees dyed crimson; In the evening I watch the petals fall, the tree returns to emptiness.
If one compares these blossoms to the affairs of the human world, The flowers and human affairs are one and the same.
Willow colors hold the mist, flowers smile upon their branches; The oriole sings beneath the trees—how few know this? Those of later generations should rightly seek the path of mystery;
Do not cast away your time in vain.
My aspiration for the Gate of Emptiness is a vow that shall never cease. Do not allow trivial matters to hang upon your mind. White clouds are the companions for your practice;
let them pass as time flows on, leaving nothing behind.
Knowing the body is an illusion, one seeks not fame; like bubbles rising and sinking, how long can they last? I ask those who study the Way among the clouds and mountains:
when will your cultivation reach fulfillment?
While dreaming, how could one know the dream is empty? Only upon awakening does one realize there was nothing within the dream. When deluded, one is just like a person in a dream;
after enlightenment, one is like a man who has woken from sleep.

Those deluded have not yet understood, yet they urge the blind and the deaf; it is like adding another layer of mud upon the earth. Those who understand have an intention that is like the intention of the deluded;
they remain within delusion and do not encounter it.
Human sentiments are deep, while the Way’s sentiment is subtle; the Way employs human sentiment, yet the world does not know it.
Though there may be human sentiment, if it lacks the employment of the Way, how long can such sentiment endure?

Those who achieve Buddhahood are rare, while those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are many. Yet, if one practices for a long time with such [conceptual] mindfulness, it instead becomes a demonic obstacle.
If you now wish to easily achieve Buddhahood, there is no need to compare it with the mind of non-mindfulness.
A solitary old man sits amidst his furniture; long hair grows from between his brows, white and disheveled. How could his mind find rest and his will find peace?
It is simply because all things within his heart have become empty.
At the two times of day, whether the meal of gruel and rice be long or short, one should rest from seeking within the three realms; this is the great essence.
Among those in the world who have many desires, none shall find satisfaction until the arrival of impermanence.
If you have not yet realized it, go forth at once to pay homage in person; there is no need to sit upright and preserve a life of pure poverty.
How can the secret practice of Rāhula compare to Kāśyapa’s hearing what cannot be heard?
If one seeks the Way while acting as if seeking fame, no one in this world will achieve it. With a tranquil mind, one has never reached the site of practice;
instead, one wanders idly along the dusty paths of the world.
The cypress and pine grow straight up, reflecting the mountain peaks; their uniform, eternal green is beheld by the Wayfarer. Through the waxing and waning of the four seasons, they remain unchanged;
how could they compare to ordinary trees, which possess many varieties?
Among them all, the compassionate mother was moved by her son’s feelings; losing him, she wept piteously, startling everyone wherever she went.

Among the many people at the market, though none were his mother, as she gazed upon them, her tears still filled her eyes. When the mother arrived and saw her son, she immediately turned her face away and remained silent.
The flame-light body with the white tuft between the eyebrows—phenomenal reality may seem more prominent than principle, yet phenomenal reality exists only because principle exists.
Through the compassionate skillful means of principle, one transforms devas and humans; when one day there is great awakening and all is dissolved, only then can one be called a person of no affairs.
"Śramaṇa, do not trouble yourself by staying far from Jetavana. Observe the four dignified postures of your own body; if the thistle grows among the hemp, it will never stand straight.
For the monks to separate themselves from the pure assembly is most groundless. From ancient times in the past, all the former masters have found peace within the monasteries."
Humans and devas must rely upon provisional forms for practice; if there were no forms and no shapes, how could the world ever know? Śāriputra attained realization while sitting in the mountains;
the falling rain of flowers was due to his being slow to see. Those of the Three Vehicles who wish to study such matters must become like Śāriputra before they can truly know them.
I traveled to every famous mountain on foot; through many years of hardship, I wore out my socks.
Now that I am old and can no longer walk, I hold a broken wooden ladle in my hand. This broken wooden ladle distributes the medicine of ambrosia to all sentient beings.
Once they have eaten it, all shall become fully awakened; all confusion and delusion shall be utterly lost.
Without cause, he was sent to the edge of the ink pool; his body and robes were dyed black as smoke.

He went back to wash them in clear water upstream, yet his body and mind remained stained just as before. He was ordered to strip them off and don fresh white ones, yet he could not avoid returning to the same pure conditions.
Since both the paths of defilement and purity remain unresolved, one must ultimately attain the mystery of one’s own mind.
I intend to dwell in the City God’s precincts to guard against what is not right; seeing where the clouds arise, I again think of returning home.

My three-thatched cottage still stands with joy; the nine-fold green vines still encircle it. The pines and cypresses, planted but recently, are already flourishing; the hibiscus flowers at the start of autumn have never withered.
Though the mountain clouds hang thick and spreading, who knows who it is that receives and gathers them?
Since realizing that initial awakening is itself ignorance, I have wandered with this single robe, following conditions as they arise. When reviled by others, I have no mind for contention;

hearing talk of the Unconditioned, I do not seek to dispute it. It would be best to remain ignorant and dwell in a dark room, yet because of the need to distinguish between the ordained and the laity, I inform you practitioners who come and go:
only when you find a teacher who has no intentional purpose will you reach the state of non-arising.
A fine drizzle falls for many days; the hundred plants sprout branches and grow without being noticed. When transformation cannot be stirred, the people provide for themselves;
that the people provide for themselves is likewise so. Heaven regards the myriad things as straw dogs; though it covers them, it has no heart, yet one still looks to it.
Were it not for this state of non-action beneath the trees, how could one perceive that kings and lords possess such resources?
Provisions of rice, firewood, and tea are abundant; my thatched hut and reed door do not startle the world. At dawn there is congee, and at mealtime there is rice;
these sustain me as I remain in the natural flow of my being. In winter, I rest the mind and pass the time according to my lot; when spring comes, I must labor with all my strength.
If I can sustain myself thus through this life, in the next life I shall still be like one who has nothing to do.
Studying the Way is like drilling for fire: when smoke appears, do not stop. Only when the golden star manifests will you reach home at last.
The great treasure of Jambudvīpa is rarely seen by those who encounter it; if someone were to offer it to me, I would attain Buddhahood in a single moment.

Awakening takes but a single moment, yet it can resolve doubts spanning ten thousand kalpas. If a person’s doubts from ten thousand kalpas cannot be resolved in a single moment, how could the ancient masters have discussed them?
To inform those who study the profound mystery: you must harbor a sense of remorse at this time.
To seek a cow, one must follow its tracks; to study the Way, one must seek the mindless state. When the tracks are found, the cow returns; when the mind is absent, the Way is easily sought.
Only mindful of the tree by the gate, which can accommodate birds to perch and roost, those who come do not call out with a seeking mind; they leap forth and have no longing to return.
If one’s mind is like a tree, it will not conflict with the Way.
When the night grows cold, one should tend the fire; protect the assembly until daybreak. At dawn, the body feels warm, and the mind becomes alert; as the mind awakens, its clarity increases further.

How could this be a matter of having no ambition? It is because excessive seeking loses the spirit of the Way. I have observed those who seek much: though their years are advanced, their undertakings do not succeed.

They are like old trees by the river; when the wind shakes them, their branches are surely in peril. When the bank collapses, they follow the water away; once they have entered the sea, no one can pursue them.
Death on the road is like withered wood; how could the surging waves ever turn back? Though the people of this age disregard me, I am able to bring rest to the blind turtle in the sea.
I have newly built a three-room hut; with much mud, I fear there may be drafts. There are no noble guests at my door, so my clumsy nature is too weary to go out and meet them.
I eat my rice according to the season; when my robes are worn, I sew them alone. If anyone comes to question me, I beckon with my hand and tell them I am deaf.
In the tenth month, the night is bright and deep; the mountain cold pierces the heart. Abandoning all ties to seek the Great Way, I have but a single robe and no quilt.

Having realized the intent of the Tathāgata, one knows that neither cold nor heat can invade; having awakened to the fact that there is no one who attains Buddhahood, one must maintain a sincere disposition toward the physical reality.

Emperor Gaozong of the Tang dynasty dispatched the palace attendant Xue Jian to deliver an imperial edict to the Sixth Patriarch Chan Master. The Master declined the invitation on the grounds of illness.
Xue Jian then asked the Master, "What is the realization of the Mahayana? The Master replied, "The nature of clarity and ignorance..."
It is non-dual. This nature of non-duality is itself Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). As for this Buddha-nature: it does not diminish while dwelling among the foolish and ordinary;

it does not increase while abiding among the worthy and holy. It is not disturbed while remaining amidst afflictions (*kleśa*), nor is it quiescent while residing in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

It is neither annihilated nor eternal, neither coming nor going. It does not abide in the middle, nor in the internal or external. It is neither born nor extinguished; its nature and characteristics are such as this.
That which is thus, eternally abiding and unchanging, is called the Way. Jian asked: "The Master speaks of neither arising nor ceasing; how does this differ from the non-Buddhists? The Master said:
"When the non-Buddhists speak of neither arising nor ceasing, they use cessation to stop arising, and use arising to manifest cessation.

When the youth Bingding came seeking fire, he suddenly attained realization upon hearing these words. He served [the Master] for ten years. Later, King Li invited him to open the hall for formal instruction. The King and Yijun were both present in the assembly. A monk asked, "The dragon roars and the mist rises; the tiger roars and the wind arises. I know this to be a matter concerning the transcendence of the world, yet why is it that I do not understand it? The Master then said: "Fire is here. The monk immediately attained great enlightenment. The King and Yijun also attained realization. Subsequently, the Master was appointed as the Abbot of the Great Xingshan Monastery. One day, while sitting in the Dharma Hall, he addressed the assembly: "The Buddhas of the three periods of time all transmit the mind-seal of the Tathāgata. This mind-seal is precisely the mind of sentient beings. It is neither produced nor extinguished, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. It is originally complete and perfect. Because sentient beings give rise to false thoughts, they lose sight of their original nature. Therefore, the Buddhas appear in the world to instruct them in the Way, so that they may realize their own minds and see their nature. What is the mind? It is the mind of sentient beings. What is seeing one's nature? It is seeing one's own nature. If you can see your own nature, you will become a Buddha. If you do not see your own nature, you will remain a sentient being. You must each examine yourselves within. Do not seek outside. If you seek outside, you will be far removed from the Way. If you seek within, you will immediately attain it. Why is this? Because the Way is fundamentally within oneself. At that time, there was a monk named Zhizang who had been practicing meditation for many years. He rose from his seat and said, "I have been practicing meditation for thirty years, yet I have never seen my own nature. The Master said, "If you have not seen your own nature after thirty years of practice, how could you ever see it now? Zhizang was greatly enlightened by these words. He bowed and withdrew. The Master then struck the gavel and descended from the seat. Later, when the Master was about to pass away, he called his disciples together and said, "I am now eighty-four years old. My life span has reached its end. I have no regrets regarding my past deeds. However, I do regret that I did not encounter the Great Master Mazu earlier in my life. Had I met him, I would have avoided all these hardships. Having spoken thus, he passed away peacefully. His remains were enshrined at Xingshan Monastery. He was posthumously titled Chan Master Daoyuan. His dharma heirs numbered over a thousand. Among them, the most prominent were the Chan Master of Mount Guo, the Chan Master of Mount Dong, the Chan Master of Mount Shuangfeng, the Chan Master of Mount Huangbo, and the Chan Master of Mount Nanquan. Each of them propagated the dharma extensively, and their influence spread throughout the world. Thus, the lineage of the Baizhang school flourished and became the foundation of the Zen tradition in China.
