There is no need for fine silks to serve as robes—how profoundly deep and inconceivable! Within this, one may learn the truly marvelous: the genuine treasure store remains within one’s own breast.
All day long one begs from others for coarse cloth; grasping at objective realms, deluded sentiments arise—just like a single wave forming upon the surface of the water.

If one can remain unattached to objects as they appear, it is just like the surface of the water returning to its original state of stillness. Whether responding to a large body or a small body, it remains thus.
Its functioning is just like the wish-fulfilling jewel: though its forms differ—whether wearing fur or bearing horns—the essence of its responding to objects is no different.
When it responds to the eye, it is like a thousand suns; the myriad images cannot escape its shadow and substance. Ordinary people simply have not yet observed this;
how can they disparage themselves and become discouraged? When it responds to the ear, it is like a deep valley; there is no sound, great or small, that it does not [reflect].
Sufficient! Throughout the ten directions, bells and drums sound all at once; the numinous light moves and flows, constantly continuing.

When it accords with the mind, discrimination ceases; it illuminates the myriad phenomena, never resting. It penetrates through mountains, rivers, and stone walls; yet, while it shines, it is eternally still.
The objects of perception vanish of their own accord—there is no need for fear. From dawn until dusk, this illumination has no counterpart. Even so, let it sustain its floating course.
The illusory body: its functions are all centered on the tongue, body, and mind.
In Master Zhaozhou’s *Song of the Twelve Hours*, for the hour of *Chou* (the Cock-Crow):
"I am distressed to see that even rising from bed is still a leakage. I have neither skirt nor upper robe; only the form of a *kāṣāya* remains."
He looks somewhat presentable, yet his trousers have no waistband and his pants have no opening. On his head are three or five pecks of green ash.
He hoped to practice cultivation for the benefit of others; who would have known he would turn out to be such a failure?
At dawn, at the hour of Yin (5–7 a.m.), this desolate village and ruined monastery are truly difficult to describe. There is not a single grain of rice for the morning meal;
I sit alone facing empty windows and the dust in the crevices. Only the sparrows chirp; no one is near. Sitting by myself, I hear the leaves falling frequently.
Who would say that those who have left the household life have severed all likes and dislikes? As I reflect on this, I cannot help but find my tears dampening my robe.
The sun rises at dawn; purity is turned instead into affliction. Meritorious deeds of the conditioned are shrouded by the dust of defilement;

the boundless fields have never been swept. Frowns abound, while satisfaction is rare. One cannot bear this old man from the eastern village—black and yellow—who has never brought any offerings, yet lets his donkey graze on the grass before my hall.

At the hour of eating, one vainly gazes at the smoke and fire of the four neighbors. Having parted from my steamed buns and dumplings last year, today I contemplate them and swallow my saliva in vain.
My recitations are few, yet sighs of lamentation are frequent; among a hundred households, there is not a single good person.
Those who come merely say they are seeking tea to drink; when they do not get tea, they depart and yet remain resentful.
The hour of Youzhong (the fourth watch). Who would have known that shaving one's hair would lead to such a state? Without cause, I was invited to become a village monk;
humiliated, hungry, and despondent, I am nearly dead. Hu Zhangsan and Hei Lisì never gave rise to even a trace of respect.
Just now they suddenly arrived at my door, saying nothing but "Lend us some tea and lend us some paper."
It is noon in Jinnan. The serving of tea and rice proceeds in rotation without fixed order; one goes from the house to the south to the house to the north.
Indeed, when arriving at the northern house, there is no delay. There is bitter sand salt, barley vinegar, millet rice, and pickled lettuce.
These are called offerings that are not ordinary; the Master’s resolve must be firm and steadfast.

It is not yet past noon. This fellow does not tread upon the ground of fleeting time. I have heard it said that "once full, one forgets a hundred hungers," and today this old monk’s body is exactly like that.
He practices no Zen; he discusses no doctrine. He simply spreads out a tattered mat and sleeps in the sun.
I suspect that even if one were to ascend to Tuṣita Heaven by supernatural power, there would be no such thing as having one's back roasted by the sun as it is here today.
In the hour of Shēn (the fifth watch), there were also those burning incense and prostrating.
Five old women, three with goiters, and a pair with faces as dark and coarse as weathered wood. Sesame tea—truly a treasure! O Vajra, do not strain your muscles in vain.
May the silkworms and wheat ripen for me next year; may the child Róuhòu receive one coin.
The sun sets in the hour of You (5–7 p.m.). Beyond this desolation, what else remains to be guarded? The lofty currents of clouds and water will surely flow on without end;
yet the novices passing through the temples remain forever present. These words of principle never reach their mouths; they merely continue the lineage of the Muni’s descendants.
With a single staff as coarse as a wild thorn, they not only climb mountains but also beat dogs.
At dusk, during the hour of Xu, I sit alone in a solitary, dark room. The light of the sun’s flames never meets my eyes;
before me, there is nothing but the lacquer of Jinzhou. I do not hear the bell; days are spent in vain. I hear only the clamor of mice scurrying about.
Relying on what else could I have the heart to contemplate and recite a *pāramitā*?
At the hour of Ren-ding (the tenth watch), the bright moon before the gate—who loves it?
As I turn inward, I only grieve that when I lie down to sleep, there is no robe to wear and nothing to cover me. Layman Liu and Upāsaka Zhao: you speak of goodness with such strange eloquence;
yet no matter how empty my mountain monk’s bag may be, when questioned, you know nothing at all.
At the midnight hour, when have my mind and thoughts ever found even a moment’s rest?

When I reflect upon the renunciants throughout the world, how many could there be who serve as abbots like me? My earthen platform bed has broken reed mats; my old elmwood pillow lacks a cover entirely.
I do not burn安息香 (anxiang) incense before the sacred images; from within the ashes, one smells only the odor of cow dung.
The Song of Realizing the Way by the Great Master True Enlightenment of Yongjia:
Have you not seen the idle man of the Way, who has severed study and attained non-action? He does not eliminate delusive thoughts, nor does he seek the Truth.

The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. When the Dharma-body is awakened to, there is not a single thing; this is the original source.
The self-nature is the original, true Buddha. The five aggregates are floating clouds, coming and going in emptiness; the three poisons are bubbles, vainly appearing and disappearing.

Realizing the true mark, there is neither person nor dharma; in an instant, the karma of Avīci hell is extinguished. Yet, if one uses false words to deceive sentient beings, one will personally incur the punishment of having one’s tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
When sudden awakening is attained, the Tathāgata-dhyāna is complete within the essence of the six perfections and myriad practices. It is like a dream...
Within, there are clearly the six realms; after awakening, all is empty, with not even a great chiliocosm to be found. There is no sin or merit, no loss or gain.
Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire. Until now, the mirror of dust has never been polished; today, you must clearly analyze and discern it.
Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If in truth there is neither birth nor non-birth, call upon the wooden puppet with its mechanical joints and ask it:
"Seeking the Buddha through effort, when will it be accomplished? Let go of the four elements; do not grasp at them. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty; this is precisely the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment. This is the definitive teaching that manifests the true Sangha.
Some people are unwilling to accept it, instead investigating according to their own whims. I cannot pluck leaves or seek branches; I must directly cut through to the root, as sealed by the Buddha.
The mani jewel—people do not recognize it—yet it is personally obtained within the Tathāgata-garbha. Its six kinds of divine functions are empty yet not non-existent.
Emptiness. A single orb of light, neither form nor non-form, purifies the five eyes and attains the five powers; only through realization can it be known, for it is difficult to fathom.

To behold one’s own reflection in a mirror is not hard, but who can grasp the moon in water? He always walks alone, always strides forth; those who attain him travel together upon the path to Nirvana.
His tune is ancient and his spirit pure, his wind naturally lofty; his countenance is haggard, yet his bones are firm—a man of rare character.
He pays no heed. This destitute Śākya son claims in speech to be poor; yet in truth, while his body is poor, his Way is not poor. Poor in body, he constantly wears coarse, tattered robes;
rich in Way, his mind harbors a priceless treasure. This priceless treasure is inexhaustible; he bestows it upon all beings according to conditions, never begrudging it.

The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within his essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of his mind-ground. When the superior man makes this single resolution—
All is understood. Those of middling and inferior capacity have heard much but lack faith; they merely harbor within their breasts the notion of having removed the soiled garments.
Who can boast of diligence toward others? Let them slander; let them be wrong. To hold fire and burn the heavens is but to exhaust oneself in vain.
When I hear this, it is like drinking nectar; it melts away and instantly enters the inconceivable. To view evil words as merit—this then becomes...
My good spiritual friend does not give rise to enmity or attachment because of slander or defamation. How can this manifest the power of the compassion and patience of non-arising?

He is proficient in the fundamental principle and proficient in its exposition; his concentration and wisdom are perfectly clear and luminous, never stagnating in emptiness. It is not that I alone have now attained realization;

the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical. With the lion’s roar he speaks without fear; when the hundred beasts hear it, their heads split open. The fragrant elephant...

Rushing about, one loses their majestic power; when devas and dragons listen in silence, they give rise to joy. Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and streams, seeking teachers and visiting paths to practice Zen.
Since recognizing the road to Caoxi, one understands that birth and death are not interconnected.
Walking is Zen; sitting is Zen; in speech and silence, movement and stillness, the essence remains serene. Even if one encounters a sharp blade, one is always composed and at ease. If...
Though filled with poisonous drugs, all is tranquil and still. My Master beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara; through many kalpas he was once the Immortal of Forbearance.
How many times was he born? How many times did he die? Birth and death flowed on without end or rest. Since his sudden awakening to the absence of birth, [all has been stilled].

What cause for sorrow or joy amidst all honors and insults? Entering deep mountains, dwelling in an araṇya, beneath towering and secluded pines, one leisurely sits in stillness within the home of a wild monk.
To dwell in such profound silence is truly serene and detached. Upon awakening, one realizes this; no effort need be exerted.
All conditioned phenomena are distinct. Giving with a mind fixed on abiding leads to the merit of rebirth in heaven; it is like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void.
When its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down, bringing about an unfavorable future life. How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark?
Therein one transcends directly and enters the stage of the Tathāgata. If you obtain the root, do not worry about the branches. It is like pure lapis lazuli containing precious gems.
The Moon. I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; benefiting self and others, it never exhausts. The river moon shines; the pine wind blows.
Throughout the eternal night, what is there to do? The Buddha-nature is the precept-jewel, the seal of the mind-ground. Mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the garments upon one’s body.
The dragon-subduing bowl, the tiger-releasing staff, the two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly. This is not a mere empty display of form.

The Sustainer of Affairs: The personal traces of the Tathāgata’s precious staff. Not seeking the true, not severing the delusive—understanding that these two dharmas are empty and signless (*animitta*).
Signless, empty, and yet not non-empty; this is the true mark of the Tathāgata. The mirror of the mind is bright, reflecting without obstruction;
vast and translucent, it pervades the entire dharma-realm. Within its reflection, the myriad phenomena appear in dense array—a single sphere of perfect radiance.

To claim there is neither internal nor external, to embrace a vast emptiness that negates cause and effect, is to invite calamity and disaster through such reckless wandering. To abandon existence for the sake of attaining emptiness is likewise a sickness;
it is like fleeing from drowning only to throw oneself into a fire. To discard the deluded mind and grasp at the True Principle is to allow the mind of grasping and rejecting to create artificiality.

When practitioners do not understand this and yet apply themselves to cultivation, they deeply fall into the error of recognizing a thief and taking him for their son, thereby depleting the wealth of the Dharma.

The extinction of all merit does not fail to proceed from this mind-consciousness. Therefore, through the Gate of Dhyāna, one brings the mind to an end and enters suddenly into the power of non-arising insight.
A great man wields the sword of wisdom; the blade of Prajñā is like the radiance of a diamond.

It not only utterly destroys the minds of externalists, but has long since struck down the courage of the celestial Māras. He thunders the Dharma-thunder, beats the Dharma-drum, and spreads the clouds of compassion.
Ah! Sprinkling sweet dew, the treading of the dragon-elephants brings boundless moisture. Those of the three vehicles and five natures all awaken;

the snow-mountain fatness is now free from all admixture. Pure ghee alone emerges, which I constantly receive. One nature is perfectly pervasive throughout all natures; one dharma universally contains all dharmas.
The single moon appears everywhere in all waters, yet all the moons in the water are subsumed within that one moon.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my nature; my nature is identical and united with that of the Tathāgata.
In a single stage, one is fully endowed with all stages; it is neither form nor mind, neither karma nor action. In the snap of a finger, the eighty thousand gates are perfectly accomplished;

in a single instant, the three great kalpas are extinguished. All numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases—what connection do they have with my numinous awakening? It is indestructible. It cannot be...
Praiseworthy! Its essence is like empty space—do not seek its boundaries. Without leaving this very place, it is eternally serene;
if you seek it, you will know that it cannot be seen. It cannot be grasped, nor can it be relinquished; within this state where nothing can be attained, there is simply attainment.
To speak in silence, and to remain silent while speaking—the Great Gate of Generosity stands open without obstruction. When someone asks me what school I understand, I reply: "Mahāyāna."
The power of Prajñā—whether right or wrong, humans cannot discern it; whether acting contrary to or in accord with the flow, even the heavens cannot fathom it.
I have already practiced through many kalpas in the past; this is no idle deception. I raise the Dharma banner and establish the fundamental tenet:
clearly, Caoxi is the Buddha’s command. Kāśyapa was the first to transmit the lamp; twenty-eight generations are recorded in the West. It has passed through the Yangtze...
The Ocean. Entering this land, Bodhidharma was the First Patriarch. The transmission of the robe through six generations was renowned throughout the world;

as for those who later attained the Way, their number is beyond reckoning. Truth cannot be established; delusion is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside, yet it is not a mere emptiness.
One does not cling to the twenty gates of emptiness; the single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently the same. The mind is the root; phenomena are the dust. These two kinds—

It is like a blemish upon a mirror; only when the stains of the blemish are entirely removed does the light finally appear. When both mind and phenomena vanish together, the nature is itself the Truth. Alas for the Dharma of the final age!
In this evil world, sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline. They are far removed from the Sages, and their false views are deep.

Demons are strong and the Dharma is weak, with much resentment and harm. Hearing speak of the Tathāgata’s gate of sudden teaching, they resent it, wishing to destroy it so that not even a shard remains.
The deed is formed in the mind; the calamity rests upon the body. There is no need for resentment or complaint, nor should one lay the blame on others.

If you wish not to incur karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata. In a sandalwood forest there are no other trees; dense, lush, and profound, it is the dwelling place of the lion.
Wandering alone in the quietude of the forest, beasts and birds all flee far away. O lion cub, followed by the pack, at three years old you can already roar with great power.
If a wild jackal pursues the Dharma King, that beast of a hundred-year-old ghost merely opens its mouth in vain.
The Perfect and Sudden Teaching has no room for human sentiment; if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must simply contend for it. This is not the mountain monk showing off his prowess.

I have practiced the Way fearing the pitfall of falling into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism. It is neither "not" nor "is," neither "is" nor "not. To err by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand li.
Thus, the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood instantaneously, while Shanxing fell into ruin in that very moment. Since my early years, I have accumulated learning;
I have also investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and treatises. Yet I distinguished names and characteristics without ceasing, like one who enters the sea to count its sands.

In vain you exhaust yourself; you are instead harshly rebuked by the Tathāgata. What benefit is there in enumerating the treasures of others? From the beginning you have stumbled, realizing your journey was in vain;
for many years you have needlessly been a guest of the wind and dust. Your nature is perverse and your understanding mistaken; you do not comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching.
Do not speak of the resolve for enlightenment in those of the Two Vehicles who are diligent; nor in the outsiders who are clever but lack true wisdom—they too are deluded.
Foolish and even slightly deluded, you produce a false understanding from an empty fist pointing at the moon; grasping the finger as the moon, you labor in vain.
Amidst the phenomena of sense bases and objects, you falsely concoct strange fabrications. Only when you do not see a single dharma can you be called Avalokiteśvara.
Once realized, karmic obstacles are originally empty; if not realized, one must still repay past debts. Like a hungry person who encounters a royal feast yet cannot eat.
When one encounters the King of Physicians while ill, how could one fail to recover? Through the power of wisdom and insight, one practices dhyāna amidst desire;
like a lotus born from fire, it is never destroyed. Vīryadatta committed a grave offense yet awakened to non-arising; he attained Buddhahood long ago and remains even now.

With the lion’s roar, he speaks fearlessly, deeply lamenting those who are ignorant, stubborn, and callous—those who know only that committing grave offenses obstructs Bodhi, yet fail to see the Tathāgata’s opening [of the path].
The Secret Instruction: Two bhikṣus committed the offenses of lust and killing; Upāli and Śrīprabha increased their karmic bonds.

The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow. This inconceivable power of liberation has a wondrous function as boundless as the sands of the Ganges.
To provide the fourfold offerings, I dare not decline the toil; even ten thousand loads of gold would be spent to repay it. I would grind my bones to powder—
The body is not yet sufficient as recompense; a single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds. This King of Dharmas is most supreme;
Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have all together testified to it. I now understand this wish-fulfilling jewel; those who believe and accept it will all be in accord.
Seeing clearly, there is not a single thing; there is no person, and there is no Buddha. The great trichiliocosm and its myriad realms are but bubbles on the ocean. All the sages—
Virtue is like a flash of lightning; even if an iron wheel were to spin upon one’s head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost.

The sun may grow cold, the moon may grow hot, but no demons can destroy the True Teaching. While the carriage of the Great Elephant advances majestically along its path, who could see a cicada attempting to block its tracks?
A great elephant does not travel the narrow paths of a rabbit; a great awakening is not constrained by petty formalities. Do not—
To slander the vast blue sky with my narrow views—let me now resolve this for you.
Zen Master Beidu’s song of the single bowl resounds *e-la-la* and clamors *nua-kua-kua*;
it is all nothing but idle fabrication and fabrication upon fabrication. It is like a hungry man eating salt—the craving only increases.

Wasted all your life in vain; in the end, you cannot know the beginning or the end. Casting aside this corpse, where will you find liberation? Strive with all your might to exhort yourself toward deliverance.
Mundane affairs must ultimately be brought to a conclusion. When fire falls upon your body, you must push it away immediately.
Do not wait until the last moment to cry out for the Bodhisattvas. A man of spirit must speak with clarity and resolve; do not emulate the foolish.
I receive massages and rubs, yet I must wrap myself in time; I must push and pull. Sometimes I learn gentleness, sometimes I am coarse.

I shave my head, and I wear coarse cloth. I also learn from ordinary people how to make a living. I speak directly to you, but you have not yet understood. Therefore, I shall sing a long song about this single bowl.
A Song of the Single Bowl: Within the many, there is one; within the one, there are many. Do not laugh at this wild man’s song of the single bowl.
Relying on this bowl, I cross over the Sahā world. The azure sky is bright and clear as the moon rises high; at this moment, the realm of emptiness contains ten thousand images.
Where do the delusions of floating life arise from their own right and wrong? The single source of true nature has no coming or going. Do not further use the mind to create bubbles upon the water.
Why let blood flow from every pore for someone else’s sake? It is better to sit in stillness upon the ground of True Suchness, leaving the top of one's head to others.
The magpie builds its nest; for ten thousand generations, he is the Golden Wheel Sage Prince. This very one is True Suchness and numinous awakening.

Beneath the Bodhi tree, he delivers sentient beings; having delivered all beings, he neither dies nor is born. Neither born nor dead, he is the true man; formless and signless, he is the Great Vairocana.
When worldly toil is extinguished, True Suchness manifests—a single, perfectly luminous, priceless pearl within the eye.
Not seen; not heard by the ear. This non-seeing and non-hearing is true seeing and hearing. From the beginning, there has been but one bowl, free from speech.
Today, with a thousand words, I am forced to make distinctions. You must listen attentively: every person possesses the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is just like gold within the ore;
through repeated smelting, the essence of the gold becomes pure. Truth is delusion; delusion is truth. If one were to eliminate truth and delusion—
There is no further person; let not the true mind give rise to vexation. Clothe and feed the physical body according to the times. Whether it be good or bad, wear it;
in all things, be without mind and without attachment. There is neither evil nor good; the path of equality is serene throughout the three periods of time.
Whether coarse or fine, eat it; do not follow the commoners in observing external appearances. There is neither coarse nor fine.
There is no subtlety. Above, in the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) realm, there are no roots or bands; one walks while sitting, and sits while walking.
Under the tree of birth-and-death is the fruit of Bodhi; there is neither sitting nor birth. Since there is no birth, what use is there to seek non-birth? One attains birth, and one attains death.
Everywhere one shall come to see Maitreya; there is neither birth nor death. The Tathāgatas of the three realms are all thus.
This: to distance oneself is attachment; to be attached is distancing. Within the gateway of illusory transformation, substantial meaning arises.

There is no distancing; there is no attachment. Where else could one seek the medicine to cure the illness? When speaking, there is silence; when silent, there is speech. Seeking the traces of speech and silence, there is no location.
There is neither speech nor silence. Do not call east and west by the names of south and north. When angry, one is joyful; when joyful, one is angry.

I myself subdue demons and turn the wheel of Dharma, yet there is neither anger nor joy. Water does not depart from its waves; the waves are themselves water. When stingy, one is generous; when generous, one is stingy.
This is not separate from the internal, the external, or that which lies between. There is neither stinginess nor generosity—utter stillness.
Silent and still, there is nothing to grasp. In suffering there is joy; in joy there is suffering. This very practice cuts off the gateways [of dualistic thought].
There is neither suffering nor joy. Originally, these two natures are without entanglement. When defiled, it is pure; when pure, it is defiled.
At the ultimate limit, both sides have no before or after. There is neither defilement nor purity. The great trichiliocosm is one single *tathatā* (suchness) nature. Medicine is itself the illness.
Illness is the medicine. In the end, both matters are entirely cast aside; there is neither medicine nor illness. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s numinous, awakened nature.
When Mara acts as Buddha and Buddha acts as Mara, it is like seeking a form within a mirror or waves upon water.
There is neither Mara nor Buddha. The three periods of time have originally not a single thing. The ordinary is the holy, and the holy is the ordinary. It is like clear water within colored glass.

The lining is salty; there is neither ordinary nor holy. Among the ten thousand practices of total retention, there is not a single practice. Within the real is the provisional; within the provisional is the real.

It is simply that ordinary beings give rise to delusive dust; thus, there is neither reality nor provisionality. When you seek to call out for it, who will respond? Originally, there is no nature and no name.
Just go along in this state of carefree wandering, stepping where the feet lead. Sometimes in the marketplace, sometimes in the village lanes.
In a butcher’s stall, a single red lotus blooms amidst the flames. He once took up his staff to wander through the capitals of Jing and Luo;
his body is like drifting clouds, with no fixed dwelling. These illusory transformations are but temporary lodgings; where else could there be such purity and emptiness? If you seek the precepts—
When will the sores of the three poisons be healed? If you seek Chan, I myself sleep freely and unrestrainedly—how pitiable!
It is not madness; it is the world-transcending one, the God among Gods. People of this age do not understand the meaning herein: striking the south, the north is moved.
If you seek the Dharma, ask Kāśyapa at the peak of Mount Kukkuṭapāda; the Great Being holds his robe here.
In the midst [of this], from the very beginning there is no need to seek a specific focus. If you seek the Sūtras, the true source of the Dharma-nature cannot be heard.
If you seek the Vinaya, the impoverished son does not need to be taught to run out. If you seek cultivation, where can the eighty-four thousand stūpas be found?

You only know how to use yellow leaves to stop a child’s crying; you do not realize that black clouds are obscuring the sun. Do not take offense at these mad words lacking order; they are like sifting through...

The basket gradually enters into the coarse within the subtle; yet even this "coarse within the subtle" does not exist. This is precisely the perfectly luminous, true reality (*satya*). True reality is fundamentally not "true";
it is merely a name, and that which is heard is itself a dust-mote. If one seeks to understand true reality within the midst of these dust-motes, [one will never find it].
This is indeed one who has loftily transcended the world. Do not fabricate anything. Walking alone, stepping forth alone, empty and desolate;
no birth, no death, no nirvana. Originally, birth and death do not interfere with one another. No right, no wrong, no movement, no stillness. Do not vainly cast your body into an empty well.
No good, no evil, no coming, no going—nor is there a bright mirror hanging upon a high terrace. Thus says the mountain monk.
My view is simply this: I do not believe in following others to create "kalpa-ash" (world-ending ashes).
With the Buddha-eye, I have thrice examined this body and its lifespan;
it is like a horse's hoof passing through a crack. What leisure is there for idle sentiments or to falsely engage in miscellaneous affairs? Since I have honored the Śākya lineage...
One must investigate the tradition of the Xu Shao Gate and scrutinize the teachings of the former patriarchs. What is their standard?

Since our spiritual work remains unfinished and the time since the Sage has long passed, one must truly not abandon the instruction of virtuous friends and teachers; one should exert oneself with self-motivation.
Mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness is something known only to oneself; let not the great resolve falter.
Conditions for repayment are illusory—how can they be forced? How long does this fleeting world last? Let one follow the family’s abundance or scarcity, and face suffering or joy, adversity or favor.
The Way lies within it. In movement and stillness, in cold and warmth, one should feel self-reproach and repentance.
Master Daoyuan of Mount Gui cautioned us:
"Bound by karma, one receives a body and cannot avoid the burdens of form. One inherits the physical frame bestowed by one's parents and relies upon a multitude of conditions."
Although one is sustained by the four great elements, they are constantly in opposition; impermanence, old age, and sickness do not wait for man’s appointment.

One may exist in the morning and perish in the evening; in a single kṣaṇa, one passes into another world. Like spring frost or morning dew that vanishes in an instant, how could trees on a riverbank or vines hanging from a well endure for long?
Every thought-moment is swift; within a single kṣaṇa, with the turning of a breath, one enters the next life. How [can one remain]?
Thus, he passed his time in idle tranquility. His parents did not provide him with fine delicacies, and his six relations had already abandoned him.
Unable to bring peace to the state or manage the family estate, he suddenly renounced his lineage. Leaving his native village far behind, he shaved his head and received the precepts from a master.

Internally, he applied himself to the practice of mindfulness; externally, he propagated the virtue of non-contention. Having transcended the mundane world, he hoped for liberation. Yet, how is it that—just as...?

Upon ascending to the stage of the precepts, they immediately claim, "I am a bhikṣu. They consume whatever is required by the *dānapati* (donors) from the monastery's permanent assets, yet they lack the understanding to reflect upon their source.
They say it is "natural" (*dharmatā*) that such things should be provided for them. Having finished eating, they gather together in a noisy clamor, speaking nothing but mundane, trivial talk.
Thus, for a time, they pursue pleasure, unaware that this pleasure is the cause of suffering. Throughout past kalpas, they have pursued the dust of the world, never once turning back.
Reflect! Time is swallowed by oblivion; years slip away in vain. Yet one’s enjoyments are abundant and the benefits of offerings are rich;

they persist for years and decades, and one has no intention of relinquishing them. Thus, accumulations grow ever greater as one maintains this illusory body. The Teacher issued a decree to exhort the bhikṣus: advance on the Path and adorn yourself.
The three things are always insufficient, yet many people remain immersed in this state, slumbering without ceasing as days pass and months go by.
Now that I have arrived, my hair is already white with age; those of later generations have not yet heard the essential meaning. One must extensively consult those who possess prior knowledge.

It was thought that leaving the household life was merely for the sake of seeking food and clothing. Yet the Buddha first established the Vinaya to initiate and enlighten the ignorant. Its rules and majestic decorum are as pure as ice and snow.
Through the observance of prohibitions and the performance of duties, the beginner's mind is restrained. These subtle and minute regulations eliminate all vulgar defects—the Dharma of the Vinaya.
I have never once had the honor of attending his assembly. How could I possibly discern the ultimate meaning of the Supreme Vehicle? Alas, my life has passed in vain; regret is difficult to undo.

I have never applied myself to the teachings and principles, nor have I found a way to realize the profound Path. Now that I am advanced in years and senior in ordination, my mind is puffed up with emptiness;
I refuse to draw near to virtuous friends, knowing only how to act with arrogance. Unfamiliar with the rules of discipline, I remain constrained by ignorance.
There is a complete lack of restraint. Some speak loudly and at a high pitch; their speech is unrestrained, and they show no respect for seniors, equals, or juniors.

They are no different from assemblies of Brahmins. Their bowls and alms-basins clatter as they eat; they rise before the meal is finished; their conduct is erratic and improper; they possess none of the character of a monk.
Whether rising or sitting, they cause agitation and disturb the minds of others; they observe not the slightest rule of decorum, nor do they maintain even minor points of dignified demeanor.
How can one restrain oneself? If future generations of new students have no cause for emulation or instruction, and as soon as they are observed, they immediately claim, "I am a mountain monk;

I have not heard the Buddha's teachings," and their practice remains consistently rooted in coarse conduct—such people are surely those whose initial resolve was indolent and who, driven by greed and complacency, have drifted through the world until they become rustic and uncultivated, unaware that they have stumbled into old age.

Decayed and worn out, he was like a wall facing every direction when confronted with affairs; when later students sought his counsel, he had no words to guide them. Even when he did speak, it did not touch upon the classical scriptures.
If he were suddenly addressed with even a slight remark, he would immediately reproach the younger generation for their lack of propriety, his anger flaring up and his words directed at others.
One day, as he lay bedridden with illness, he was besieged by a multitude of sufferings. Day and night he brooded over this, his mind filled with agitation and distress. Previously...
The road stretches out vast and boundless; one knows not where it leads. From this point on, one finally realizes the need for repentance. To dig a well only when parched with thirst—what is the use?
I regret that I did not cultivate myself early on. In my later years, I have committed many transgressions. At the moment of departure, I am wavering and distraught, terrified and panicked.

Like a bird escaping through a rent in a silken garment, the conscious mind follows its karma. It is like a person burdened by debt: the stronger creditor drags them away first. The mental continuum is manifold and complex; [the weight of] heavy...
Dwelling in partiality and falling into ruin, the ghost of impermanence slays us; every thought-moment passes without ceasing, life cannot be extended, and time cannot be waited for.

Within the three realms of existence—humans, devas, and the rest—one shall surely not escape this. To receive such a body is beyond the reckoning of kalpas. How deeply moving and lamentable! Alas, it cuts to the core of one’s heart;
how could one remain silent? We must exhort and admonish one another. What we regret is that we were born together in this age of semblance-dharma, far removed from the time of the Sage.

Yao: The Buddha-Dharma is sparse and many people are indolent; I shall briefly set forth my humble views to enlighten those who come after. If one does not eliminate self-conceit, it will truly be difficult to escape the cycle of rebirth.
Now, those who have left the household life do so with the intent to transcend the mundane world, making their minds and forms distinct from the secular.

They propagate the lineage of the Sages and strike terror into the armies of Māra, thereby repaying the four debts of gratitude and rescuing beings from the three realms of existence. If one does not act in this manner, they merely defile the ranks of the Saṃgha.
Lun, your words and deeds are negligent and coarse; you have vainly partaken of the offerings of the faithful. At the places where you once practiced, not a single step has been taken forward.

Your entire life has passed in a daze—upon what can you rely? Moreover, your dignified monastic appearance and observant countenance are all the result of wholesome causes planted in former lives, which have brought about this extraordinary retribution.
Yet you intend to remain merely with hands folded in stillness, failing to value even a moment of time. Your endeavors are not diligent, and your merit...
If the fruit is not achieved through its cause, how can one spend a lifetime in vain? Moreover, it would fail to benefit one's future karma.

Having bid farewell to my kin and resolved to don the black robes [of the monastic order], I pondered day and night: toward what goal do I seek to transcend equally? How could I allow time to pass by procrastinating?

My heart’s aspiration is to become a pillar for the Buddha-dharma and to serve as a mirror for those who come after. Constantly reflecting in this way, I have been unable to achieve even a small portion [of my aim].

One’s speech ought to engage with the classical canons, and one’s discourse should be grounded in historical precedents. One’s physical bearing should be distinguished and noble, and one’s spirit should be lofty and serene.
When traveling afar, one must rely on virtuous companions to frequently purify one’s ears and eyes;

when dwelling at home, one must choose one’s associates to occasionally hear what has not yet been heard. Thus it is said: "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who bring me to fulfillment are my friends. This is because of the intimacy [of such bonds].

Those who associate with the virtuous are like those walking amidst mist and dew: though they do not soak their clothes, they are moistened from time to time. Those who habitually consort with the wicked cultivate evil views and knowledge;
they commit evil morning and night, receiving retribution even in this life, and after death they sink into the depths. Once one loses the human body, it is difficult to regain.
Ten thousand kalpas may pass without restoration. Loyal words are contrary to the ear; how could one not engrave them upon the heart?

By doing so, one can cleanse the mind and nurture virtue, obscure one's traces and conceal one's fame, preserve inner purity and clarify the spirit, and bring all clamor and noise to a complete halt. in all your actions, look to those of the highest caliber rather than following the vulgar and base. You must reach a definitive decision this very lifetime. Consider this well.

Do not rely on others; quiet the mind and forget external conditions. Do not set yourself in opposition to the various sensory objects. When the mind is empty and the environment is still, it is only because you have long been stalled and obstructed.

Nevertheless, how could one be without anxiety and fear? Thus, the Sūtra says: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten;
when causes and conditions meet, one must receive the retribution oneself. Therefore, know that the punishments and fetters of the three realms kill the person.

Thoroughly investigate the principles of the Dharma, taking awakening as your standard. Abandon both mind and objects; neither record nor recollect.
The six faculties are serene; in walking and standing, they are silent and still. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are all stilled.
Record of Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s Attainment of Enlightenment, composed by Wang Bo of Taiyuan during the Tang Dynasty.
Observing the manifestation of Śākyamuni Tathāgata in the world: his body of the pure dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing. Out of great compassion...
Through the power of his vows, he manifested birth; reaching the Tuṣita Heaven, he became the Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra. He descended upon the kingdom of Kapilavastu and was named Sarvārthasiddha.
The son of the Golden Orb (Suvarṇapuṣpa) chose his family, and the noble King Śuddhodana became his father.
The jade elephant rode the sun to manifest his arrival within the womb of Mahāmāyā; the golden wheel turned as King when he was first born beneath the Aśoka tree.
His eighty secondary marks of excellence were as brilliant as fragrant flowers, and his thirty-two marks of a Great Man were as radiant as the full moon.
He took seven steps in each of the ten directions and was bathed by the waters of the nine seas all at once.
He manifested the *udumbara* flower and let out a lion’s roar, declaring that his existence within the womb was already exhausted and that he had early realized the eternal body;

yet, for the sake of saving sentient beings, he returned once more. Now, as he descends to manifest his traces of transformation, he returns to the swaddling clothes, appearing like an infant for the purpose of having his physiognomy read.
He felt sorrowful before the seer Asita; he went to the suburban sacrifices; and he caused a stir at the temple of Maheśvara.
Sometimes he was a youth; sometimes he studied the science of grammar (śabda-vidyā). For the purpose of military instruction, the archery towers and arrow wells still remain.

For the purpose of competing in strength, the elephant tracks and elephant pits still exist. At the age of ten, he experienced sensual pleasures; at twenty-nine, he manifested his travels and observations at the four gates.
Delighting in the body of a śramaṇa and weary of old age, sickness, and death, the Devaputra Kamaṇḍaluka then roused him by manifesting the ugly countenance of the celestial maidens;
the Śuddhāvāsa devas supported him as he leaped forth, urging Channa to prepare the carriage.

Thus they passed beyond the city of Kapilavastu on the eighth night and dwelt upon the Snowy Peaks for six years. Men expressed their sorrowful longing for their lord, while the horse licked the pearls that had fallen from his mane.

Shedding tears, he brandished his precious sword and cut off his dark-blue hair; a stupa rose like a celestial palace. He traded his imperial robes for a fur garment and took on the form of a mountain deer.
He sought what the forest immortals had attained, realizing that worldly stability is not true. Eating wheat and hemp, he subdued suffering and transcended pleasure.
Furthermore, when a jade lute plays a melody, the song is completed only through the eyes of the master; so too, the fruit of Buddhahood is perfected through its causes.
By means of the provisional and the middle, the fruit was fulfilled. Thus, he selected his location: he passed by the Dragon Cave to bathe his body;
he entered the Nairañjanā River to demonstrate his taking of food; he accepted the milk-rice from Nanda to demonstrate his seat; and he received the auspicious kusha grass.
With his final and supreme body, he proceeded to the Bodhi-maṇḍala to perfect the profound cause of liberation and ascended.

Upon the adamantine jewel throne, possessing one hundred and forty unique merits not shared with the two vehicles, and transcending the ten stages through eighty-four thousand Dharma gates, the demonic armies were intimidated by the power of his compassion and retreated in grief and fear;
the seductive maidens were neutralized by his concentrated mind and their beauty transformed into ugliness and frailty. Thereupon, the Earth Deity Sthāvarā leaped for joy and bore witness.
The Devaputra Ākāśa successively announced this news. Like a lotus emerging from the water, he was resplendent beyond measure;
like the crescent moon suspended in the sky, his radiance was penetrating and clear. After seven days had passed, he accepted the parched grain and honey offered by Trapusa.
With words of few syllables, he awakened them; with a single voice, he bestowed upon the merchants the precepts for returning home. He granted them the blessings of both gods and humans. Thus it was.

Having attained Buddhahood, he surveyed the conditions for those to be transformed. He felt compassion for the two sages who had failed to encounter the Thunderous Voice, yet rejoiced that the five men were capable of following his Dharma transformation.
However, because their sensory faculties were dull and inferior while the Sage’s realization was profound and deep, if he followed the Dharma, it would not accord with their faculties;
if he followed their faculties, they would not penetrate the Dharma. There was none among them who was not deeply submerged in the river of craving, conditioned by delusion and pleasure.

Thus blinded, if what was to be heard were not beneficial, he would instead employ expedient words to enter into cessation. Thereupon, Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, led a host from the thirty-three heavens like a gathering cloud;
the King of the Sahā World surrounded by the eighteen Brahmās like a mist, bowed his head in prostration and paid homage with single-minded devotion.
He requested that the Wheel of Dharma be turned and exhorted him to preach according to what is appropriate. The Tathāgata then reflected upon the goodness [of this request].
He passed through the universal norms and followed the sublime counsel of the ancient Buddhas, responding to the base desires of all sentient beings.
Thereupon, the Buddhas of the ten directions appeared and together offered words of praise. The single Vehicle of Dharma was divided to jointly establish the realm of worldly toil.

From this, he arose at the Bodhi tree and proceeded to the Deer Park; for three months he disciplined his faculties, and the five companions attained deliverance. Kātyāyana realized the... of the Compassionate Honored One.
The first to sing the hymn initiated the exposition by establishing the names [of the truths]. Śāriputra encountered Aśvajit and transmitted the words; he realized the Truths while on the road.

Kauṇḍinya followed in his footsteps and served him as a disciple, leading his followers to return together to the same path. Mahākāśyapa gathered his traces to subdue his mind, taking his fire-worshipping disciples back to the assembly.
There was none who did not receive the great downpour of nectar, with the wish-fulfilling jewel responding universally. Thus, the celestial realms...
In the human realm—whether in groves of warblers, in cemeteries, or by lakes of herons; on the Vulture Peak, or on the shores of the ocean, or in monastic gardens;
by the Monkey River, or in the caves of fire-dragons; dwelling in Vārāṇasī, or residing in Magadha;
relying on the Saṃkhyāvana forest, or staying at the Māyā-tree; on the peak of Laṅkā by the seashore, or on the cliff of Potalaka at the edge of the mountains; or in a monastery...
Whether at the Bamboo Grove of Rājagṛha or in the Golden Land of Śrāvastī; whether appearing as empty space through recollection or emerging from a mountain to enter a palace;
whether preaching the Dharma by means of the six directions or transforming the body to become three feet tall;
whether the palm covers the fingers or light flows as the Buddha arrives; whether a single body universally gathers into many bodies, or this realm is again illuminated.
In other realms, some transform the impure so that purity covers the defiled, while others accord with worldly conventions to reveal the truth through those very conventions.

The Discourse on the Mind; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* as the foremost of all practices; the *Anantārtha-sūtra* of the One Vehicle;

The distinction between reciting and repeated recitation is like the three animals—the elephant, horse, and rabbit—crossing a river; it is like the three vehicles—the sheep, deer, and ox—leaving their home.
Some call it existence, maintaining the center while empty; some call it non-existence, revolving in illumination and upholding [the truth].

Hearing it, one hears it eternally. Whether through being sustained so as to be relied upon, or through being empowered so as not to forget, there is nothing small that is not great, and nothing boundless that is not central.

mountains shook and the earth quaked, as all raised cries of agony. Creatures of different species changed their forms, and all manifested blood like *śirīṣa* flowers.
He accepted the final offering of Cunda and received the secret words of Vipaśyin. Chanting the four virtues, he revealed the three *ī*.
Pointing to the myriad phenomena to show their return to a single nature, he answered the forty-two inquiries of Mahākāśyapa; having completed his teachings, he delivered Subhadra.
At eighty-one, when his transformative mission was nearing its end, he shattered the erroneous calculations of the ten sages so that they might attain awakening upon hearing the morning drum.
He established the noble model of the four stupas to nourish future generations for a long time. Thus, he sought to clarify that all conditioned things possess cessation and to manifest...
Through signlessness and non-arising, he ascended to the Vajra-body and traversed the realm of empty space. Even the sun and moon would fall;
how could a firefly remain for long? He cautioned that one possesses a constant body and must not be negligent.

Thereupon, he returned to the Jade Throne and lay his head upon the Crane Forest (Heli). He traveled extensively through the gates of samādhi, intending to restore the nature of the Single Reality, entering against the flow and following the natural order.

He entered [parinirvāṇa]. Having transcended entirely and partially, he relied upon the meditative equipoise of the fourth dhyāna to rest in the profound stillness of the three points of perfect quiescence.
At that moment, humans and devas cried out and collapsed; birds and beasts wailed in grief. Gale-force winds and sudden clouds arose; mountains roared and waves surged backward.

Following the ancient rites of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), they were about to await the funeral ceremonies; they ordered the Mallas to lift [the coffin], yet none could move it. Thus, the golden coffin—

Meanwhile, Ajātaśatru was in Rājagṛha, where he first conceived a dream-vision of the World-Honored One of Ten Epithets;

from afar, Mahākāśyapa descended to Mount Kukkuṭapāda to behold and pay homage to the thousand-spoked wheels upon the Buddha’s feet. Finally, with fine *tūla* cotton cloth, the sacred fire spontaneously consumed him.

His power of aspiration still remains and his compassionate heart still perfumes all; thus, he shattered his supreme diamond body into the precious relics of gold-like bone.

Beginning from the omen of the collapsing beam and ending with the sign of the flowing milk, the vessels differ while the water remains the same, and the lamps vary while the light is ultimately one.

The school analyzes the subtle with the hair-splitting precision of gold. Whether it be the Sthavira or Mahāsāṃghika as its original branches, or the ten divisions that widely expounded the doctrine, or the thousand schools that flourished;
whether it be Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna who succeeded to its fragrance, or Asaṅga and Vasubandhu who spread its beauty;

Regarding the external traditions: some ten masters assisted with the final verses; some, upon hearing the sutras, ascended to Tuṣita at night;

some awaited the Buddha while dwelling in caves among the asuras; some vowed their heads to swords as a solemn pledge; and some offered gold on the backs of elephants to request the teachings of Śākyamuni.
Some were rewarded for their abilities and granted fiefdoms; some erected victory banners upon triumph.

Some discussed the principles of Prajñāpāramitā, titled *The Lamp*, while others investigated the fallacies of the Abhidharmakośa, titled *The Hail*. Though their paths diverged and their methods differed, they all ultimately converged at a single source.
Both existence and emptiness alike converge in the myriad virtues. From the Shang and Zhou dynasties, we saw the rainbow piercing the heavens; during the Han, Emperor Wu dreamed of the golden man.
When the teaching reached the land of Shenzhou, its fame spread throughout Huaxia. I, Bo, was born in this degenerate age and have had the fortune to receive the true discourse.

Although I have recorded and continued these accounts to narrate the golden words, I remain adrift and have not encountered the Jade Countenance in person. My knowledge is limited to what I have seen and heard, yet the ultimate purport of the doctrine is clearly manifest.
Thus, I have set aside these writings and shall not speak of them further in detail. Yet, I compose this inscription: Transformation arises from the fundamental source;
Success is achieved in response to the Bhadrakalpa. The myriad practices manifest the True Doctrine; Three great eons accumulate vast merit.
For the sake of the Dharma, you appeared in the world; Descending in spirit, you manifested the birth from the side.
Eyebrows arched like the bow of the Lord of Devas, eyes adorned with blue lotus petals; when the Immortal Master shed tears, the heavenly deities vied to receive them.
His consecration shall take place within the palace; his flying wheel transforms all into tranquility.
Inheriting the lineage of Heaven and Sun, he is noble; his trunk pierces the lion’s cheek. Who can transmit these sublime teachings?

He reviled those who were merely bold and chivalrous; his travels and observations brought him face to face with old age and death. He scaled the city walls and abandoned his ministers and concubines;

he shaved his hair and gave away his precious sword. He traded clothes and encountered a hunting party; he took refuge among the deer and grew intimate with them. He mortified his body to display weakness and frailty;
when the people saw him eating deer meat, they all knew his intent. Yet as he sat cross-legged in the midst of the grass, even the sages were struck with awe.
Pure as a lotus emerging from the water, Bright as a mirror opened from its case, Mountains and seas are like his loftiness and depth;
clouds and thunder equal his refined discourse. The teachings of the three periods are extensively expounded, And the faculties of the myriad classes are naturally satisfied.
I now briefly seek to respond to the four questions, As the ten immortals follow one after another in their deliverance, And the record of Maitreya’s succession to the position is fulfilled.

The final instructions were entrusted to Kāśyapa; Lying beneath the tree, he bore the spring alone. The fragrant wood has already been consumed by fire, yet his compassionate heart remains vast and far-reaching.
The śarīra relics shine with brilliant splendor; I alone was born at a later time, yet I have fortunately been moistened by the lingering waves of his grace.

"Matters concerning livelihood and profit are not for a śramaṇa to discuss; matters of state affairs and weaponry are surely not for a practitioner of the Way to debate.
Fame and wealth in the human world are like dreams and illusions; they are not worth extolling. The right and wrong of the worldly path are like flashes of lightning; how [can they be grasped]?"
One must distinguish between them. Disciples and followers are like birds nesting on high branches; relatives and kin are like travelers meeting on a crossroads.
The three robes are combined into a single patchwork garment, for the intent of the Zen school lies in reducing external conditions.

Mending rags to ward off the cold is valued only to avoid burdening donors. One should eat and drink according to circumstances, drifting and sinking as nature dictates. Should one desire to seek much more, there is fear that—
Though it may obstruct the Way, I briefly set forth my humble views to instruct beginners. If they might serve as a model, I hope you will follow them in practice.
Composed by Yangshan while dining at Zhongda.
Yangshan’s Rice: Grain by grain, like pearls, like silver; Those who eat must know how difficult it was for it to come.
Let me briefly offer a few observations for everyone: When spring arrives at the eastern fields and western plots, the plowmen and their wives are cold and hungry.

As the soil softens and agricultural work begins, oxen with sores on their necks still pull the plows. In summer, when the seedlings are lush and about to bear fruit, there is no rain and all four directions are scorching sun.
With backs parched and faces cracked, sweat flows down their chests; they toil and weed, fearing only—
Weeds and tares sprout forth; in deep autumn, the rice ripens yellow as clouds. By day it is harvested, by night it is pounded—sweet, bitter, and pungent.
Village headmen press and urge the king’s taxes with urgency; both official debts and private arrears fall upon one's person. When official debts remain unpaid, one suffers the lash and the cudgel;

when private debts remain unpaid, one sells fields and houses. How often have parents, wives, and children been satiated? In every household, they leave behind only rice and coarse gruel to subsist. They dwell...

The elderly monk wanders from door to door seeking alms; the mendicant gathers his provisions as he begs for food. With calloused hands and cracked feet, he dares not sit in meditation; through wind and rain, he never rests.
At the fifth watch, the gates of the Cloud Hall are still closed, yet those in the kitchen have already risen to prepare the universal offerings.
Fearing that the rice gruel for the assembly will be late, this is how it is every day and every morning. Rice wash-water overflows the ground and solidifies.
Like fat, the coarse is removed and the subtle remains as one stokes the firewood to cook. The cauldrons emit steam and flames; the steamer and pots grow hot.

One exerts effort and labor in their tasks. The sound of the long board ends with the roar of the wooden fish. Sitting upright on the meditation seat, one receives the alms bowl. One minutely discusses the merit of transforming the raw into the cooked.
Only fearing that the *śrāmaṇera* will find it difficult to take a bite. It does not come from the world of Gṛdhrakūṭa, nor is it...
The ghosts and spirits receive your offerings at the midday meal; from a single spoonful and ladle up to a single cup, all are the wealth sought by the donor for merit.

When the Rector strikes the mallet with a sound like thunder, you are too lazy to open your mouth for ten recitations of the Buddha’s name. When the distribution of benefits is even slightly delayed, anger arises.

In the second thought-moment, it all is forgotten. The ancients were originally busy for the sake of studying the Way; they traveled everywhere seeking spiritual friends and wandered through all lands.
They used tree bark and grass leaves to provide fuel for their cauldrons—how could there have been such rice to fill their hungry bellies? A hundred years of life are like a dream or an illusion;
you should prepare your practice of inquiry and study early on. If your mind-ground has not yet been clarified, even a Buddha would find it difficult to digest [the offerings].
Yangshan’s Meal.
Master Baoning Yong instructs on the method of reading sutras (the *yulu* is identical).
Regarding the method of reading sutras, those in later generations must know it: one should purify the three karmas. If the three karmas are without deficiency, then [one will attain] the hundred...
May merit be gathered in abundance. As for the three types of action—namely, those of body, speech, and mind:
first, sit upright with the body, as if facing the countenance of the Honored One; this is the purification of bodily action.
Second, let the mouth be free from idle chatter and sever all frivolous laughter; this is the purification of vocal action.
Third, the mind is not distracted; by stilling false conditions, the mental karma (*manas-karman*) is purified.

Once the inner mind is tranquil, external objects are simultaneously relinquished; only then does one accord with and awaken to the true source, and hope to investigate and exhaustively master the principles of the Dharma.

It may be said that the waters are clear as crystal and the pearls are lustrous; the clouds have dispersed and the moon shines bright. The ocean of meaning surges within the breast, and the mountain of wisdom solidifies before the ears and eyes.
One must not treat this lightly; it is truly no small matter. When both mind and phenomena are forgotten, self and others are both benefited.
If one can act thus, it is a true repayment of the Buddha’s grace.
1. Washing the hands while they are not dry; 2. Spreading out the cloth for prostrations before it is fully extended;
3. Touching the hands to the edges of the cloth; 4. Letting the cords hang unevenly above or below; 5. Turning the scripture over while reading; 6. Reading in the midday sun or before a fire; 7.
Reading in a place shrouded by clouds, mist, or heat; 8. Folding the pages with uneven creases; 9. Holding the scripture in the mouth or wrapping it around the neck.
10. Altering or destroying the [monastic] staff; 11. The sash not aligned with the door.
