Preface to the Mountain Dwelling Poems of Master Chan Yue, Recorded by Shi Ruyou of the Five Peaks.
In the Xian-tong era, I composed these poems while at Mount Zhong. Having set my brush aside, the draft was circulated orally until it reached one or two others.
The characters and phrases contained many errors; they were corrected at Sanshu-ji during my mountain retreat in the Xinchou year of the Qiandao era. This results in twenty-four poems.

Their style and tone are vulgar and clumsy; I do not dare present them to great and refined gentlemen who compose such works. It suffices that their spirit is unified, and one may chant them aloud with clarity.
Mountain Dweller’s Poems, Part One:
Cease speaking of clamor; all things are difficult. A mountain elder ought only to dwell in the deep mountains.

Amidst the sound of clear chimes beyond right and wrong, there is but one idle man between heaven and earth. Green gardens and empty steps where clouds drift slowly; strange birds and numinous herbs by the water.
A murmuring stream flows; no one is there to speak to the assembly of scholars. The cassia branches on the cliff are high, yet they are easy to climb.
The second difficulty is that when one speaks of resting, one simply rests. Singing alone in purity at the head of the emerald stream, there is no one in the three rooms of the thatched cottage.
Arriving at the Pine Gate, I wander alone for ten li. The bright moon and clear breeze are the society of Zong Bing; The setting sun and autumn colors belong to the tower of Yu Gong.
My cultivation of the mind has not yet reached the groundless state; Ten thousand kinds and a thousand variations follow the flowing water.
Thirdly, the song of a fine bird awakens my long-slumbering eyes; with fine tea like milk, I sit upon the moss. Hearing neither honor nor disgrace, the watches of the night pass away;

I see only bears coming in their herds. The principles of poetry have long surpassed the "White Snow," and the sentiment of the Way shall ultimately be made to resemble— (Note: The final line of the provided text appears incomplete, as it ends with "似" [resemble].)
An infant; from of old, few have been those who understand this matter. It is not that the True Wind departs and does not return. Fourth:
when the myriad realms forget their artifice, it is the Flower of the Way. Amidst the azure lotus, the sun slants empty through the air. Deep and profound, a path leads to the Immortals.
In the cave, silent and deserted, strange flowers fall. A flash of lightning and drifting clouds are truly apt metaphors. Like dragons and like phoenixes, there is no need for boastful praise.
Behold the tombs of heroes by the river; there are only the roots of pines and the stumps of cypresses.

After the fifth lash, he followed others with his naturally white hair; clear waves surged toward the emerald depths, their coldness seeping through the curtains. No one loved his lofty and extraordinary verses;
the world detested his tranquil and detached spirit. On the high White Stone Bridge, his chanting was never enough; beneath the warm shadows of red clouds, he lay down to rest.
I am never weary. Dwelling in the mountains, I have a distinct sense that differs from the common perception of mountain life; do not mistakenly compare me to Song Xian.
For forty autumns amidst the dust outside the sixth island, I have also held the lords of Han in high esteem. Though such a disposition is pure, [it remains so].
How clumsy! A true man of great character ought to be free. The rhizomes of *Atractylis* and the sprouts of *Brassica juncea* grow lushly; from the embroidered pouch, musk scents and voices chirp.
In the end, one must reach the heart of the Elder of Caoxi, whose thousand-year *zhú* roots have snow filling his hair.
The seventh [verse] is exceedingly indolent; like Ji Kang, he ultimately does not turn back. What prevents his inner mind from being like cold ashes?

Mountain spirits emerge daily as young children, and immortals occasionally bring jade vessels. With a broom of bamboo he sweeps the flowers, startling the sleeping deer; in the earthen stove he burns tree branches.
Withered moss. It has been a long time since he frequented the morning markets. Where are the Xu, Shi, Jin, and Zhang families now?

In the eighth consciousness, mind after mind does not abide; in the realm of the mysterious and the ineffable, craggy stone dwellings hang with white hair. Cherishing the bamboo, he does not clear it from the path.

Bamboo shoots; loving the pines, one leaves behind their branches that obstruct the path. Incense burns as I unroll my scrolls, rosy clouds arise upon the steps. The blinds are drawn back and the mind is serene, the moon shining upon the pond.
How many old friends have their hair turned entirely white? I know not where they have gone this day.
The ninth dragon-treasury casket pervades the nine realms; frost-bells and golden drums resound upon the Jade Terrace.

How lamentable that no one has attained this single phrase—thus it was that our Master came here specifically. The hornless iron ox sleeps at Shaoshi; the stone woman gives birth to a child and grows old.
Huangmei makes one longingly recall Layman Pang; neither in heaven nor among men can they be matched. On the fifteenth peak, mists and clouds stretch on without end;

the mountain caves of the Three Peaks must surely be interconnected. Leaning one's pillow against a slanting stone window, the sparse [moonlight]— *Note: The final line appears incomplete in the source text.*
Rain falls; the water-mill is empty, a vast wind howls. A youth recites sutras deep within the bamboo groves; a macaque picks lice in the setting sun.
Reflecting thus on past events, I have cast away my mental strength; for six or seven years now, I have been by the eastern waters of Chu.
The eleventh: within the dust there is further dust. At times, his two eyebrows knit together like a bow. Fortunately, the years fly by like arrows; what state of mind could still be called human?
Returning to Xian and attending the ancestral rites, he speaks from time to time. Bees and scorpions sting, and wolves greedily prey—day after day.
Ever-renewing. The will of Heaven is stern; how can such a person remain? It is only fit for sorrow, beyond all description. Number twelve:

Verdant Caverns and Misty Cliffs cannot be painted. The fragrance of cassia mingles with the spray of waterfalls in a blend of sweet scents. Pushing through the rosy clouds, sweeping away the snow, one blends with the mists.
The mother digs through stone and shifts pines to find *fuling* fungus; a fine bird resembling a flower peers at the jade chime. Tender moss is like water submerging a golden pitcher.
Let others laugh, let them laugh; though earth is overturned and heaven is turned upside down, all is but peace.
Thirteenth:
Stepping slowly with a vacant and unburdened gait, the subtle signs of awakening dissolve as one knows them only within.

Though the golden elixir of Nāgārjuna has not yet been prepared, the earthen cave of Sūn Deng is well-suited for now. The mountain cloak of *bìluó* vines can be woven with ease; acorns and chestnuts shall suffice as provisions for the year.
Coarse branches. Having already attained the good news of the True Man, there is no further doubt between the human realm and the heavens.

Verse 14: The misty peaks are fresh and the breeze light, like emerald gauze; the golden statue in the snow-capped tower is veiled by mists and clouds. From the *ge* vines, jade-like powder produces a fragrant scent.
Mounds of mushrooms cluster like silver nails upon the clean stumps. The whole world knows only to lament the flowing waters; no one subtly understands that they are empty flowers.
How pitiable, amidst the turmoil of dust and grime, our twin hair-tufts are as white as silver while our affairs are as tangled as hemp.

Fifteenth: The path through ten thousand crags and myriad gullies is steep and narrow; amidst the misty pines and cypresses, I close my door alone. A child gathers medicinal herbs, disappearing into a fissure in the stream;
bees seeking flowers return through the smoke of the forest fires. Wandering at ease, I follow the course of the water; sitting in stillness, I rest my chin upon my hand until—
Falling Glows. I long remember the fine words of Nanquan; such dull-witted people as these are rare indeed (Nanquan once said:
"Among those who study the Way, those who are dull-witted are difficult to find").
116. From the darkened eyes gazing into the vast void, a mushroom-pillow rests upon a pine bed amidst the green of mossy crags. Young deer move unseen through the snowy paths of tamarisk trees;
a fine spray from a waterfall mists the sutras within the stone pavilion. Walking idly, one does not realize the celestial well has passed; a long, deep cry can truly stir the depths.
Yue Ling: One should fear that no one understands this intent; neither ordinary nor sage, alone awake among those who sleep.
XVII: Slothfully carves lotus blossoms to pass the eternal watches; do not boast of elegant prose, for I despise the style of Tangxiu. For now, let me fill my small granary with crimson.
The chestnuts—there is a rare bird here, superior even to the white gull. Gathering chestnuts, it seeks far into the depths of the ravines; playing with monkeys, it frequents the small peaks.
It cannot emerge any further from the midst of the dust. A metal tempered a hundred times becomes as soft as a finger.
The eighteenth:
The fire of the mind, fueled by the wood of karma, burns and sears like the sun; vain deaths and empty lives have been thus since antiquity. Lu Ji’s claim that he was a dragon was ultimately false;
the Han house’s acquisition of the deer was even more hollow. The layman in white speaks from the depths; the blue-eyed barbarian monk looks on from afar.
Far-reaching transmission. Upon the firm earth, no one understands this meaning; how can one endure such sorrow before the falling flowers?
(19) Dewdrops on red orchids, jade fills the fields; idly trailing my elephant-slippered feet, I reach the western peak. Only let the mind be like a lotus flower.
Purity! Why must one’s body be like withered wood? In ancient ditches, fine incense lingers; by red trees, age has set in. On half a peak, remnants of snow remain as white monkeys cry out.
Though this is not the Peach Blossom Cave, when spring arrives, peach blossoms will fill the stream.
Verse Twenty:
Resting in myself, finding my own completion, I arrange my own affairs. I always wish to dwell in the mountains, where my circumstances harmonize.

Monks gather *shuyi* (tree-moss) from the edge of the precipice—(at Mount Jinhua, tree-moss grows; monks often harvest it for vegetables, which is exceptionally delicious)— while langurs scramble for mountain fruits that fall upon the empty steps. Leisurely, I carry my tea vessels.
Facing the azure cliffs, he sits upon the green precipice in his quiet monastic robe. His composing of new poems in vain invites reclusion;
those who emerge from it mostly act contrary to this mind. Twenty-one.
Stone hearths and golden cauldrons amidst tender maple leaves; incense chambers and tea pavilions line the green ridges. Wild rats scurry down the gushing torrents from the burning woods;
mountain chickens scramble over the scattered wildflowers. Beyond the circle of Master Zhuang, those who understand me are few; on the road of Ruan Ji, my purpose has grown dim.
Surely there will come a man of the world seeking me—how many layers of water and mountains shall I lose myself in?
Twenty-two: Since antiquity, how many have been vain and ostentatious? The surging waves depart all day long, flowing on and on. In the abandoned gardens of the Han kings, autumn grasses grow;
into the desolate palaces of the Wu rulers, night tides enter. Gold fills the halls, yet the looms never cease; yet a single strand of white hair brings one’s spirit low.
It remains lofty. How could one know that the Golden Immortal beyond the mundane world willingly lets the fragrance of heaven fill his woolen robe? Twenty-three:
Like a fool, how could he merely be as straight as a string? He should only hide deep before the green cliffs; there, one sees him always present within the mountains.
Snow. Who knows what year it is in this world? The rustic man loves to smile before his hermitage; red monkeys frequently come to sleep beside his patched robe.
This very one is a fine companion for carefree wandering; why need one ask further about the heavens within the cave?

In the twenty-fourth branch, the sentiment of Zhigong releasing his cranes is similar [to ours], yet Fan Tai’s discourse on friendship differs in its intent. Where there is attachment, one is entirely bound by the shackles of affliction;
only when free from contrivance is one called a Crystal Palace. Incense of *campaka* burns as the various peaks dawn; the *vajra* is grasped with beads as ten thousand...
The elephant is empty; if one asks about its sustenance, words fail. For kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, its use is inexhaustible.
This is Master Zhigong’s fourteen topical verses on the non-duality of bodhi and affliction.
Sentient beings do not understand how to cultivate the Way, yet they wish to sever and eliminate afflictions. Afflictions are originally empty and quiescent;
they seek the Way while already possessing the Way, wishing to find the Way anew. The single thought-moment is it—why must one search for it elsewhere?

The Great Way is clearly present before one’s eyes, yet deluded fools do not realize it. Buddha-nature is genuine and spontaneous; it is neither produced by causes and conditions nor created through cultivation.
Failing to recognize that the three poisons are illusory, one falsely clings to the cycles of birth, aging, and death. In former times, one was deluded into thinking it was already late;
today, one finally realizes it is not yet too early.
Thus, upholding and violating the precepts are non-dual.

The Great Man employs them without obstruction; he is not constrained by the precepts and rules. Upholding and violating are fundamentally non-arising from the start. The foolish person is bound by others' prohibitions;
the wise person finds all creations to be empty. The Śrāvaka encounters obstructions at every turn; the Mahāsattva’s physical eyes possess perfect penetration.
The divine eyes of the Two Vehicles are clouded with cataracts. They falsely cling to existence and non-existence within emptiness, failing to realize that form and mind are unimpeded.
The Bodhisattva dwells together with the mundane, yet remains pure and never defiled by the world. The foolish person craves attachment to nirvana;
the wise person finds the reality-limit within birth and death. The nature of phenomena is fundamentally beyond words and speech; this verse is composed briefly based on dependent origination.
A child of a hundred years may lack wisdom, while a child of one year may possess it.
The Buddha and the assembly are non-dual; sentient beings and the Buddha are no different.
Great wisdom is not distinct from folly. Why seek the jewel elsewhere? Within the field of one’s own body, there is naturally a bright pearl.
The right path and the deviant path are non-dual; understand that ordinary people and sages travel the same road. Delusion and awakening are fundamentally non-existent.
As for the distinctions: Nirvana and birth-and-death are of one suchness. Ultimately, the objects of perception are empty and still; one seeks only the purity and vacuity of mental conceptions.
Since not a single dharma can be obtained, one enters spontaneously and freely into the realm of no-remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).

In the non-duality of phenomena and principle, the King of Mind is sovereign and carefree. The nature of dharmas is originally free from the ten entanglements; everything is nothing other than the Buddha-work.

Why then need one restrain the mind through seated meditation? Delusive thoughts are fundamentally empty and still; there is no need to sever them or eliminate objective conditions. The wise person has no such mind.
It can be attained. It is naturally free from contention and clamor. If one does not recognize the Great Way of non-action (*wuwei*), when will one realize its profound mystery?

Buddhas and sentient beings are of one kind; sentient beings are themselves the World-Honored One. Ordinary people deludedly give rise to discrimination, clinging to existence within non-existence and wandering in confusion.
Once one thoroughly understands that greed and anger are empty and still, where would there not be the Gate of Truth?
Stillness and turmoil are non-dual.
When śrāvakas loathe clamor and seek stillness, it is like discarding flour while seeking bread; yet the bread is fundamentally nothing other than flour.
Its manifestation varies according to the person’s efforts, but afflictions are themselves bodhi. Where there is no mind, there is no object; thus, birth-and-death are not different [from nirvana].
Nirvana. Greed and anger are like flames and shadows. The wise have no mind to seek a Buddha;

the ignorant cling to what is false and what is true, laboring in vain throughout their lives and failing to behold the wondrous crown of the Tathāgata. When one fully realizes that the nature of lust is empty, the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals will naturally grow cold.
Good and evil are non-dual;
my own body and mind are blissful. Transcendently free, there is neither good nor evil. The Dharma-body is sovereign and without fixed location;

everything encountered by the eye is none other than perfect awakening. The six sense-objects are originally empty and still, yet ordinary beings falsely give rise to attachments regarding nirvana and birth-and-death.
All is equal. Throughout the four seas, who is favored and who is slighted? The unconditioned Great Way is spontaneous; there is no need to employ the mind to calculate or measure it.

Bodhisattvas are relaxed and open through, their actions always imbued with wondrous enlightenment. Śrāvakas cling to dharmas while practicing seated meditation, like silkworms spinning silk to bind themselves.
The nature of phenomena is originally perfect and luminous; once the illness has been cured, why persist in clinging to the medicine? Thus one fully understands all dharmas.
Equanimity. It is transcendent, pure, empty, and joyful.
Form and emptiness are non-dual;

the dharma-nature is fundamentally devoid of blue or yellow. Sentient beings vainly compose their own treatises, while I and others speak of his *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, according to our own inclinations.
In a state of restless agitation and madness, they do not recognize the wondrous principle of perfect penetration. When will they realize the true and eternal?
Unable to treat their own illness, they instead seek medicinal prescriptions from others; outwardly they appear to be virtuous, yet within their hearts they remain like wolves and jackals.
The fool fears hell; the wise person finds no delight in heaven. When the mind does not arise in response to sense objects, every step taken is a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual; it is sentient beings themselves who create separation between them.

If one wishes to eliminate the three poisons, yet remains far removed from this truth, one will not escape calamity. The wise know that the mind is the Buddha; the fool delights in going to the Western Paradise.

Birth and death are non-dual; all worldly phenomena are like illusions. Birth and death are like lightning; the *dharmakāya* is sovereign and perfectly penetrating, passing through mountains and rivers without obstruction.
Inverted deluded thoughts are fundamentally empty; *prajñā* is without confusion or disorder. The three poisons are originally...

Liberation! Why is it necessary to collect the mind through meditative contemplation? It is only because fools do not understand; they follow the dictates of others' precepts and fail to recognize the true suchness of quiescence.
When will they ever reach the other shore? For the wise person, there is no evil to be severed. They employ their faculties according to the mind, whether in gathering or dispersing.
The nature of phenomena is originally empty and still, and thus they are not fettered by birth and death. If one wishes to sever [delusions],...
Afflictions—these are the ignorance of a deluded man. Afflictions are themselves bodhi; what need is there to seek dhyāna-contemplation elsewhere?
In the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) there is neither Buddha nor Māra; the essence of mind is formless and without parts.
Having severed duality, this Great Man acts with majestic dignity; he wanders at ease and with sovereign freedom, unhindered by anything. Nothing can cause him harm;
he is as firm and solid as a vajra. He does not cling to the two extremes, but abides in the Middle Way—serene, neither annihilated nor eternal. As for the five desires, greed, and anger...
This is the Buddha. Hell is no different from heaven; it is only the deluded person who falsely gives rise to discrimination, wandering through birth and death in a state of frantic madness.

The wise person realizes that form is without obstruction, yet among the śrāvakas there are none who are not filled with trepidation. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally free from blemish or obscuration, yet sentient beings falsely cling to blue and yellow.
The Tathāgata guides the deluded and ignorant, sometimes speaking of hell and heaven within the body of Maitreya.
It exists inherently; why must one seek it elsewhere through deliberation? To cast aside True Suchness (Tathatā) and the Buddha-image is to be a madman.
Within the minds of the Śrāvakas, this is not understood; they merely pursue words and phrases. Words and phrases are not the true Path;

they only increase contention and stubbornness. Within their hearts dwell vipers, snakes, and scorpions; once stung, they immediately suffer injury. They do not understand the meaning within the texts.
Grasping at meaning, when will one attain realization of the true and eternal? Upon death, one enters the Avīci Hell, where the consciousness suffers calamities in vain.

Although the Dharma Master preaches that the ultimate and conventional truths are non-dual, his mind is not free from afflictions; while his mouth speaks of words and characters to transform others, he only becomes further [entangled].
They increase the birth and aging of others. Truth and delusion are fundamentally non-dual; yet ordinary beings abandon delusion to seek the Way.

The fourfold assembly gathers like clouds to listen to the lectures, and the high seats debate the principles with great clamor. Those seated to the south and those seated to the north contend with one another, while the fourfold assembly speaks for them, claiming each side is right.
Though their mouths speak of the nectar of immortality, their hearts remain habitually parched. Having not a single coin themselves, they spend day and night counting the treasures of others.
They are like ignorant fools who cast away true gold to carry straw upon their shoulders.
With the three poisons unabandoned within their minds, I do not know when they will attain the Way.

The Vinaya Master Jiebo (Liberation from Bonds) adheres to the precepts while binding himself; thus, he binds himself and is able to bind others as well. Outwardly, he displays a demeanor of dignified tranquility, yet within his mind there are waves like a surging flood.
Without boarding the raft of birth-and-death, how can he cross the river of craving? He does not understand the True Doctrine.
The *Nyāya* (Right Principle) school abounds in heterodox views and verbose rhetoric. There were two bhikṣus who had violated the Vinaya;
they went to Upāli to inquire about it, and Upāli explained their offenses according to the Vinaya. This, in turn, increased the web of regulations for the bhikṣus.

When the layman Vimalakīrti came to the chamber of the *śāstrin* (the presiding monk) and rebuked them, Upāli remained silent and offered no reply. Vimalakīrti’s exposition of the Dharma was without fault, yet regarding the nature of that precept:
Like space, it does not abide within or without the Sahā world. I urge you to eliminate birth and cessation; do not be unwilling. If you suddenly awaken, you will be identical to Śākyamuni.
When the object and the illumination are non-dual, the essence of the Chan master is free from ignorance. From where could afflictions arise? Hell and heaven are of one single mark—Nirvana.
Birth and death are empty names; there is neither greed nor anger to be severed, nor is there any Buddha-way to be accomplished. Sentient beings and Buddhas are equal.
Natural, sagely wisdom is ever-awake and is not defiled by the six sense objects. In every phrase, one uniquely accords with the unborn.

In a single thought, one attains the profound understanding of perfect enlightenment; the three periods of time are thus revealed as entirely level and even. Neither dharma nor discipline, one self-restrains;
with effortless spontaneity, one truly enters the state of perfect fulfillment. Transcending these four propositions and a hundred negations, one is like space—without action and without reliance.
In the unimpeded application [of the Dharma], I now flow with ease and mastery. I do not envy dukes, kings, ministers, or officials. The four seasons remain as steadfast as a vajra;
my mind is ever unchanged by suffering or joy. The Jewel of the Dharma is like Mount Sumeru; wisdom is vaster than the rivers and seas. I am not moved by the eight winds.
One is led along without either diligence or indolence; following one's nature, drifting and sinking, or even toppling over, one is unrestrained, sprawling, and free.
Even if a sword were placed upon one's head, I would remain naturally at ease and pay it no heed.

Delusion and awakening are non-dual: in delusion, one takes emptiness to be form; in awakening, one takes form to be emptiness. Delusion and awakening are fundamentally without distinction; form and emptiness ultimately remain the same.
The fool calls south north, while the wise person realizes there is neither east nor west. If you wish to seek the Tathāgata...
The wondrous principle is always within a single thought-moment. A mirage is fundamentally not water, yet the thirsty deer frantically pursues it in haste.
One’s own body is false and insubstantial, yet one seeks emptiness within emptiness. The delusion of worldly people is extreme, like a dog barking at the roar of thunder.

The Monk Teng Teng’s Song on Cultivating the Way: In the Way, there is nothing to cultivate; in the Dharma, there is nothing to inquire about. Those who are deluded do not understand that form is emptiness; those who have awakened find that fundamentally there is neither opposition nor compliance.
Among the eighty-four thousand gates of the Dharma, the ultimate principle does not depart from the square inch of the heart-mind. Recognize your own home!
As for city walls and moats, do not vainly seek them in other lands or districts. There is no need for extensive learning across many gates;
it does not depend on eloquence or cleverness. One need not know the large and small months of the lunar calendar, nor concern oneself with the intercalary days of the year.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; pure flowers grow from mud and dung. When people come to ask me how it is, I cannot engage them in discussion. At dawn, one uses gruel.
It satisfied my hunger. At the time of the midday meal, I ate yet another head. Today I am carefree and buoyant; tomorrow I shall be buoyant and carefree.
My mind is clear and understands it all. For now, let me remain thus—half-witted and half-dull.
The Song of the Thatched Hermitage by Master Shitou:
I have built a thatched hermitage with no treasures; When the meal is finished, I leisurely seek the joy of sleep. When it was first completed, the thatch and grass were new;
When it falls apart, I shall cover it again with thatch and grass. The one who dwells in the hermitage is ever-present; He belongs neither to the middle nor to the inside.
Externally: Where worldly people dwell, I do not dwell; where worldly people find delight, I find no delight. Though this hermitage is small, it contains the entire Dharma-realm.

The Elder of Fangzhang understands its essence through his realization. For Bodhisattvas of the highest vehicle, there is no doubt; those of middle or lower capacity will surely feel strange upon hearing this. Ask whether this hermitage can be destroyed or not:
whether it is destroyed or not, the Master remains fundamentally present, dwelling neither in the south nor the north.
East and West: the foundation is most secure when it is firm. Beneath the green pines, within the bright windows—marble palaces and vermilion towers do not compare.
With the cassock on and the head covered, all affairs cease; at this moment, even the mountain monk does not understand. Dwell in this hermitage and refrain from forming interpretations.
Who would boast of setting up a stall to entice others to buy? Turn the light back upon itself and return home; the spiritual root is vast and penetrating.

Neither turning toward nor turning away, you encounter the Patriarch and receive his personal instruction. Weave grass to make a hermitage and do not give rise to retreat. After a hundred years, cast it all aside;
moving freely in all directions, one departs with a wave of the hand and incurs no fault. A thousand words and ten thousand explanations are intended only to ensure that you remain forever undeluded.
If you wish to know the immortal person within the hermitage, how could they be separate from this present skin-bag?
Stonehead Monk’s *Cantong qi* (The Accordance of Penetration), with the topical outline by Chan Master Langya Huijue.

The mind of the Great Sage of the land of Chu (India) was secretly transmitted from east to west. Though human faculties may be sharp or dull, the Way has neither Northern nor Southern patriarchs.
**Section Two: Establishing Expedient Means Without Departing from the True Source** (divided into seven parts) **Section One:
Clarifying that the True Source and Original Enlightenment Are Essentially Non-delusive** (four statements; from "The luminous source" to "nor is it speech")
The spiritual source is bright and pure; its branches and streams flow on in obscurity. To grasp at phenomena is fundamentally delusion;
to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. Second, regarding the non-abiding of faculties and objects (there are four lines):
"In every gate and every object, whether they revolve or do not revolve, they interpenetrate one another; otherwise, they abide according to their respective positions."
Third, the non-obstruction of form and sound (consists of four phrases, from the line on the essence of form to the line on clarity and turbidity):

The essence of form differs in its substantial appearance; The source of sound varies in pleasure and pain. "Darkness" corresponds to the terms "superior" and "middling"; "Clarity" refers to the phrase on "clarity and turbidity."
The fourth is the Great Elements Free from Dust (consisting of four phrases, from "the nature of the four great elements" to "firmness"):
the nature of the four great elements returns to itself, like a child finding its mother; fire is heat, wind is movement, water is moisture, and earth is firmness.
The fifty-second section: Establishing [the bases] based on reality (consists of six phrases, from eye and form to speech).
Eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and salty/sour [tastes]. Yet, for each and every phenomenon, they are distributed according to their faculties and objects.
The root and the branches must both return to the source; honor and humility are expressed through their words.
The sixth [point] does not stagnate in being or non-being (there are six phrases, from "When brightness is manifest" to "before and after").
When brightness is manifest, there is darkness within it; do not encounter it with darkness. When darkness is manifest, there is brightness within it; do not perceive it with brightness.
Light and darkness face each other, like front and back steps.
In the seventh [verse], the myriad dharmas are without distinction and the true mind alone is revealed. (There are four lines; from "The myriad things" to "the arrowhead meeting the point"):

The myriad things possess their own function; one should speak of where that function is applied. In phenomena, it is like the lid fitting the box; in principle, it is like the arrowhead meeting the point.
Third, clarifying that the cause must be understood through the fruit for the ultimate discourse to be revealed (one section, two sentences):
"One must rely on the words to understand the essence; do not establish your own arbitrary rules.

When you meet it with your eyes, you do not realize the Way; when you set foot upon it, how can you know the path? Advancing forward is neither far nor near; it is only through delusion that mountains and rivers stand between you.
I respectfully address those who study the profound mystery: do not let your time be spent in vain.
The Monk Suxi (the junior disciple of Wuxie) sang this "Song of Mupohu":
Listen to the monk Mupohu; he wanders freely and at ease, dwelling nowhere. A single hundred-patch robe and a water jar are his entire livelihood and equipment.
Seeking the ultimate principle, he has traveled in search of it, undaunted by the hardships of cold and heat. Has he ever [reached] the four seas?
Wandering everywhere, mountains, waters, winds, and clouds fill my belly. Within, I maintain the precepts with rigorous discipline, yet I do not study formal deportment or gait.

The followers of the Three Vehicles laugh at me for being incapable; I laugh at the Three Vehicles for their pretentiousness. The wise establish provisional stages for the sake of others, yet the Great Way is fundamentally free from delusion or enlightenment.
Those who have attained it do not rely on cultivation or rectification; it does not depend on eloquence or speech. One simply strips off the hempen robe and looks directly with the eyes.
Amidst the clouds and mists, let it be—kings and lords may take no notice. The original substance of the Way-person is thus: it is not a matter of knowing where the Buddha goes.
Living is like putting on a robe; dying is like taking off one's trousers. In birth and death there is neither joy nor sorrow; how could the eight winds cause alarm or fear?
Outwardly he may resemble a fool, but within he is exceedingly sharp and resourceful. Though he possesses no worldly means of livelihood...
"One coin—dare I compete with the Sovereign in wealth? The fool waves his hands in disdain; the wise man nods in agreement.

smash the painted vase and go home."
Master Yuepu’s Song on Floating Bubbles: Clouds in the sky, rain falls upon the courtyard water;
Upon the water, floating and drifting, bubbles arise. The former has already vanished as the latter is born;
In succession from before to after, they continue without end. Originally, drops of rain caused the water to form bubbles; Now, driven by the wind, the bubbles dissolve back into the water.
It returns to the water; one does not know that the bubble and the nature of water are no different. Following its transformation by external conditions, it is taken to be something distinct.

Clear and bright on the outside, containing emptiness within, it is transparent inside and out like a precious jewel. When it is upon the still waves, it seems to exist; yet when touched and moved, it is as if non-existent.
Existence and non-existence, motion and stillness—these matters are difficult to clarify. Within formlessness, forms take shape. One knows only the bubble.
It emerges from within the water; how could one know that the water, too, arises from the bubble?

Temporarily using the bubble and the water as analogies for my own body—the five aggregates are a hollow collection, conventionally established as a "person"—only by understanding that the aggregates are empty and the bubble is unreal can one clearly perceive the original reality.
Dana Hermit’s “Verses on Playing with the Pearl,” Two Poems The wondrous *prajñā* pearl is difficult to fathom;
within the ocean of the *dharmatā*, it is personally realized. Hidden or manifest, it constantly wanders amidst the five aggregates;
its inner and outer radiance is a great spiritual power. This pearl is neither large nor small; its radiance shines throughout day and night.
It illuminates all; when sought, there is neither object nor trace. Arising and sitting, it follows along, always clear and distinct.

Once, the Yellow Emperor traveled to the Red Water; though they vied to listen and vied to seek, none succeeded. Wǎngxiàng, being without mind, instead obtained the pearl. To be able to see and hear is but falsehood.
My Master used a provisional finger-pointing as a metaphor for the *maṇi* jewel; countless seekers have drowned in the spring pond, vying to grasp it.
Rubble and debris shall become jewels; the wise obtain them with serene composure. The myriad phenomena of the universe manifest within the light;
essence and function are suchness, revolving yet not revolving. Ten thousand functions are resolved within a single inch of the heart; at all times, there is skillful means.
It burns the six thieves and incinerates the multitudes of Māras; it can shatter the mountain of the self and dry up the river of craving.

The Naga Queen personally offered it to the Buddha at Vulture Peak, yet for the poor child beneath his robes, how many times has it been nearly lost! It is called "nature" and it is called "mind," yet it is neither nature nor mind, transcending past and present.
When the whole body is luminous, that luminosity cannot be grasped; for the time being, it is titled "A Verse on Playing with a Pearl.
Second:
Once the treasure within the garment is recognized, the intoxication of ignorance naturally awakens. Though the hundred members of the body may all crumble away, one thing remains eternally numinous.

Know that the objective realm is fundamentally not the essence; the divine pearl has no fixed form. To awaken is to be the Buddha of the Three Bodies; to be deluded is to be lost in ten thousand volumes of scripture.

When it resides in the mind, the mind can fathom it; when it passes through the ear, the ear finds it hard to hear. Its formless radiance illuminates heaven and earth; its profound spring emerges from the depths of the void.
The fundamental adamancy is not forged; primordial purity is beyond stillness. It abides like a wheel reflecting the morning sun; it is translucent, mirroring the dawn stars.
Auspicious light flows on without ceasing; true energy is regenerated upon contact. It reflects the silence of Mount Kongtong; it encompasses the luminosity of the Dharma-realm.

The merit of subduing the mundane is inexhaustible; the transcendence of the holy fruit is not full. The dragon maiden offered it with a heart of intimacy; the serpent king presented it from his own mouth.
The man who protected the geese was restored to life; yet the yellow sparrow’s intent remained light. Understanding speech does not depend on the tongue; the ability to speak is not merely sound.

Severing all extremes, it is vast and boundless; without limit, it is as level as space. The unfolding of the teaching is not for the sake of verbal explanation; upon hearing its name, do not mistake the name for the reality.

Do not establish yourself in either of the two extremes, and there is no need to travel the Middle Way. When you see the moon, cease looking at the pointing finger; once you have returned home, stop inquiring about the journey.
When consciousness is the mind, that mind is the Buddha; what other Buddha could possibly be accomplished?
Master Daowu’s Song of Delighting in the Way:
"I, this mountain monk, follow my nature freely. Heaven turns and earth revolves—let them do as they please. I lie idly upon a solitary peak, without companion."
Alone, I sing a single song of non-arising. This song of non-arising is the supramundane joy. It is laughable that people of this age do not harmonize with it;
they let their passions run wild while claiming to delight in the Way, thus wasting the remainder of their lives. They have completely forgotten the likes of Zhang San and Li Si.

A great man must possess spirit and resolve; do not follow worldly sentiments, and do not create obstacles. You say that compliance is itself Bodhi, but I maintain that from the very beginning it has been so.
Facing each other in opposition; at times stubborn, at times deluded—how could I know this along the way? Throughout my life, I have simply followed the natural flow.
As a wild guest, there is no hometown to which I can return. Today, this mountain monk is just like this; what more could the original mountain monk do?
Probing the ancestral pivot, the Prince of Emptiness, his essence is like drifting clouds vanishing into the recesses. From of old, he has long been clothed in the vast expanse.
A single robe has weathered many cycles of cold and heat; it is neither true nor false.
As drums beat for the gods and prostrations are made, there is clearly a single cloud over the Han River. The green mountains and clear waters are unlike anything else; its nature is thus formed.
There is no erasing or correcting. The interlocking knots and cross-hatched patterns do not obstruct one another. One may employ the minds of compassion, joy, and equanimity;
or, upon encountering a person, one strikes them with a staff. Compassion and affection fall into entanglements; striking with the staff teaches them to break through such affection.
This is reported to those travelers under the moon: if there is any lingering attachment, I shall amend it for you.
Master Fu’s Inscription on the Mind-King:

Contemplate the King of the Empty Mind; it is profound and wondrous, difficult to fathom. It has neither form nor appearance, yet possesses great supernatural power capable of extinguishing a thousand calamities.
Having accomplished the ten thousand virtues, though its essential nature is empty, it can bestow the Dharma rules. Contemplated, it has no form; called upon, it has sound.
Acting as a great general of the Dharma, it transmits the sutras through the precepts of the mind. It is like the flavor of salt in water or the clarity of glue within color; it definitely exists.

Its form is not seen. The mind-king is likewise: it dwells within the body, yet enters and exits through the gateway of the face; responding to objects according to circumstances, it is sovereign and unimpeded, accomplishing all that it does.
Having realized the fundamental consciousness-mind, one sees the Buddha through the consciousness-mind; this very mind is the Buddha.
This Buddha is the mind; in every thought-moment, the Buddha-mind is present. The Buddha-mind recollects the Buddha. If you wish to achieve success early, restrain yourself with the mind of precepts;
purify the precepts and purify the mind. The mind is itself the Buddha; apart from this sovereign mind, there is no other Buddha. If you seek to attain Buddhahood, [you must realize this].
Do not be stained by a single thing. Although the nature of the mind is empty, the essence of greed and anger is real. Upon entering this Dharma-gate, one attains Buddhahood while sitting upright.
Having reached the other shore, one obtains the *pāramitās*. A true seeker of the Way observes their own mind and knows that the Buddha resides within.
Do not seek outward; the mind itself is the Buddha, and the Buddha himself is the mind. When the mind is clear, one recognizes the Buddha; when one understands thoroughly, one recognizes the mind.

Apart from the mind there is no Buddha; apart from the Buddha there is no mind. That which is not the Buddha cannot be fathomed; it is incapable of being grasped. To cling to emptiness and stagnate in quiescence—this is delusion.
Sinking and floating within this [world], the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not find peace here. The Great Being who clarifies the mind awakens to this profound resonance;
the nature of body and mind is wondrous, its functioning never subject to change. Therefore, the wise let the mind rest in freedom; do not speak of a "mind-king."

Emptiness has no inherent nature, yet it can cause the physical body to act either erroneously or correctly; it is neither existent nor non-existent, appearing and disappearing without fixed certainty.
Although the nature of the mind is empty, it can manifest as both ordinary and sagely. Therefore, I exhort you: take care to guard yourself with vigilance at every moment of action.
Yet they drift and sink once more. The pure and clear mind-intelligence is like the gold of the world; the Dharma-treasury of Prajñā resides within both body and mind.

This treasure of unconditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is neither shallow nor deep. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have realized this original mind; those who encounter it through the proper conditions [shall likewise realize it].
Neither past, future, nor present.
The Song of Master Lan’an Zan of Mount Nanyue:
"Utterly still and without affairs, there is no change. Since there are no affairs, what need is there to discuss even a single segment? The direct mind is free from distraction. He—
There is no need to sever anything. The past has already passed; the future is not yet to be reckoned. Sit upright and without concern; who has ever called you?
To seek effort outwardly is the mark of a fool or a blockhead. Without storing a single grain of rice, one simply knows how to eat when food is encountered.
Those in the world with many affairs cannot keep up with their own pursuits. I do not delight in birth.
Heaven! Nor does he cherish fields of merit. When hunger comes, he eats; when weariness comes, he sleeps. Fools laugh at me, but the wise understand.
It is not that I am dull-witted; my fundamental nature is simply thus. If I wish to go, I go; if I wish to stay, I stay.
My body is clad in a single tattered robe, and my feet wear my mother’s birth-cloths. To speak much and chatter excessively has, from the beginning, led to mutual delusion. If you wish...
To deliver sentient beings, there is nothing better than first delivering oneself. Do not vainly seek the True Buddha; the True Buddha cannot be seen.
As for the wondrous nature and the spiritual citadel, when have they ever been subject to perfuming or refinement? The mind is a mind of non-action; the face is the face one was born with.
Even if the kalpa-stone could be moved, that which lies within it never changes. Non-action is fundamentally without affairs; why need one read written words? Erase them!

The person and the self are fundamentally one; their meaning is darkly merged within this state. All manner of toil and strain of body and sinew is not as good as sleeping soundly beneath the forest trees.
When you lift your head and see the sun is high, go from door to door to beg for food. To apply effort upon effort leads only to further confusion and obscurity.

If you try to grasp it, you cannot get it; if you do not grasp it, it is naturally understood. I have a single word: cut off deliberation and let go of conditions. It cannot be obtained through clever speech; simply use it.

The Mind-Transmission. There is yet another phrase: there is nothing better than giving it directly. Subtle as a fine hair, vast and without fixed location, it is fundamentally perfected from the start, requiring no laborious weaving.
Worldly affairs are wearying; they are not as good as a mountain ridge. Green pines block out the sun; azure ravines flow on forever.
Mountain clouds serve as a curtain; the night moon acts as a hook. Lying beneath the wisteria vines, with a boulder for a pillow, one does not attend court.
O Son of Heaven, why envy kings and lords? With no anxieties regarding birth and death, what more is there to worry about?

Like the moon in water, it has no fixed form; I am always simply at peace. All phenomena are thus: they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning. Sitting upright and free from affairs, when spring comes, the grass turns green of its own accord.
The Verses of Great Master Zhixian of Xiangyan Shideng (Nineteen Stanzas):

Pointing to the bones of the ancients, many are wondrous and extraordinary. Wise descendants have secretly established this one school, fulfilling filial piety and righteousness. People have not yet...
Attain it. Do not falter. One must be firm in resolve and cast away doubt. Thus one attains tranquility and avoids peril. Seeking it leads to the distant; seeking it leads to separation.
To grasp it is urgent; to lose it is tardy. There is no calculating; forget all sensory awareness. The turbid flow of consciousness is the falsehood of antiquity and today.
In a single kṣaṇa, it pervades all transformations. From the jagged peaks of the mountain, the breath of a flint-fire issues from within, burning the piled-up crags without obstruction;

it burns the ocean floor, for the net of Dharma is vast and the divine flames are subtle. One lies through the sixth month without clothing or bedding, yet cannot be covered by them—therein is no pretense or falsehood.
The man who has attained the Way proclaims the ancestral meaning; this is the tradition of my Master, a taboo since ancient times. Only such a person can skillfully establish it.
Sufficient in the wealth of Dharma; endowed with shame and remorse; not giving in vain; using [resources] with discernment. When someone asks, one should respond with a slight sigh;
then, having reflected further, one says, "Rice is expensive."

The final word has but one phrase. It is entirely complete in its pattern. Cease your deliberations; do not grant yourself permission [to rest]. When meeting a person who has attained the Way on the road, they raise their eyebrows to examine where you have come from.
If you cannot step upon it, doubts will abound. Yet you turn back to contemplate it, bringing along your companions. Thus, the task of a lifetime of study remains unfulfilled.
Accomplished! With earnest devotion, he embraced the sandalwood tree.
Changxuan and Cui Dafu were men of great realization;

they were indeterminate in whether they remained hidden or manifested, and did not allow their physical forms to be revealed. In their speech, they left no trace behind, secretly and closely providing protection and sustenance.

A movement of the countenance reveals the ancient path; only through clarity and subtlety is it truly known. Responding to things, one merely establishes provisional means; do not call this "inconceivable.

The practitioner who has reached the site of enlightenment and the outskirts of the city finds the principle profound and beyond calculation. Seeking the root along the long path, one thereby realizes the vast distance [between them]. There is no help for being confined by boundaries.
Human life must be exceptional and penetrating; in rising and sitting, one perceives its fragrant essence. The sons of the Tathāgata, pure and serene, sit peacefully within the site of enlightenment.
To Judge Official Xue:
drop by drop of water, flame by flame of fire—the one who drinks the water grows drunk, the one who faces the fire grows old; yet he neither drinks nor faces it.

"To you, O man who travels to Linru County—how lamentable!

Because of this, the eyes are opened. This old monk’s hand is stiff with rheumatism, and my writing is faltering. Yet there is meaning beneath the words; they truly emerge from the cage of affliction.

The revealed intent is far-reaching, and the divine countenance is profound. Through refined emptiness, one’s practice becomes pervasive. Seeing and hearing transcend images; the secret boundary precedes all traces of speech.

Attaining mastery within the sensory realm is subtle; meeting the opportune moment, one reveals the countenance of the Way. Concealing brilliance yet illuminating, one awakens with a start; only by being willing can one reach the True宗 (Zong).

The meaning following the "three phrases" is expressed through written words that are largely empty; within this emptiness, there is both being and non-being. Yet, one must realize it before the writing appears, letting go of the pearl within the mind.
In response to the questions of Officer Zheng (two poems):

Traces are buried within words; forms are revealed before sounds. In this moment of wondrous realization, one shares the same spirit as the ancients. Responding to conditions like an echo, one acts in accordance with the opportune moment.
With neither self nor other schools, he rebukes the startled serpent; with vigorous strides he becomes a dragon.
Within his words lie the sinews and bones; his voice colors his countenance. At that moment, when the subtle meaning is perfectly realized, he claps his hands to chase away the perverse dragon.
The Way of Tan Dao has no dualistic inclusion; how can it rely on solitary operation? When meeting a person who has realized the Way, do not respond with speech or silence.
This is the profound mechanism for students.

The wondrous intent is swift; words come too late. As soon as one follows the words to understand, the divine mechanism is lost. When the eyebrows are raised in response to a question, there is a joyful radiance face-to-face.
What kind of realm is this? Only those on the same path can know.
The clarity of the Way seems to leave traces with every thought, yet its luminous essence is unknown where it dwells. I ask you, guest who reveals the source: look back slowly and silently;
therein lies the profound principle.
Going, going, there is no destination; coming, coming, it is simply coming. When someone asks me for instruction, I do not speak, but laugh heartily.

Like the mendicant from Dengzhou who realized his own body was deluded beneath the trees, I have never carried the pearl of the mind. My mouth opens but has nothing to say; my pen-tip has nothing to write.

The one of superior capacity exclaims, "Alas! Do not err! Suddenly there is no-thought; words are spoken from within emptiness. A single stroke startles the dragon; a slight whisper issues the summons.
Its subtlety is absolute and its name is remote. Lofty is this stream of the Way; it cannot be peeled away or stripped bare.

Having shattered the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), above there are no father or mother; below there are no son or daughter. One stands alone as a single person; one must by all means bring this to final resolution.
Hearing these words of mine, everyone vies with one another to grasp them. To meet each of them with a single phrase, I do not speak of the absence of speech.

The one-legged chick pecks at its mother’s beak; the chick awakens to find no grain, and both mother and child perish. Thus, conditions do not fail to correspond. Those of the same path sing in harmony;

A Verse on the Ground of Awakening by Chan Master Weijing of Nanyue (Seven Lines), Briefly Clarifying the Names and Differences of the Ground of Awakening:
Awakening arises and returns, beginning and ending, mutually exchanging birth. The Ocean of Nature first establishes the title "Increased" (*zeng*);

Wondrous Awakening (*miaojue*) still relies upon the clarity of Nature-Awakening (*xingjue*). The essence and awakening both contain clarity and wondrousness; Clarity-Awakening and Wondrous-Awakening are both present.

The dual functioning: the wondrous awakening awakens to the wondrous, primal luminosity of the essence. This entirely constitutes the single, true, pure quintessence of the outflow-free. Luminous awakening awakens to that which is luminous and that which is understood.
Sometimes, due to the perception of characteristics, one loses the primal luminosity. The two types of awakening—the wondrous and the luminous—are the primary essence and the fundamental body.

The awakening of the essence and the awakening of the nature are both identical in their luminosity. This profound awakening is perfect and round, without increase or decrease. Within this, there is neither Buddha nor sentient being. Non-awakening...
From beginning to end, it is not clearly manifest; if one does not hear it, how can there be delusion or awakening, or any state of alertness? This is called the Tathāgatagarbha of the Mind-ground;
it is devoid of both cognitive illumination and non-arising. It is neither arising nor ceasing—the ocean of True Suchness (Tathatā)—serenely and eternally abiding, named yet nameless.
In the great void, before awakening, the first speck of dawn appears; how could one hear the slightest sound of outflow from a mote of dust?

A bubble in the sky is not separate from the ocean of awakening; movement and stillness are fundamentally one true luminosity. The essence of awakened luminosity inherently contains the flames of sentience; yet when awakened luminosity pursues these flames, it leads to deficiency and fullness.
To deviate from this and fail to return is called "non-awakening"; to realize it and restore the source is the arising of "initial awakening. Fundamental awakening arises through causes.

Initial awakening arises; correct awakening, in turn, relies upon the clarity of combined awakening. Due to these two types of stages, differences arise, ultimately causing the whole to be designated by the name "ālaya-vijñāna.
It contains both defiled and pure paths within its dual branches. Where the clarity of awakening is contained, divergent ways begin to sprout.

The nature-arising, non-arising, immovable wisdom does not depart from the essence of awakening, which is fundamentally perfected. As nature-arising turns toward awakening, it reverses to produce the objective realm. Thus...
It causes those with outflows to fall into delusion and blindness. Ignorance is moistened by the cause of craving; name-and-form, as its root, arises gradually.
Where the seven consciousnesses revolve, they obscure the perfect mirror; when the five and six arise, they shroud the luminosity of awakening.

Contact, sensation, grasping, and existence arise in mutual dependence; birth, old age, sickness, and death continue their course. The karmic consciousness, vast and boundless, sinks into the sea of suffering; following this great torrent, it eventually...
Floating Clouds: The Great Sage, out of compassion, manifests salvation; from the single body, the three bodies emerge.

The Wisdom Body arises from the Dharma Body, and the Practice Body is produced in reliance upon the Wisdom Body. These two bodies—Wisdom and Practice—are fused without duality, returning to the one essence that is fundamentally level.
All phenomena are equally contained within the True Sea-Seal; the One Mind universally manifests all things in total, perfect clarity. A profound radiance.

Where does this blazing flame depend? In the vast expanse of emptiness, there is nowhere for it to rest. In every place it manifests the signs of birth, yet in every place it manifests the form of non-birth.

In every place it manifests cessation, yet in every place it has no form of cessation. Like a jewel or a mirror, it reflects instantaneously without coming or going; like drifting clouds gathering and dispersing, it follows no fixed course.

Appearing and disappearing according to reality, they are like the moon in water; responding to conditions like echoes, they transform the myriad emotions. The fundamental nature of sentient beings is originally undefiled;

it is only because of floating delusions that the true essence is obscured. Failing to realize that the five aggregates are like an empty village, how could one know that the four elements are like a city of *gandharvas*?
The mountain of self-conceit and ignorance stands towering and firm; the ocean of ignorance and desire is vast and profound. One constantly pursues the *caṇḍāla*.
Deceived by pride and delusion, one constantly follows fierce beasts and utters piteous cries. The nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*) transforms into illusion;

the illusory scenes of one's own mind cause the mind itself to be startled. Realizing that this illusory nature is like a mirage, the flowers in the sky and the waves of consciousness are again perfected.

Suddenly, in the great void, one perceives the drifting clouds dispersing; one then realizes that empty space was originally pure. From ancient times to the present, it remains profoundly still, eternally bright and lucid. Not...
He attained renown among the ordinary and the sagely, the ancient and the modern.
Upon the monk’s passing, his name was inscribed as a "Stele for the Subduing of the Mind" (*Xixin Ming*).
Within the Dharma-realm there was a man who possessed the wish-fulfilling jewel; he long kept his person in silence and engraved upon his breast: "The subduing of the mind of antiquity..."
You are a human being. Be on guard! Be on guard! Do not harbor excessive thoughts; do not seek excessive knowledge. Excessive knowledge brings excessive affairs; it is better to let the mind rest.
Excessive deliberation leads to excessive failure; it is better to maintain the One. When deliberation is excessive, the will is scattered; when knowledge is excessive, the mind is disturbed.

A disturbed mind gives rise to affliction; a scattered will obstructs the Way. Do not say, "What harm is there? for its suffering is long-lasting. Do not say, "What is there to fear? for its calamity—
The cauldron boils; not a drop ceases to fall. The four seas are about to overflow; not a speck of dust is brushed away. The five sacred peaks are about to be formed.
Guard the end by staying with the root; though small, do not treat it lightly. Close your seven apertures and shut off your six passions.
Do not gaze upon forms; do not listen to sounds. He who hears sounds is deaf; he who sees forms is blind. A single letter or a single art is but a gnat in the sky; a single skill...
A single ability is like a solitary lamp beneath the sun; the talents and arts of the eminent and wise serve only to obscure the foolish.

They abandon simplicity and purity, becoming immersed in licentious beauty. It is easy for a horse to bolt, but the mind-monkey is difficult to restrain. When the spirit is exhausted by toil, the physical form will surely perish.

Erroneous conduct leads ultimately to delusion, and the long journey is forever mired in mud. Do not prize mere talent, lest one grow increasingly dull and obscured day by day. To boast of one's own clumsiness while envying the skillful—such is their virtue.
Not expansive, it is called "thick conduct being thin. Such a state will swiftly collapse. Within, one harbors arrogance and self-aggrandizement; without, one incurs resentment and hatred.
Whether spoken from the mouth or written by the hand, seeking the reputation of others is most shameful. What the common folk call auspicious, the sages call a fault.
Pleasure and play last but a moment, while sorrow endures for a long time. Fearing the shadow and fearing the tracks, one goes further and further away. Sit upright.

Beneath the shade of trees, footprints vanish and shadows subside. One grows weary of birth and apprehensive of old age; as thoughts arise, so do karmic acts. If the workings of the mind are extinguished, the cycle of birth and death will be forever severed.

There is neither death nor birth; there is no form and no name. The single Way is empty and still; all things are equal and level. What is noble and what is base? What is disgraceful and what is honorable?
What is superior and what is inferior? What is heavy and what is light? The clear sky feels abashed before such purity; the bright sun [is eclipsed].
Preface by Ming’an: Resting upon the peaks of Mount Dai, he is like that city of gold. I respectfully present this to the worthy and wise;
may this Way be beneficial and auspicious. Ten Poems by Chan Master Defu of Yunding Mountain The words and silences are difficult to fathom.
Sitting in silence, profoundly still, even the sages do not know it. Though words are uttered, there is nothing to compare it to. A wooden man holds a board and strikes it amidst the clouds;
a stone woman holds a flute and blows it beneath the water. If you say you do not hear it, you have not yet understood;
if you seek its resonance, you will surely be filled with doubt. I bid you sing and respond—you must respond! Do not ask about the notes of *gong* and *shang*, nor of bamboo and silk strings.

The Patriarchal Teaching is utterly distinct; the Patriarchal Intent is far-reaching. Transmitting a single phrase, the teachings are widely disseminated, arrayed as the Three Vehicles. Vimalakīrti topples the mountains with his thunderous roar;
Śāriputra’s solitary pond reflects the moon’s image in clarity. In the marketplace, the fish-seller forgets his pursuit; in the mountain crags, the tiger-keeper gazes [at the beast].
Transcending and ascending, though one knows the provisional skillful means of the same essence, it is like a lamp in the midday sun of the heavens.
It is difficult to learn;
those who find a subtle resting place and study the Way are as numerous as dust motes. How many recognize Caoxi? If one were to make the sacred and the profane free from obstruction...

Obstructed! Thus, even if one were to take bricks and tiles as the cultivation of truth, the moment a single thought of deviant reflection flickers up, it already belongs to the causes of heedlessness over many lifetimes.
Without encountering the Patriarch’s direct and personal instruction, it is difficult to speak at all when the critical moment arrives.
When responding, do not boast that your response is clear; clinging to phrases and seeking words will only lead you astray and destroy you. It is only fitting that Mañjuśrī should speak thus:
"The layman has failed; he is utterly silent. When meeting others, one must cast away the objects used for knocking at the door; once the path is known, one forgets even the milestone markers.
My son’s name. If you do not doubt that words exhaust their meaning, what prevents you from passing through this floating life in silence?

Since there is no fixed point to things, they do not abide in the north, south, east, or west; how could the upper and lower reaches of empty space ever be equal? Even when appearing as a tiny hair-tip, it is still said:
Vastly expanding, it transforms the heavens beyond the outer limits, yet one still deems it too low. Suddenly drying up the four seas, red dust rises;
it can exhaust the three realms of suffering and dispel the delusions of black karma. All such myriad things belong to the realm of destruction; you must press further forward and inquire at Caoxi.

Delighting in my own eccentric attachments, I have harbored such fixations for a lifetime and lack all grace. For several decades, I have been too lazy to step through the pines at the mountain gate. Sometimes I am too weary even to join my palms and inquire of the Buddha;
who would deign to bow their waist and pay court to kings and lords? The world is as transient as a flash of lightning in a dream; the fires of desire among the masses are already ablaze.
Evening rest. As for the inherently enlightened nature of one's own being, one cannot allow it to remain even momentarily suspended upon the mind.

One must know that in questions and answers regarding arising and falling, one must be taught to recognize arising and falling. To have a dragon’s head and a snake’s tail is self-deception; it is like a king wielding a sword—it depends entirely on the king.

The mind is like a mirror set upon its stand, awaiting the reflection; yet in the blink of an eye, it is separated by a thousand miles, and in a moment of thought, obstructed by ten thousand layers of barriers.
If you seek deep insight within this Way, you will do no more than become a wild jackal on the path ahead.

For words and deeds to support one another, and for words and deeds to accord with one another, is not easy to practice. Like the light of both the crow and the hare, it is attained through diligent effort regardless of day or night;
how could it arise from greed, anger, or indolence? Even Bodhisattvas find it difficult to describe, so how would Śrāvakas dare to attempt it?
Commentary: Yet, while sitting idly for a long time in no particular state, who would have expected the dragon-gods to come forth to welcome him?

One phrase, another phrase—this mystery cannot be grasped through intellectual understanding. Once it is realized with a sudden clarity, what can be done about it? Not only do worldly affairs become non-existent; [all things are thus resolved].

The matter is this: in the ancestral teachings, the mind-demon is the Buddha-demon. This was directly pointed out in the Parable of the Poor Son and clearly displayed in the Verse on Offering the Pearl.
The path to the Gate of Emptiness is level and broad; who, when earnestly invited with such urgency, would refuse to pass through?
The Great Meaning of Past and Present:

Throughout ancient and modern times, the whisk has been used to point toward the southeast. This great meaning is profound and subtle; how could it be easily grasped? A flicking finger and a shaking head are fundamentally one;
a sidelong glance and a clapping of hands are certainly not three. Daowu’s dancing with his ritual tablet is understood by those of like mind; Shigong’s drawing of his bow is likewise so.
This is the recitation. If this Way were not transmitted through the seal of a teacher’s instruction, by what could one perceive it or engage in profound discourse?
A Verse by Chan Master Zhichang of Guizong on Returning to the Source:
The affairs and principles of Guizong are cut off; The sun’s orb is at its zenith. He is as free and sovereign as a lion, Requiring no reliance upon external things.
Striding alone atop the four mountain peaks, he wanders freely upon the three great paths. When he falters, flying birds fall; when he winces, the multitudes of evil spirits tremble with fear.

His mechanism is like an upright arrow, easily reaching its mark; his shadow vanishes like a hand that cannot cover it. His deployment is like a master craftsman’s skill; his cutting and shaping are as precise as a ruler and measure.
Skillfully carved in myriad forms, they return to the source as mere earth. Where speech and silence, and all sounds, are utterly extinguished, the wondrous meaning is beyond the reach of sentiment.
To discard the eye is to become deaf; to grasp the ear is to become dull. A single arrowhead pierces the three barriers—clearly, this is the path behind the arrow.
How pitiable are those who claim to be great men! Only the primordial source of the mind is the true ancestor.
The First Poem on Mountain Dwelling by Venerable Jiufeng Quan of Junzhou (formerly at Qixian Chan Monastery on Mount Lu).

The true source is like profound stillness; when stillness reaches its ultimate limit, it radiates brilliance. As clouds disperse, the solitary peak emerges; as the mountain rises high, the myriad ridges converge.
Wildflowers bloom along the mossy path; fragrant trees conceal the wattle gate. Pointing back toward the realm of the vast void, the pine wind stirs the misty heights.
Secondly, let us inquire of the recluse dwelling in the mountains: What mountain is this? Before the curtain, rain falls on Mount Lu; beyond the heavens, waves roll upon Lake Dongting.
The bright clouds are drawn in and diminished; the green crags are spread wide and abundant. Looking back at the path by the cliffside, flowing waters mingle with the misty vines.
A third mountain-dweller has arrived as a guest; meeting me, he asks of my abode. The sedges before my courtyard are fine and sparse; the rain upon the islet is light and thin.

Years and months have passed, leaving human affairs behind; wind and frost have hindered the sending of letters. I hear again that the "Picked-up Child" has returned, once more concealing himself on Mount Kuanglu.
Fourth, I wish to present a few questions; I rely on you to examine them with meticulous care. Among the Taihu rocks before the hermitage, which one is the yellow arsenic?

When the color of the grass meets autumn, it shortens; when the roots of the clouds enter summer, they grow long. This sentiment reaches the ultimate discernment; its flavor is fully realized as the sun slants toward the west.
Fifth, the Stilling of the Waves: Looking south, the northern ridges rise high; cranes fly from their crests beyond the clouds, while mountains press down upon the giant tortoises of the sea.
The resonance of pines arises from the secluded valley; cold light penetrates my woolen robe. Hearing of the humble Xu Ruzi, I instead say he was a master of *fengsao*.
The sixth [verse] goes alone toward the mountain peaks. For what reason does he increasingly cling to words? The bird clings to his fur and licks his feathers;

his form yields to its shadow as its teacher. There are lines that flow like fragrant leaves; there are no words to speak of what is contemplated. Returning to sit within the crags, he remains in silent stillness, twirling his long beard.
Where do we not meet in the seventh place? Amidst smoke, mists, and bitter fogs. Gazing at flowers, one forgets the fruit; lost among leaves, one turns away from the secluded thickets.
Washing weeds in the clear, fresh rain; striking pines in the white-dew wind. Once this mind is enlightened and penetrating, who would again speak of failure or success?

Eighth Question: What capacity do I possess? I alone am called a monk, yet I am but a monk among monks. With my head raised toward the mountains and two islands, I hold a single branch of rattan in hand.
A wild crane peers at my meditation seat; idle clouds embrace the ridges of the rocks. In these secluded crags, there is much chill and austerity; I pass through the sweltering heat as best I can.
Ninth, as for the path of exhaustion, I dwell in the mountains. Dwelling in the mountains is also difficult; I have not yet clarified what you asked. Why speak so many points?

The moonlight is white, joining with the clouds; the sound of the wind is cold, carrying the rain. My cultivation of the mind has not yet reached this state; I linger on the winding paths of the crags and valleys.
The tenth mountain path lies clearly before us; those lost on their way do not yet know it. The eyes gaze into the distant, dimming blue; the mind’s waves are like white-haired children.
In late autumn, the wind and frost are severe; at twilight, the monkeys and gibbons lament. From antiquity to the present, the cycle is far from exhausted; where else shall we go as we come and go?
Eleventh: Fragrant grasses compete in their lush growth; flowers bloom and a hundred birds sing. In years past we sought seclusion together; our old friend now dwells to the west of the crags.
As I take a step, I secretly suspect the distance has grown; as I sit upright, I become even more lost. In silence I sit beneath the cliff; flowing water fills the long stream.
Twelfth: Dwelling Deeply Beyond Discourse Secluded and tranquil, it endures forever. Beyond the clouds, from the break of dawn, In the mountains, the gates remain closed.
The sound of water divides at the mouth of the cave; Tree shadows sweep across the base of the crags. No one understands this meaning; I sleep idly as the day fades into dusk.
Thirteenth: Where does the mind dwell? Amidst the wind and the rushing waterfalls. One desires to go but never arrives; only by non-abiding does one truly reside in the mountains.
Ancient trees sprout long leaves; floating clouds close the great gates. In such silence, where can one be seen? Beneath the crags, the hair at the temples has turned white.
Fourteen: Discourse on Enduring the Worldly Condition. Seeking profit and fame, I have not yet severed the path of rosy clouds; Already I grieve over the growth of white hair.
The cold wind adds to the traveler’s thoughts; The evening light hastens the cry of the cicadas. Who will accompany this mountain-dweller As he wanders deep within the waters and clouds?
Fifteenth: The Vast Void Shows Nothing. The Tathāgata speaks of the primordial source; The path divides into three trails amidst the weeds. The gate is closed, yet a hundred flowers bloom.
A crane’s feathers hang like snow; White brows arch like jade rings. Dwelling in seclusion beneath layered peaks, I long remember being on Mount Tiantai.
Sixteenth:
Desiring to proceed to the front cliff, deep within the thickets of *bìlì* vines, I add several handfuls of water to my jar and strike the wind with a single branch of my staff.
The stone path is lost in the traces of clouds; the stream is so clear its color reflects the void. Looking back beneath the old forest, there sits upright an old man with white hair.

Seventeenth: Dwelling at Kuangfeng, all manner of affairs are set aside. Radiant light turns across the distant sky and the mountains before me. Monkeys cry out, naturally delighting upon the cold crags;
children play, left to their own devices within the bamboo huts. The vulgar world has never shown affection for water and stone; where could one find such a path among divergent ways?
The mind is at ease; now that it has already grown withered and faded, I stew yellow mustard greens to nourish my sickly countenance.
Eighteenth, dwelling on Mount Kuang like one in a thatched hut, with a wooden gate and a cool pillow to the east of Tiger Creek, my dreams of the Five Lakes have been severed by the pond.

The moon; the cry of gibbons in the Three Gorges; the wind through the pines and cypresses. I do not employ my writings to stir the depths of others' hearts; Never have fame or fortune reached this mountain elder.
Sitting alone in deep seclusion to settle the mind, Moss encircles the cliff as half the rocks turn crimson.

The nineteenth dwelling, situated on Kuang Peak: how should one conduct affairs here? One lingers among springs and rocks, cherishing the prolonging of time. Let others pursue worldly fame and profit;
who else has such leisure of mind as I do at Shaoshi? Tending seedlings in the medicinal garden, one guards against rain and snow; adding provisions to the autumn kitchen—this is the way.
Quince and pear; at my thatched gate, I do not wish for it to ring out again. I shall let the gray moss fill the paths and forks.

(Verse 20) Having resided near Kuang Peak for nearly ten years, the newly planted pines and bamboos have fully harmonized with the sound of the flute. The mountain pheasant calls out as dawn breaks, its song trailing off.

In the moonlight, the youth brews tea and draws water from the Lianquan spring; fallen leaves cling to the cliffs, startling the birds at rest. As the clouds of his sword retreat into the cavern, he reveals his tranquil meditation.
He seldom desires to gaze upon the flowing stream, for his reflection cast upon the clear pool reveals his hair already white.
Twenty-first:
Dwelling at Kuāngfēng, he followed the conduct of the Patriarchs; though the white sandalwood was consumed to ashes, its fragrance remained unheard.

Sēngyáo failed to grasp the subtleties of his divine traces, and the Qin mirror instead became a source of long-standing resentment. When matters reach the gates of Yǐng, one must grant or withhold; when a game of chess meets a worthy opponent, victory is certain.
