Realgar. Now these words are but a vain scratching of the head; for now, I shall lie among the trees as the evening sun sets.
Twenty-second: Dwelling at Kuangfeng, I closed my retreat; my life’s labors have circled in vain. How many times can the soul wander in dreams throughout a hundred years?

Day by day, a span of cold ashes should be kept near the mountain. Filtering water to brew tea awakens the eyes from sleep; listening to the spring’s flow, one remains with guests to speak of the leisure of the body.
When I reflect further upon the matters of the unseen realm, the pines and bamboos stand dense and tall, beyond reach.
The Four Marks of Existence by Master Fu:
Consciousness arises, entrusting itself to floating bubbles; birth comes from craving and desire. In former times one was already grown, yet today one is again an infant.
Star-like eyes follow people as they turn; crimson lips part toward the breast. Because one is deluded regarding the nature of true awakening, one returns once more to undergo the cycle of saṃsāra.

Old age comes when looking in the mirror and the countenance has changed; ascending the steps, one’s physical strength declines. Alas! Now that one is already old, even the performance of prostrations and obeisances is failing.
The body is like a tree on a precipice; the mind is like a tortoise dwelling in water. Yet one still clings to outflows (*sāsrava*), refusing to study the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Suddenly struck by a deep and chronic illness, one thus becomes bedridden. Wife and children grieve in silence; friends weary of being near.
Piercing pain draws through a thousand vessels; moans resound to the four neighboring houses. Unaware of the perils ahead, one still indulges in greed and anger.
The vital essence and soul depart from the path of life; the wandering spirit enters the barrier of death. One hears only of millions departing, yet sees not a single person returning.

The precious horse stands neighing in vain; the courtyard flowers can never again be plucked. Having early sought the Unsurpassed Way, one should surely be spared from the mountains of the four directions.
*Record of the Dharma Hall of Yong’an in Fuzhou*, composed by the Layman Wujin (Linchuan Chen Zongyu).
While among the assembly of Elder Chang at Yong’an, Chen Zongyu attained great joy in the Dharma and donated his family assets.
He was building a *zhàngshì* (master’s chamber) and constructing a square, long corridor; meanwhile, he was amassing funds to renovate the Dharma Hall. However, Zongyu died.
His two sons wailed and appealed to Chang, saying, "Before our late father honored the Buddha, he was peaceful and strong.
Once he honored the Buddha, he became ill and passed away. Can the cause-and-effect of the Buddha be trusted? Or is it untrustworthy? Chang replied, "I..."
I am but a rustic elder; I am insufficient to serve as a model for you. You, my disciple, shall fulfill your father’s aspirations and complete my hall.
My late master had a chief disciple who attained the Dharma, known as the Layman Wujin. He had deeply entered the non-dual state and possessed unimpeded eloquence;

he skillfully expounded the Dharma according to the capacities of beings through his melodic voice. Once the hall is completed, I shall write a letter on your behalf to seek his instruction, so that he may resolve your doubts and ensure the succession of the lineage.
In the spring of the first year of the Xingyuan era, Chang sent Mingjian to Shanyang with a letter.
At that time, I had just been summoned back as a censor and had no leisure. The following year, Mingjian arrived in the capital again and waited for a reply at the Chizhai Chan monastery.

At that moment, the lay practitioner sat in silence within a single room, clearly perceiving the illusory nature of phenomena; though the iron wheel turned upon his crown, his body and mind remained in tranquil concentration. Mingjian—

Shedding tears and weeping with grief, he earnestly and repeatedly entreated the Great Compassionate Layman to serve as an external protector of the Buddha-dharma by entrusting it to kings and ministers.
"Now these sentient beings drift through the sea of suffering; they crave existence yet fear death, and are deluded regarding cause and effect.
I only pray that you, Layman, will act as a great King of Physicians and bestow upon them the medicine of the Dharma. The Layman replied, "Excellent, excellent! You are indeed capable of this."
From a distance of a thousand li, you have come as a disciple of the Chen family to inquire about the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, secret, and profound essentials of the Dharma.
Listen attentively to my words and hold them fast to inform others. Good son, within the great void of emptiness and stillness, the four marks arise delusively:

the accumulation of qi becomes wind; the accumulation of form becomes earth; the accumulation of yang becomes fire; and the accumulation of yin becomes water. These establish the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human) and disperse as...

All myriad things and all sentient beings are produced by the mutual friction of water and fire and the conjunction of form and breath. Possessing the four minor characteristics and the four great elements, they depend on birth for nourishment;
depending on nourishment, they require wealth; depending on wealth, they require accumulation; depending on accumulation, greed arises;

depending on greed, competition arises; depending on competition, anger arises; depending on anger, cruelty arises; depending on cruelty, delusion arises; depending on delusion, ignorance arises. This greed—
Hatred and delusion—these the Buddhas declare to be three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

Within a human lifespan of a hundred years, or ten years, or twenty years, or thirty or forty years, or fifty or sixty years, or seventy or eighty years, each such duration of life constitutes a minor kalpa (antarakalpa) for that person.
Within such a kalpa, humans may give rise to immeasurable transgressions.
Kalpa. It is like an earthworm wishing to ascend into smoke and clouds; such a thing is impossible.

The Buddhas, out of compassion, reveal the great gateway of skillful means of the *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) and exhort you to relinquish wealth. If you can relinquish your wealth, you can relinquish your attachment.
If you can relinquish your attachment, you can relinquish the [attachment to] dharmas. If you can relinquish your dharmas, you can relinquish the mind. If you can relinquish your mind...
One who can relinquish the body can, by relinquishing the body, relinquish the mind; one who can relinquish the mind can thereby accord with the Way.
Long ago, when the Venerable Kāśyapa was traveling to convert others, an old woman offered him rice gruel from a broken vessel.

After the Venerable had finished drinking it, he leapt into the void and manifested the eighteen transformations. As the old woman gazed up at him, her heart was filled with great joy. The Venerable said:

He said, "The merit of your giving is immeasurable. Whether as a human or a deva, as a Wheel-Turning King or Śakra, as one of the four fruits of sainthood, or even the Bodhi of a Buddha—whatever you wish for, there is nothing you shall not obtain. The old woman replied, "I seek only birth in heaven."
The Venerable One said, "It shall be as you desire; after seven days have passed, your life will end and you will be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to experience supreme and wondrous bliss.

Furthermore, the King of Kaśmīra was present in the Buddha’s assembly listening to the Dharma. Rising from his place, he said, "A Great Sage appears in the world once in a thousand kalpas, difficult to encounter.
Now I wish to resolve my mind to construct a vihāra; I pray that the Buddha grant me permission. The Buddha said, "Do as you see fit."
The King of Kaśmīra held a single stalk of bamboo and planted it before the Buddha, saying, "The vihāra is now completed. The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is.

Because this monastery contains and harmonizes with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and because such an offering surpasses the sands of the Ganges in merit, I have reflected upon these two principles for you.
Return and tell the donor: let him choose wisely for himself. As for the hall established by your father—

If one compares the merit of filling the halls, corridors, and eaves with a single vessel of rice-water, the blessing obtained is exceedingly great; there is no doubt that one will be reborn in heaven to enjoy bliss.
If compared to King Kapiṣa of Kaśmīra planting a single stalk of bamboo, which is able to encompass and harmonize the infinite Dharma-realm—if you wish to advance toward this, listen to my verse:
A single pole of tall bamboo erected for a monastery; The wind sweeps a gnat into the South Sea, where the foul water splashes it into a second.
Those of dull faculties miss the mark when asking about the first three.
Recorded by Huazang Wujinding as the Dharma Seal of Chan Master Zhenxie Liao of Changlu.
It has been over three hundred years since Dongping shattered the mirror, and over four hundred years since Longtan extinguished the lamp.
Descendants of later generations have become deluded regarding the true eye, claiming that the mirror was broken and the lamp extinguished;

they do not realize that while walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one radiates great light—the lamp has never truly been extinguished. Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing manifest before all phenomena; the mirror has never...

It has been broken before. Although a lamp has no shadow, it can illuminate the long night of birth and death; although a mirror has no pedestal, it can discern the delusions of birth, death, and Māra.
The light of the mirror and the lamp are eternally quiescent; clarity and the reflection of illusions are both like *tathatā*.
To shine upon things without end is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp"; to reflect them without end is called the "Inexhaustible Mirror. Daily life is never obscured; it is luminous and clear.
This is clearly manifest within the space between the mind and the eyes; yet sentient beings are deluded and do not know it.

Therefore, there is the teaching of the *Sūtras* which opens up skillful means that are like illusions: establishing an illusory *maṇḍala*, delivering illusory sentient beings, and performing illusory Buddha-activities.

It is like placing a single lamp at the center of the four cardinal directions—east, south, west, north—and the four intermediate directions, above and below, with ten mirrors set outside; these ten mirrors serve as a metaphor.

Regarding the ten dharma-realms: take a single lamp as a metaphor for the one true mind. While the principle of the one true mind is indivisible, the phenomena of the ten dharma-realms manifest in myriad forms.
Nevertheless, there are no phenomena outside of principle; there are no lamps outside of the mirror.

Although within each and every mirror there are infinite lamps, they are but a single lamp. Within each and every phenomenon there are inexhaustible principles, yet they are but a single principle. By means of this...
Because a single principle can accomplish diverse phenomena, there is the non-obstruction of thing and thing (*shishi wuai*).
Because a single lamp fully illuminates diverse mirrors, the mirrors intersect with one another. A single mirror, though motionless, is able to transform, contain, encompass, and enter [all others].
Without destroying a single phenomenon, that very thing is both this and that, both one and many; lords and retinues are harmoniously integrated, and every phenomenon is inexhaustible.
Alas! Sentient beings dwell amidst all atoms of dust, yet they do not know that these are all the inexhaustible ocean of lands of Vairocana.
Although Samantabhadra reveals a single pore, they do not know that within each and every pore there are three [realms] containing sentient beings.

Though they are obscured within the physical body, the daily activities of all sentient beings occur within the pores of Samantabhadra, emerge and subside within the radiance of Vairocana, and come forth from and enter into the pavilion of Maitreya. They traverse back and forth upon the edge of Mañjuśrī’s sword.
In every thought-moment, they arise together with all Buddhas, realize *bodhi*, turn the wheel of Dharma, and enter parinirvāṇa—like mirror reflecting mirror, like lamp meeting lamp.
The lamp. Throughout all things, at all times, it is universally pervasive, harmonious, and unobstructed; it is truly called the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation.
Were it not for sentient beings of great resolve, none could reach this mirror. Someone asks:
"Is the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing of our daily activities ultimately the lamp or not the lamp? Is it the mirror or not the mirror? The verse says:
The mirror, the lamp, the lamp, and the mirror are fundamentally without difference;
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are flowers before the eyes, yellow leaves drifting everywhere throughout the courtyard. A single sound of a mortar and pestle falls—whose house is it?
*Gāthās and Verses of the Various Patriarchs of the Chan Gate*, Part One of the Upper Section.
Recorded by Shi Ruyou of Wufeng, from the *Gāthās of the Patriarchs of the Chan Gate*, Volume IV, Part V:
The Lamp Record of Chan Master Dengming of Fodeng (Gushan).
Every person possesses an ancient mirror, shining brightly within the space between heart and mind; every individual possesses a true lamp, radiating brilliantly amidst the dust of sensory phenomena.
It is only because of a single thought that turns away from awakening and unites with the dust that this ancient mirror fails to manifest its clarity.

If the true lamp does not shine, there is no means to illuminate the darkness and delusion of birth and death. If the ancient mirror does not manifest its clarity, there is no means to reflect upon the false delusions of form and sound.
For this reason, beings remain immersed in the six realms and submerged in the three miserable paths; through hundreds and thousands of kalpas and lifetimes, by what means could they escape?
There was, however, a bodhisattva whose vow of compassion was vast and whose resolve to rescue and deliver all beings arose within his heart. Following the example of the former sages...
Regarding the ritual procedures: they are established like the metaphors of a lamp and a mirror. The lamp is the principle of the single reality; the mirror is the phenomena of differentiation.
To see the lamp but not the mirror is the totalization of principle; to see the mirror but not the lamp is the totalization of phenomena.

"A single lamp universally entering ten mirrors" means abandoning phenomena to accord with principle. "Ten mirrors universally encompassing a single lamp" means abandoning principle to accord with phenomena.
Mirrors and lamps interpenetrate one another, mutually harmonizing and fusing in infinite layers; this infinite layering is the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena.
Thus, within this, one perceives that every movement, turn, bow, or gesture is eternally [the manifestation of such non-obstruction].
Dwelling in the wondrous field of perfect enlightenment, all movements, shifts, and activities do not depart from the nature-ocean of Vairocana.

The skillful means of the mirror and lamp have reached their ultimate expression in these affairs. Having finished speaking thus in his mountain retreat’s secluded chamber, suddenly an old man appeared, questioning him with doubt:
"If a sudden Vairambha wind were to arise, where would the lamp be? When all patterns are melted away, where would the mirror be? Here—
"The principle is ineffable; the phenomena are ineffable; the site of perfect enlightenment is ineffable; the ocean of Vairocana is ineffable.
Ultimately, what is it? Huishì did not answer. After a long silence, he revealed it to him through a verse:
Tall pines and verdant bamboos intermingle; The bright moon and clear breeze share one household.
Deep in the night, the ancient hall is silent and still; Moths flutter their wings as they fall upon the lamp-flames.
*Written by Gāomài of the Chángmíng Lamps Sequence.*
The eyes of Li Lou may, while in a dark chamber, be unable to perceive the brilliance of a lamp;

the palm of Master Cheng may, in the deep of night, be unable to illuminate a lamp that is clearly present. Therefore, the Great Hero (the Buddha), through the power of skillful means, rescues those in the realm of darkness.
Relying upon his light, he guides those people. This is the lamp-light possessed by the Buddha, the light of the Dharma.
There is the meaning of the "transmission of the lamp. Generally speaking, the eternally burning lamp embodies its essence. Now, the sun presides over the day;
when the essence of the great yang reaches its midpoint, it rises in the south, and when it is in the south, it sets. Yet my eternally burning lamp does not set. The moon presides over the night;

when the essence of the great yin is full, it wanes, and when it wanes, it is exhausted. Yet my eternally burning lamp is never exhausted. If even the sun and moon are thus, how much more so the minor lights and minor [lamps]?

How clear! It is essential to know that the accumulation of suffering forms an ocean; yet when one lifts a foot, one finds oneself drowning in it. The accumulation of the heterodox forms a mountain; yet when one lifts a foot, one encounters its obstruction.
In the end, one cannot even approximate [the truth], or if one approximates it, one fails to achieve its fulfillment. To speak of this is enough to evoke a long sigh.
Within my own community, there is a preeminent talent who presides over this offering of lamps, having achieved mastery through diligent practice at Baorong Temple.
The Treasure Hall. Now, as for the incense of orchids burning with fire, I have seen its abundance, but never its depletion.

An iron basin filled with oil—I have seen it increase, but never see it diminish. Within a single lantern, the four seasons are perpetually spring; throughout the entire chamber, the year-long cycle is never night.
When people see this, they perform a prostration once, and their eyes receive benefit; they perform a prostration a second time, and their minds receive beauty. Thus, the mind...
The eye illuminates its own characteristics; thus, both the internal and external are thoroughly penetrated. Consequently, though one sees a lamp all day long, one has never failed to see the lamp;
though one does not see a lamp all day long, one has never failed to see the lamp. Such is the vision of the adept.

It is my thought that this does not stop at this alone; it shines directly upward, illuminating the first heaven, the second heaven, and even up to the thirty-three heavens, where no gate remains unopened.
Through this, as many virtuous people as there are grains of sand in the Ganges enter.

It shines directly downward, illuminating the first earth, the second earth, and even down to the eighteen hells, where every hell is opened. Through this, those who have committed sins for many kalpas emerge. If this is so, then...
"Can the empty space of the four intermediate directions, above, and below be measured, or can it not? My long-lasting jewel-marked lamp of merit is likewise so.
For several years I have desired to compose an inscription and eulogy for it, but I was pressed by base affairs and failed to do so.
One morning, I suffered from an eye ailment and my vision became blurred; I could not discern from where this [vision] had come. Thereupon, I dreamed of a divine being."
He said to Yu Mai, "Do you not owe something to this perpetual lamp? At these words, Mai attained awakening.
Awakening, he rose; rising, he composed a verse. The next day, his eyes were healed. The verse says: [Verse omitted as per instructions]
One sees the outer lamp shining eternally; one sees the inner lamp shining eternally. All evils are extinguished within this light; all virtues arise from within this light.
One does not see a single lamp, yet there are hundreds, thousands, ten millions, billions, and even an infinite number of lamps. One does not see a single person.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of people have returned to the Great Unity. Emptiness is form; form is emptiness.
Your disciple composes this verse: "Truly uphold that which is the Middle Way."
Section on Honoring the Sangha, composed by Master Mingjiao Song:
Teaching must honor the Sangha. Why is this so? As for the Sangha, they take the Tathāgata as their family, the Dharma as their body, wisdom as their life, and the joy of meditation as their food.
Therefore, they do not rely on secular surnames, do not cultivate a worldly lineage, and do not maintain physical form.
He was free from attachment to life and unafraid of death; he did not crave the five flavors. In guarding his person, he possessed precepts;

in restraining his mind, he possessed meditative concentration (*samādhi*); in discerning the truth, he possessed wisdom (*prajñā*). Regarding his precepts: they purified the three delusions so that his person remained untainted for the rest of his life. Regarding his concentration:
it stilled his thoughts and rectified his spiritual clarity, remaining undisturbed throughout the day. Regarding his wisdom: it honored virtue and distinguished the truth.
To be deluded yet certain—practicing with this is called the cause; accomplishing through this is called the fruit.
Regarding all things, there is kindness, there is compassion, there are great vows, and there is great benevolence. As for kindness, it is the constant desire to bring peace to all beings.
"Compassion" means constantly desiring to rescue all from suffering. "Vow" means vowing to see the True Dharma together with all under heaven.

"Beneficence" means bestowing the Right Dharma upon all living beings. To manifest it through spiritual penetration, even Heaven and Earth cannot obscure it; to practice it in secrecy, it remains hidden yet effective.
Spirits and deities could not fathom him. In expounding the Dharma, his eloquence was unimpeded;
in protecting the Dharma, he acted with reckless disregard for his own person. He could endure what others cannot endure and perform what others cannot perform.
Regarding his right livelihood, he ate food obtained by begging without feeling shame; regarding his few desires, he wore robes made of rags and mended bowls without considering himself poor. His...
He is without contention; he may be humiliated, but he must not be treated with contempt. He is without resentment; he may be made whole, but he must not be diminished.
He treats all things with sincerity and cultivates himself with supreme compassion. Therefore, throughout the world, he is able to ensure harmony and universal respect.
His words were never false; thus he was trustworthy. He reached the realization of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); thus he was humble.

Truly, he possessed a majesty worthy of reverence and a decorum worthy of emulation. When gods and humans beheld him, they were struck with solemn awe. He was able to bestow blessings upon the world and guide the common people.
In his state of formlessness, he would feed birds and beasts without stinting. In his recitation of the scriptures, he braved both cold and heat.
He does not abandon [the world], for he emerges from it by means of the Dharma. He wanders among humans through every village;
he regards fame as an echo in a valley, profit as drifting dust, and material forms as a mirage. He nurtures the poor and the sick.

Whether dwelling in a humble hovel or a noble palace, he does not feel abased, for he establishes himself by means of the Way. Even in deep mountains or remote valleys, wearing clothes of grass and eating food from the trees, he remains serene.

Yet they attain this for themselves; it cannot be enticed by profit, nor can it be bent by power. They decline the honors of the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords without considering themselves aloof.
In their solitude, they overcome themselves through the Way, so that even though their physical form and shadow lament together, they do not feel lonely.
In their communal living, they gather people from all under heaven without becoming confused with the crowd. That which can be learned—even the Three Pitakas and the Ten [Stages]—is...
He was not ignorant of the two vehicles or the various scriptures of the hundred schools and heterodox paths; he was not unacquainted with the languages of other regions and different customs.
In his ancestral transmission of the Dharma, there were both texts and chapters; in his practice of the Middle Way, he maintained that it is neither empty nor existent.
His ultimate learning was free from discursive thought and pure; it was purely true and of one suchness, no longer subject to further discrimination.
Furthermore, O Monks! As for his person, it is ultimate; as for his mind, it is vast; as for his virtue, it is complete; as for his Way, it is great.
That he is called "worthy" (xian) is not the worthiness spoken of by the world; that he is called "sage" (sheng) is not the sagehood spoken of by the world.
He is the transcendent and preeminent worthy and sage. Since the Sangha is such as this, how could they not be revered?
Master Yunfeng Yue gave a small public discourse (xiaocan):

"You lot, a group of young practitioners—since you have not studied the Sutras, Vinaya, or Shastras, you do not know them. You have entered the assembly to practice Chan, yet you do not understand Chan either.
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the matter? The Master said, "Truly so, all you Chan worthies! Go!"
The time of the Sages is remote; the hearts of men have grown thin. Looking at the monastic communities (*sōrin*) of the present day, they are no longer even worth looking at.

In every place, whether there be three hundred or five hundred monks, they spread themselves out in great numbers, considering only the abundance of food and drink and the comfort of their quarters as signs of a flourishing community.
Among them, not one or half a person is diligently devoted to the Way. Even if there were three...
Five of them. Up and down they go; half green, half yellow. Having understood, they all claim, "I have understood.

Each one considers themselves to be grasping the jade of the spiritual serpent—who would be willing to admit their error? Yet when they are confronted and struck with the whip, there is not even one in ten thousand who succeeds.
How bitter, how bitter! For this reason, the forests of Prajñā decline year by year, while the wild weeds of ignorance grow ever thicker.
Year by year they grow older. Nowadays, as soon as brothers enter the assembly, they sit upright with hands folded in formal posture, receiving the offerings of others.
Everywhere they go, they do not select a single stalk of vegetables nor carry a single bundle of firewood; their ten fingers never touch water, and they harbor no concerns for any worldly affairs.
Although this may bring them a momentary sense of satisfaction, how can it prevent the three miserable realms from burdening their future selves? Have you not seen the Teaching?
The Middle Way. It would be better to wrap one's body in glowing red-hot iron than to accept the robes of a person of faith;
it would be better to pour molten copper down one's throat than to accept the food of a person of faith.

Venerable Elder, if you truly are such a person, we would not consider it excessive to transform the great earth into gold and churn the long rivers into butter and milk to provide for you. But if you are not yet such a person, even a single drop—

"A single inch of water or a single thread of silk requires one to don fur and wear horns, pulling the plow and dragging the harrow, to repay the debt before it can be settled. Have you not seen it said in the Teachings:
'If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, they shall return in another body to repay the faithful offerings'? This is a matter of certainty; it will never be in vain.
Venerable Elders, time is precious; the moment does not wait for man. One day, when the light from your eyes falls to the ground, [you will be clad in] black..."

A field has no merit if one fails to contribute even a single basket of earth; the Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) involve the suffering of a hundred punishments—do not say that this is not the Way. Be careful.
This "Record of the Hall for Examining Conduct at Mount Nanyue" was composed by the Layman Chao Ran (Zhao Lingjin).
He once said: "Among all forms of suffering, the suffering of illness is the most profound; among all acts of merit, nursing the sick is the supreme. Therefore—
The ancients regarded illness as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and taught people that nursing the sick constitutes a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

This is why monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) were established for the sake of the elderly and the infirm. Today, when the community gathers in the monasteries, whenever anyone falls ill, they are sent back to the Hall of Repentance (*xingtang*).

This is not only so that they may cultivate repentance and reform their conduct to recover from their illness, but also because one desires that, amidst the dispersal of the assembly and the stillness of night, they may be illuminated by a solitary lamp.

To investigate and seek out the Great Matter—how could this be in vain? Having appointed the Hall Master (Zhītáng) to oversee medicines and tonics, and further instructing the monastic community (*chángzhù*) to provide for all necessities, these were the regulations established by the Buddhas of the past.
In recent times, it has not been so. The hall is named "Extending Life" (*Yǎnshòu*), a vulgar and unrefined name.

The sick do not reflect upon their own faults or exert themselves in self-correction; instead, they deviate from the proper method and administer medicine recklessly, resulting only in their own decline.
There are even those who suffer from chronic and severe illnesses yet do not participate in the hall activities, excusing themselves on the grounds of seeking leisure and seclusion;

this is a great failure to grasp the intent behind the construction and naming of the hall. To know that the name of the hall remains while its actual function is abandoned is to be like a mere passerby.

When the permanent residents are preoccupied with daily necessities and fail to provide care and comfort, they further miss the spirit of Upādāya [the Elder] in attending to the elderly and the infirm. Consequently, the sick person wallows in groans and pain.

The situation at Chu has grown increasingly extreme. The fault lies with those on this side; it is not the Tathāgata’s fault. Even when relatives and acquaintances come to inquire after one's illness, they are almost invariably old friends from the same village or district.
Since their concern is not universal, matters are often neglected or mishandled. Now, the infirmary (fǎlún) has been completely renovated and made anew.

This is because there are those who have realized their fundamental nature (*běnfēn rén*); they have settled every detail of this matter so that nothing remains to be discussed, save for the illness itself.
As for a person, how should they act? One should examine oneself and reflect upon one's transgressions; those in the world with discernment can all understand this.
For a patch-robed monk, the direct karmic conditions must be realized at the very moment the head aches and the brow burns; one must grasp that which stirs within.

Amidst the cries of grievance and the wailing of suffering, one must comprehend the mind that has reached its limit. One should investigate and contemplate in secret: who is it that suffers from this ailment? Who is the person?
Since it is not seen, from where does illness come? When both person and illness have vanished together, what else remains?
Even if you were able to see this with perfect clarity, you would still be just right for tending to others.

Vow of Chan Master Rán of Yishan I take refuge in the Teachers of the Ten Directions, the World-Honored Ones who regulate and guide; In the pure and subtle, wondrous Dharma they proclaim; And in the Sangha of liberation through the One Vehicle and the four fruits of realization.
I pray that you will bestow compassion and graciously accept me. It is only I, [Name], who have contravened my true nature and entered pointlessly into the current of delusion. Following...

Swept along by the tides of birth and death, one becomes greedily stained by the pursuit of forms and sounds. The ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) accumulate to form the causes of outflow (*āsrava*).
The six sense organs and six sense objects falsely commit boundless transgressions. One wanders in delusion within the ocean of suffering, deeply submerged on the path of error.

Clinging to self and indulging in others, one upholds the crooked and sets aside the straight. Amidst the karmic obstructions of successive lives and all manner of faults, I look up to the Triple Gem with compassion.

With deep sorrow, I offer my repentance with a single-minded heart. I pray that the Benevolent One (Amitābha) may rescue and deliver me, and that virtuous friends may guide me, leading me out from the profound source of afflictions to reach the further shore of Bodhi.
May the foundations of merit, life, and status in this world each flourish;

and may the seeds of wisdom and spiritual sprouts in future lives alike hope for growth and excellence. May I be born in the Central Land and always encounter enlightened teachers, so that my true nature may emerge.
In his home, he entered the Way in the state of a *kumārabhūta* (ever-true youth). His six sense faculties were keen and unimpeded; his three karmas were pure and harmonious.

Untainted by worldly conditions, he constantly cultivated the *brahmacarya*. Upholding the prohibitive precepts, he was not invaded by the dust of karma. He strictly guarded his dignified deportment so as not to harm even the smallest flying insect.
He did not encounter the eight difficulties nor lacked the four conditions. Thus, the wisdom of *prajñā* manifested before him, and his bodhicitta never regressed. He practiced the Right...
He realized the Dharma and awakened to the Mahāyāna. He opened the gateway of practice for the six *pāramitās* and crossed the ocean of kalpas of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
He erected the banner of the Dharma everywhere and shattered the net of doubt in its many layers. He subdued all demons and caused the Three Jewels to flourish.
He served the Buddhas of the ten directions without weariness, and having studied all dharma-gates, he attained complete mastery of them. He extensively performed meritorious deeds.
Bestowing grace that universally benefits beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one attains the six supernormal powers and perfects the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.

Thereafter, without abandoning the Dharma-realm, one enters everywhere into the realm of affliction; with a compassionate heart like that of Avalokiteśvara, one practices the ocean of vows of Samantabhadra.

In other lands and this world alike, one manifests physical bodies according to the various classes and forms of beings, proclaiming the wondrous Dharma even within the miserable realms of hell and the hungry ghosts.
Within the realm of hungry ghosts, some emit great radiance while others manifest various supernatural transformations.

All those who behold my form, or even hear my name, shall give rise to the bodhicitta and forever escape the suffering of saṃsāra. The lands of fiery cauldrons and icy rivers shall be transformed into fragrant groves;
those who drink molten copper and eat iron shall be reborn in the Pure Land; and those with fur and horns, burdened by their debts...

May all enmities be exhausted and all bitterness and suffering cease, so that everyone may be moistened by benefit and joy. In an age of pestilence, may they transform into medicinal herbs to heal deep-seated ailments;
in times of famine, may they transform into rice and grain to relieve the poor and hungry. May there be nothing beneficial that is not brought forth and honored.

Next, may those who were enemies or kin in past lives, as well as one's currently living relatives, emerge from the turbulent depths of the four modes of birth and abandon ten thousand kalpas [of wandering].
Bound by this love, may all sentient beings equally attain the Buddha-way. Though empty space may come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible;
may the animate and the inanimate together perfect the seed of omniscience.
Inscription on the Master of the Moon Forest Contemplating the Way:
The superior man who investigates the profound mystery must not let his time and energy be wasted in vain. To cross the river, one must use a boat; to benefit others, one must have resolve.
Names and forms are each different; they are neither one nor two. The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not manifold; within it there is no distinct artifice. It moves and strikes at the very pivot;
it is not the natural wisdom of a teacher. This is the thoroughgoing, compassionate heart of an old woman; it touches people without any taboo.
Within a single hair-tip of the Buddha-land, there is no place to hide or escape. Sing forth the song of Deshan; a true practitioner should act thus.
When Buddhas and Patriarchs appear, one must swallow their words and draw in one’s breath. Such is the strategic maneuver; it remains unchanged through all time.
Before the primordial chaos was divided, there already existed the land deed. It is inherently complete within every person, yet none are willing to turn their heads and look back.

Each and every one reaches their own native land; take care not to become attached to names and positions. All the Tathāgatas of the past were never apart from this very "Ai" (the sound of realization) right now.
Now the various Bodhisattvas receive their predictions in succession; the wise nod their heads in silent assent, for with an empty mind they have personally passed the examination.
The foolish do not believe or accept this; they abandon their homes and flee away. Alas! Awaken with vigorous introspection; this is the true livelihood manifest before you.
The application here is inexhaustible; it is the primary meaning of the Zen school. One encounters its source at every turn, yet never departs from the marketplace.
Those with copper heads and iron brows must have their foreheads touch the ground. May the merit of this be spread to all beings.
Master Baiyang said to Shun:
"The conditions for defilement are easily formed, while the path of practice is difficult to accomplish.

If you do not comprehend the myriad distinctions before your eyes, you will see only the vast winds of external objects blowing away the forest of merit, and the blazing fires of the mind burning up the seeds of Bodhi. Thus, the thought of the Way..."

If one acts with sympathetic mindfulness, it will take much time to achieve Buddhahood; yet, if one acts for the sake of the multitude as if for oneself, both self and others will accomplish their aims.

Seeing neither the faults of others nor one's own superiority, one will naturally show respect to those above and deference to those below. Thus, the Buddha-dharma will manifest from time to time, and one will be liberated from afflictions at every moment.
When rising from bed at dawn, recite this verse and mantra from the early hour of *yin* until evening.
May all sentient beings, even those who have perished beneath one’s feet, be reborn immediately in the Pure Land. Oṃ dharikṣali svāhā.
Mantra for washing hands and face:
*Kanyūgarāye svāhā*.
Verse and mantra for donning the *kāṣāya*: [Recite].
Excellent is this robe of liberation, the signless field of merit garment. I now receive it upon my head; may I wear it constantly in every lifetime.
Oṃ siddhye svāhā.
(Verse for entering the hall)
The sons of the Buddha dwell in this stage; it is the very enjoyment of the Buddhas. Walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they are always within it.

Ascending the bed—this verse describes ascending this bed of bliss and non-obstruction. Body and mind are equal, the four elements are healthy, and they abide eternally unmoving, beyond all power [to disturb them].
Destroying [all obstacles], may all sentient beings obtain the light of wisdom. Oṃ maṇidhāri hūṃ phaṭ.
Holding the alms bowl with the verse for receiving the vessel: May all sentient beings Accomplish this vessel And receive the offerings of devas and humans.
The Verse on Hearing the Hammer:
The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu; he attained enlightenment in Magadha; he preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī; he entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara.
The Verse on Spreading the Bowl.

The Tathāgata is the vessel of proper measure; I now have the opportunity to spread forth [the offerings]. May I, together with all sentient beings, realize the emptiness and stillness of the three wheels.
(The five contemplations are contained within the six recollections.)
Gatha for Offering Food:
O assembly of spirits and deities, I now offer this sustenance to you. May this food pervade the ten directions, shared by as many spirits and deities as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Namo samantabuddhānāṃ vaḥ hūṃ.
The Verse for Dispensing Water:
I now discard this water from my bowl; Its flavor is like ambrosial nectar. I bestow it upon you, the hosts of spirits and deities;
May you all obtain refreshing coolness. Oṃ ma-hū-ra-se svāhā.
Having finished eating, their physical strength and radiance were restored; majestic and awe-inspiring, they were heroes throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.
Turning causes into fruits without false thoughts, all the assembly attained supernatural powers.
Bathing Mantra for Purifying the Body:
Oṃ śrīye svāhā. Impurity-removing mantra.
Oṃ vajra-nāgata svāhā.
Pure mantra:
Oṃ hṛdaya svāhā.
Verse for Cleansing:
Oṃ hana mṛdite svāhā. Verse upon Hearing the Sound of the Bell.
Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light, wisdom increases, and Bodhi becomes fresh. May I attain Buddhahood to deliver all sentient beings;
may they emerge from hell and leave the fiery pit. Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
At all places and at all times, one should constantly make this vow:
"May the afflictions of the three obstacles be extinguished; may true wisdom be attained with perfect clarity.
May all karmic hindrances be universally eliminated, so that in every lifetime I may always practice the Bodhisattva path."
Cishi Chan Master’s Admonitions for the Assembly (The version by Shou Wuliang is largely the same, with minor differences).

When the assembly gathers for ascending the hall, chanting, reciting sutras, or informal sermons, all members must arrive first. This applies especially to superior practitioners who have traveled from afar.

The compass and square are always with you; how can you afford to be negligent? You will surely be scrutinized by others. One lapse may be excused, but what face do you have after committing it three times?
If you do not reflect upon the true spirit of Baizhang, you will see what Touzi meant when he said: "As soon as the sign for silence is hung, everyone should remain silent."
Even if you do not have [the portrait] hanging, how can you afford to speak or laugh? The ancient Buddhas bestowed this instruction: "Guard your mouth as one would a sealed jar.

Throughout the twenty-four hours of the day, you should always maintain silence. If the three karmas are not restrained, ten thousand calamities will secretly arise. Those who thoroughly understand the style of Lu Zu will simply hang their mouths upon the wall.
Before your own desk, keep it constantly clean; install only an incense case, a meditation staff, and sutra texts—this is what is valued.
Maintain a dignified and orderly appearance. Do not place secular writings upon it. Items such as medicinal bags and incense burners, as well as various necessities, should be kept beneath the desk.

Chanting aloud and creating a clamor among many people, leaning one's back against the edge of the desk to show contempt for the assembly, or occupying a seat in vain, and hanging objects by the bright window—these do not accord with the monastic code (*vinaya*).
How could they be permitted in a monastic community (*saṃghārāma*)? One should sit upright with a focused mind and silently open [the scriptures].

Investigate the meaning of the sacred words with earnestness until they accord with the ground of your own mind; only then will your opening of the scroll not be in vain, and you will truly understand how to study the scriptures.
At all times, fellow practitioners at the neighboring desks must strictly avoid whispering to one another. When guests visit, formal greetings cannot be avoided;

once the tea and soup have been served and the conversation concluded, escort each other out of the quarters and do not remain for long. If they are former companions from the past, [farewell them] when they have traveled far.
As fellow practitioners of the Way, we invite one another to the woods or by the water, where it is sufficient to converse with open hearts.

As for engaging in trade and commerce, which attracts miscellaneous worldly people—these are entirely not the deeds of a *śramaṇa* (monk) and may be struck through with a single stroke. After the rice gruel, return to the quarters and together extend greetings;
let the senior, middle, and junior seats take reverence as their priority. If it is otherwise, one is merely being disrespectful and arrogant toward others.
When releasing the birds at the end of the evening session, one must inform the attendants of the quarters. When entering or exiting by lifting the curtain, one should let the hand behind hang down.

When ascending the platform for seated meditation, one must not let the robes trail. In all movements and walking practice, it is better to take slow steps; causing others to harbor distracting thoughts makes demonic obstacles easily arise.

As the saying goes, "The tongues of the multitude can melt gold"—what joy is there for oneself in such circumstances? When washing clothes or handling needles, these tasks should be done after the midday meal; do not be hasty with non-urgent matters.
Diligence is required. The path of practice is vast and profound; one must not use a hot water pitcher to steam clothes, nor use the washstand to cut paper for lining bedsheets.
One must not steal to cook snacks or conceal medicinal herbs. One must know whether bamboo poles are pure or defiled when touching them, and observe whether the ironing board is at leisure or busy.
To cling to a single corner and fear the common use [of communal goods] is a mistake. The ancient sages mended their robes to ward off the cold; once the patching was finished, they left it at that.

How could one spend morning and evening attending to needles and thread, or boiling tea and serving soup? Only when the formal ceremonies of the monastic community are flourishing and the great assembly has gathered may one sit in full lotus posture.
When the cups and bags are withdrawn and everyone has retired together, to privately hoard leftover tea powder is to invite derision from onlookers. With but a single hand...
Regarding the practice of bowing to others: what is this ritual protocol? If you have a reason for not attending, you must inform the administrative office (*liao*).

You may sit briefly for tea, but this must not be avoided. When a newcomer enters the quarters, they should maintain an attitude of humility. Not yet familiar with the monastic regulations, they should inquire of the elders regarding the *vinaya* appropriate to their region;

the establishment of these rules depends upon the individual. As for settling one's bedding and arranging one's desk, there is no need for haste; through patient and detailed attention, things will naturally fall into place.

It is convenient and secure. Upon entering the quarters for tea service, one should act for the sake of the assembly with sincere intent. The tea must be consumed by all until it is finished. Household affairs should be settled as before;
once the hot water pitcher has been emptied, it must be refilled immediately. When traveling through the mountains or by the water, one must guard their speech and refrain from idle chatter.
To open one’s mouth like a bow and let words fly like arrows, or to pass judgment on others as a supervisor using yellow and black ink, or to speak only of food—[these are forbidden].

They speak of money; they scold the wind and revile the rain. Yet the walls have ears, and laws show no favoritism. Suddenly, one meets with injury from a tiger’s maw, only then seeing that the blade’s edge was far too exposed.
Whenever a cremation is encountered, people go together regardless of whether it is cloudy or sunny; each harbors a sense of sorrow and collectively exercises a heart of compassion.
Fearing that the deceased before them may have lived in vain or died a hollow death, they hold sutras and mantras in their mouths and carry firewood upon their shoulders. How could this be...?

One may act recklessly, indulging in loud talk and laughter; the auctioning of robes and bowls was originally intended to break the stinginess of the heart, yet later generations, unaware of this, instead gave rise to greed and attachment.
They would secretly measure lengths and sizes, surreptitiously scrutinize old acquaintances, and bid low prices for high-value items—faults exceeding those of ordinary merchants.

Unaware of their own transgressions, they still claim to be offering "good bargains. Observers looking on feel shame and sweat upon their faces. If this were at the Gate of the Sea (the marketplace),...
Sir, you are a distinguished guest of the Zen garden; pray do not merely form karmic ties for the deceased, lest you be ridiculed by the living.
Be gentle, kind, and compliant, so that your conduct may be observed as exemplary by those above and below. Arrogance and conceit are not protected by the sages.

Within the eighty thousand subtle practices and three thousand dignified manners, you should be seen at every turn throughout the six periods of the day and night. To pass straight through the hall—how could you bear such shame? [The Master] was in the vacant hall.
To act thus would surely invite meager merit. To step onto the hall in disrobed garments, to roam the mountains in straw sandals, or to tread upon the Dharma Hall—these are all improper.

One should yield to the senior monks. Washing one's face at the fifth watch of the night is intended for the sake of cultivation; yet to spit while clutching the basin creates a clamor that disturbs the assembly.

To harbor thoughts in secret darkness is to remain ignorant of oneself. As days pass and months come, the face turns yellow and the body grows thin. Use the bath water sparingly, and let the counting sticks rest.
I pick up the subject: Though one may perform much merit, it is not as good as avoiding transgressions. Spitting in the corridors and spitting on desks violates the sages and worthies;
acting according to one's own whims, one must examine oneself at every moment and guard against faults at every step. One must truly humble the body and mind, yet broaden the capacity of one’s heart.

During the ten days of the *zhīliáo* (period of communal living), you shall provide for one another in turn; sleep late in the evening and rise early in the morning, making diligence your primary concern.
Truly, it is a matter of bitter earnestness and mental toil. Put others first and yourself last. Regarding the robes and bowls of the great assembly, one must exercise the utmost vigilance;

if even a single matter is neglected, the minds of all will be disturbed. When brewing tea, sweeping the floor, changing the water, or preparing the incense, ensure that the hot water pitcher does not grow cold, so as to spare the Chan practitioners from vexation.
Within the quarters, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) must strive to be gentle and harmonious, leading by example in the observance of regulations and setting a standard for himself.

Regarding the regulations for the meditation hall: one must follow the seasonal protocols and proceed directly to the essential points in one’s discourse. Should there be any deficiency, the assembly shall deliberate together.

When traveling through mountains or enjoying the waters, one’s comings and goings must be timely. Even a practitioner of ill temper should be exhorted with kind words; if they do not comply, report it privately to the Abbot.
Protecting the virtuous and shielding against evil ensures the trust of the donors. When shaving the hair and gathering around the brazier, propriety requires humility and deference. The above.
These regulations have been explained to you in detail. During your daily activities, each of you must remain vigilant. A single push can turn the wheel; there is no need for further praise.

If called three times and not returning, what is the use of being gathered together? Furthermore, the dust of the mind is difficult to sweep away, and the water of one's nature easily becomes turbulent.
Those of middling capacity and middling faculties may be superior or inferior; when Ke-bin failed in the battle of the Dharma, he was once punished by having his rice porridge drilled with a needle.

In one hall, Wenyuan and Shenglie contended over Chan; Shenglie lost two steamed buns. This became a model for the monastic community, and later students followed it. Jiaoshan did not speak of two kinds of Chan; he simply wanted to impose a fine of sixteen taels of oil.

The verse says: A single hall, Wenyuan and Shenglie vied for Chan; Shenglie lost two steamed buns. This became a precedent for the forest of monks; Later students followed its lead. Jiaoshan spoke of no two kinds of Chan; He only required a fine of sixteen taels of oil.
The turtle’s head was suddenly scorched by the moxa; for a thousand ages it has caused people to laugh without end.
I urge the younger generation to keep their eyes wide open: do not let yourself be fined a pound of oil.
The Inscription on Seated Meditation by Master Focin:

As for those who practice seated meditation, they straighten their bodies and rectify their intentions; they purify themselves and empty their minds. With legs crossed in the full lotus posture, they withdraw their gaze and turn their hearing inward.

Vigilant and unclouded, forever free from sinking and agitation. Even if recollections arise, cast them all away with total abandon. In a state of stillness and concentration, observe with right mindfulness:
know that it is this mind that sits, and reflect back upon this mind. Know that it is this mind which possesses existence, non-existence, middle, extremes, inner, and outer.
This mind is empty yet cognizant, quiescent yet illuminating; it is perfectly clear and lucid, falling neither into nihilism nor eternalism—a numinous awakening.

This is transcendent. It selects that which is not false or delusive. Now, when we observe those of the lineage who exert themselves in seated meditation yet fail to awaken, their ailment arises from reliance on conceptual calculations and the attachment of the mind to partiality and deviance.
They are deluded and turn their backs on the true cause, pointlessly following the dictates of cessation and activity. The failure of their lack of awakening lies precisely here.
If one can gather and clarify a single thought, one will secretly accord with the non-arising [of phenomena]. Wisdom-mirroring becomes vast and open, and the flower of the mind suddenly blossoms.

Boundless attachments are instantly ground away; the ignorance accumulated over kalpas is revealed all at once. It is like suddenly remembering what was forgotten, or like a chronic illness being cured in an instant.
Joy arises within; the mind knows for itself that one shall become a Buddha, and only then does one believe that there is no Buddha other than one's own mind.

Thereafter, one follows this awakening to cultivate further; through cultivation, realization is attained. The source of this realization is the three non-differentiated states, known as the Samādhi of Single Practice and Single Understanding, also called the Path of Effortlessness.
One is then able to transform phenomena without departing from the sense organs and their objects.

With a hand of faith, whatever is grasped becomes manifest; principal and attendant elements are mutually distinguished. The eyes of heaven and earth are cleansed, and the succession of past and present is renewed once more—a divine spirit encountered in its very essence.

The capacity [of the mind] naturally accords with its conditions; thus, Vimalakīrti said: "To manifest all dignified postures without arising from the samādhi of cessation—this is true seated meditation.
Indeed, one should know that when the water is clear, the moon appears; when the mirror is polished, the light is complete.

For those who study the Way, seated meditation is essential. If this is not so, one will wander through the long journey of saṃsāra, sinking and drowning within the four modes of birth—a sight that makes one’s nose sting with sorrow.

It pains my heart; I can hardly remain silent. I have briefly recorded these general outlines to assist in the realization of the True Source. If one does not abandon cultivation, this is precisely the *Sāṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (The Accordance of Principles).
This is the preface to Master Ci'en’s renunciation of the world.
Why leave home and renounce the world? With palms joined before the King of Emptiness, one seeks liberation. With three masters and seven witnesses, the beginner’s path is established.

Shaving the head and donning the dyed robes, one makes the great vow: to abandon greed and anger, and to eliminate base stinginess. One must be diligent and careful throughout the twelve periods of the day.
Refining the true nature until it is like empty space, one will naturally fight back and defeat the armies of Māra. Diligently study the teachings and seek out a teacher.
The Master says: This may be relied upon by the practitioner; do not allow the mind-ground to become as chaotic as tangled hemp.

A hundred years of life pass away in vain. Follow the former sages and emulate the ancient Buddhas; all that is realized relies upon hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one must be truly focused.
Only when every thought is unborn does one begin to accord with reality. The Buddha’s true scriptures, the twelve divisions, point directly and extensively toward Bodhi.
Tilou! If you do not practice, do not study, and do not act accordingly, I ask you: on what day will your mind open to awakening?

You must save yourself with urgency, as if your head were on fire; do not wait for next year or the year after. When a single breath does not return, that is the next life—who can guarantee that this body will remain firm?
Do not wear silk; do not eat the fruits of the fields. It is through the sweat and blood of weavers and plowmen that the fruit of the Path is accomplished.
The fruits of the Path have not yet been realized; how can one hope to repay what has been bestowed? Alas, father! Alas, mother! You swallowed the bitter and spat out the sweet in great hardship;
you nurtured me by taking up moisture and turning back dryness. I must inherit the family tradition and continue the lineage of my ancestors—suddenly, here it is.

I seek to shave my head and become a renunciant. At eighty or ninety years of age, with no one to rely upon, if you do not transcend the mundane and enter the stream of the sages, to remain thus in procrastination would be a complete and great error.
With the *kṣetrapatya* robe and the dragon-subduing bowl, enjoy them for the rest of your life to seek liberation.
If you bind your mind to petty gains, how can you reach the other shore of Nirvāṇa? Good son, you must know that spiritual practice is difficult.
It is as if we have encountered the present age. If one can leave the household life and don the coarse hempen robes, it is like a piece of floating wood meeting a blind turtle.

Great man, you must be fierce and sharp; restrain your body and mind with vigilance and do not be casual. If you can allow the power of practice and vows to support one another, you will certainly receive a personal prediction of enlightenment at the Dragon Flower Assembly.
The Great Master Chan Yue’s Admonition to a Novice Monk (the meaning of the twenty verses by Cishou is the same):

I urge you to leave the household life; you must resolve your will with determination. To enter under a teacher and study the Way, do not be casual. Add incense and change the water to form karmic conditions;

diligently sweep the Buddha halls and the monks’ quarters. Do not wander idly; do not play or frolic. When entering or leaving, distinguish between the formal and the informal, and speak with clarity.
Having stayed for three mornings and four nights, you have not seen him return. When has the wondrous Dharma ever been heard in even a single verse?
Venerate your seniors; let your juniors teach you. Do not vie for prestige within the Gate of Emptiness. Whether in the upper, middle, or lower seats, employ humility and harmony.

Do not disparage others to exalt yourself. Clothing and food are difficult to obtain—how could they be easy? One must feel shame regarding the measure of one’s merit. Eat and drink as circumstances permit.
Whether refined or coarse, there is no need for a thousand ways to seek the exquisite. Wear simple cloth and hemp garments; adapt to the times as they come.

When one is content, one immediately transcends the stage of karmic fruition. How could true ability be measured by fine silk robes? If one possesses the Way, what need is there for yellow brocade quilts? O laymen of pure faith and laywomen of pure belief:
to cast away one’s own body to feed a starving tiger—this causal condition is the bitterest of all sufferings. There is no need to say it again and again.
Bitter and poignant. When there is sin within the heart, one knows it by oneself; one must personally repent before the heart.

Seek out a true master and study wisdom. While others sleep, you may sleep soundly. Those who have left the household life study the wondrous principle; when practicing recitation, you must rise early.
If you sleep until the fourth watch after falling asleep at the third, return to the hall of the Honored One Śākyamuni, light a bright lamp, and change [your robes].
Pure water. Prostrate and burn incense to bring forth blessings; repay the debts of the three realms of existence and the four debts of gratitude.
May the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings rejoice. Be neither deluded nor indolent; leap directly beyond to enter the realm of the Buddha. Walking is Zen; sitting is Zen.
Thoroughly realize the True Suchness of Avalokiteśvara.
The four debts of gratitude are: heaven and earth, one's parents, the sovereign and patrons, and teachers and friends. The three jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
The three realms of existence are: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.

Emperor Renzong praised the merit and fruit of a monk’s renunciation, saying it is truly difficult to discuss: "A single piece of the *kāṣāya* is honored by all. To a layman, one speaks only of the body as not being noble;
yet once he becomes a monk, he is a descendant of the Dharma King. With hands folded before him in the hall, he pays court to the Son of Heaven; in the sanctuary, he bows with a lowered waist."
Even if one were to grind one's bones and crush one's body for thousands of millions of kalpas, it would still be difficult to repay the kindness of Śākyamuni.

Chan Master Yongming Shou’s admonition to those entering the path of study contains nothing extraordinary; he simply requires that one cleanse the sensory faculties and their objects, thereby eliminating the karma accumulated over immeasurable kalpas.
This is the seed of consciousness. You need only be able to dissolve emotional attachments and sever delusive conditions;
regarding all worldly objects of desire, let your mind be like wood or stone. Even if you have not yet clarified the eye of the Way, you will naturally achieve a pure body.
If you encounter a true and authentic teacher, you must with earnest diligence draw near to them. Even if you practice without yet reaching full penetration—

Though they have studied but not yet perfected it, these words shall pass through their ears and forever serve as seeds for the Way. From lifetime to lifetime they shall not fall into the evil realms;
from birth to birth they shall never lose their human form. As soon as they emerge from the womb, hearing this once, they shall awaken to a thousand truths.

You must know that true and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) are the greatest causal conditions among men, for they teach and transform sentient beings so that they may realize the Buddha-nature. Alas, I lament the final age, wherein [people] speak deceptively.

The first type of Chan practitioner merely studies empty verbiage and possesses no genuine understanding at all. Step by step they walk in existence, yet mouth after mouth they discourse on emptiness.

They do not reproach themselves for being dragged along by the power of karma, and furthermore, they teach others to deny cause and effect. They then claim that drinking alcohol and eating meat do not obstruct Bodhi;

that committing theft and engaging in sexual misconduct do not hinder Prajñā. Consequently, in life they encounter the king’s law, and in death they fall into the Avīci Hell, where they receive their retribution.

When the karma of the hells has been exhausted, one enters the realms of animals and hungry ghosts, where there is no prospect of escape for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, unless one turns the light back upon itself in a single thought-moment, immediately transforming the heterodox into the orthodox.
If one does not personally repent, personally regret, personally deliver oneself, and personally cultivate, [one will remain lost].
Even when the Buddhas appear in the world, there is no place where they can save you. If cutting out your heart and liver were as if dealing with wood or stone, then you might eat meat.
If drinking wine were as if drinking excrement and urine, then you might drink wine.

If seeing handsome men and women were as if seeing corpses, then you might engage in sexual misconduct. If seeing your own wealth and the wealth of others were all like dung and soil, [then you might practice non-attachment].
"You may then proceed to commit acts of aggression and theft. Even if you reach such a state, it will still not accord with your intentions.

Only when you have realized the body of immeasurable sages can you truly engage in the affairs of the world, whether they be adverse or favorable. How could the prescriptions of the ancient sages have any other intent?"

It is solely because monks and nuns in the Dharma-ending age rarely maintain the precepts and Vinaya that they fear misleading virtuous laypeople and causing many to retreat from the path of enlightenment;
therefore, extensive prohibitions and protections have been established. As stated in the thousands of sutras and expounded in the ten thousand treatises:
if one does not abandon lust, one cuts off all seeds of purity; if one does not abandon alcohol, one cuts off all seeds of wisdom; if one does not abandon theft, one cuts off...
It is the seed of all merit; if one does not remove the flesh, one cuts off the seed of all compassion.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time proclaim this with one voice, and the Chan school throughout the world expounds it with a single resonance. Why do later students largely fail to heed this, destroying the true cause for themselves and instead practicing the teachings of demons?
It is solely because of the seeds of karma from past habituation that they encounter false teachers in this life, causing their power of goodness to easily dissipate.
The roots of evil are difficult to uproot. Have you not seen the path of the ancient sages? To see a single demonic deed is like ten thousand arrows piercing the heart;

to hear a single demonic sound is like a thousand awls boring into the ears. You must distance yourselves from them with all haste; they must not be seen or heard. Each of you must investigate your own mind.
Be careful not to treat this lightly.
Master Gu (Master Jing) has declined his residence at Gushan.
My upright eye opens above the crown of my head; the Golden Grain manifests its divided bodies and arrives in such a manner. For a time, he shall bring rain to the Three Mountains.
Lu has returned at once to season the cauldron as salt and plum.

Of this old and sickly life remaining, those who transcend it are rare. I am ashamed to lack the Way and virtue to awaken the deluded masses; yet your gracious light is as vast as mountains and peaks.
I beg only to be granted the freedom of a solitary cloud to fly as I please.
Minister Hu Shangshu He requests again:

The wind and smoke over the stone drums remain grimly unopened. I, who dwell upon this mountain, truly await the Living Tathāgata. How pitiable that ten thousand monks have long since bent their hearts toward you;
Thirsting for your presence, they daily gaze at plums to quench their longing.
The single nature, perfectly luminous, is rare in this world. Why begrudge the divided lamp-light to illuminate the deluded masses? If they trust in conditions, they will surely awaken and rise;
with staff in hand, they shall soar through the void like cranes.
Dongshan’s Letter to His Parents (A Brief Summary of the Main Points; the "Ten Reasons for Not Returning" verse is not included here).
I have humbly heard that when the Buddhas appear in the world, they all receive their bodies from their parents;

when the myriad species arise and flourish, they all rely on Heaven and Earth for their protection and sustenance. Thus, none can be born without parents, and none can grow without Heaven and Earth; all are sustained by their nourishment.
We all receive the virtue of being sheltered and sustained by the grace of our parents’ upbringing. Alas! All sentient beings and the myriad forms of phenomena belong to impermanence;

none have escaped birth and death. Although the affection for nursing is heavy and the kindness of rearing is profound, even if one were to provide worldly wealth and provisions, it would ultimately be difficult to repay them.
How could serving as their sustenance through blood and food last forever? Thus, the *Classic of Filial Piety* says:
Even if one provides the nourishment of the three sacrificial animals daily, it is still not filial piety. Thus, people pull each other down into the depths, entering the cycle of *saṃsāra* forever.
To repay the boundless and profound kindness [of one's parents], nothing compares to the merit of leaving the household life.

By cutting across the river of craving in birth and death and crossing the bitter sea of afflictions, one repays the parents of a thousand lifetimes and answers the grace of compassionate kin for ten thousand kalpas. Within the three realms of existence, there is no [greater way] to repay the four debts of gratitude.
There can be no repayment for this. Thus, the Sūtra says: "If one son leaves the household life, the nine generations of his clan will be reborn in heaven.
I, Liang-jia, renounce my body and life in this present existence and vow never to return home; with these faculties and sense-objects throughout eternal kalpas, I shall suddenly realize Prajñā.

I humbly entreat you, Father and Mother, to open your hearts and joyfully relinquish [your attachment], letting your minds cease from clinging to objects. May you emulate King Śuddhodana and follow the example of the Holy Queen Māyā.
At another time, on another day, we shall meet again at the Buddha’s assembly. On this very day, at this very moment, we part for now. It is not that I am suddenly departing from my filial duty;

rather, it is because time does not wait for man. Thus it is said: "If this body is not delivered in this present life, when else will this body be delivered? I humbly hope that Your Reverence will not keep me in your memory. A verse says: When the time comes, we shall meet again; For now, we must part. I do not hastily forsake my sweet and tender parents, But time does not wait for man.
Therefore I say: "If this body is not delivered in this life, When else shall this body be delivered? I pray you, do not hold me in your thoughts. A verse says:

Failing to realize the source of the mind, I have seen the seasons pass; I sigh instead at how I have idly delayed in this pure world. How many have attained the Way within the gates of emptiness? Only I remain mired in the dust of the mundane world.
I respectfully prepare this letter to bid farewell to your affection, vowing to clarify the Great Dharma as my repayment for your parental kindness.
There is no need to shed tears or remember me often; it would be as if I had never existed from the very beginning.

White clouds beneath the crags are my constant companions; the green peaks before me serve as my neighbors. I shall avoid the pursuit of worldly fame and profit, forever parting from human love and hatred.
The Patriarch’s intent is to bring understanding directly beneath a word; the profound mystery must be penetrated through the truth within a phrase.
Should you wish to see all your kinsmen and kin, you must simply await the cause for realizing the fruit in the future.

This letter follows from the time I, Liang-jia, departed from sweet delicacies to travel south with my staff. Ten autumns have already passed since the changing of the stars and frost, and I have traversed ten thousand li along winding paths.
I humbly hope that you, my lady, have restrained your mind to yearn for the Way and gathered your thoughts to return to emptiness, ceasing all longing for separation.
Put aside these feelings of separation; do not harbor expectations like one gazing through the gate-bar. As for the affairs of the household, let them proceed as they naturally do for the time being;

they will only increase further and further, adding to your daily afflictions. Elder brother, you must diligently practice filial piety, seeking it with the persistence of a man fishing for fish in ice.

Younger brother, I shall exert all my strength to serve you, weeping like a bamboo shoot in the frost. When a wife dwells in this world, she must cultivate herself and practice filiality to remain in harmony.

Heavenly Heart. A monk dwells within the Gate of Emptiness; longing for the Way and practicing Chan, he seeks to repay the virtue of his parents' kindness. Now, separated by thousands of mountains and ten thousand waters, the two paths lie far apart.
With these eight lines on a single sheet of paper, I briefly extend my humble thoughts. The verse says:
Seeking neither fame nor profit, nor the ways of Confucius, I aspire to the Gate of Emptiness and abandon the ranks of the laity. When afflictions are exhausted, the fire of sorrow is extinguished;

where affectionate ties are severed, the river of craving dries up. Led by the fragrant breeze of the precepts and meditative concentration of the six faculties, supported by the power of wisdom that realizes non-arising in a single thought—this is my way of repaying my mother in the north chamber;
cease your longing, for she is as if dead, as if non-existent.
My daughter’s reply:
I and you have long shared a karmic affinity. Only now have we first bound ourselves together through the bonds of motherhood and affection.

Since I became pregnant, I prayed to the gods and Buddhas, vowing that a son might be born. When the months of gestation were complete, my life hung by a thread; yet, my heart’s wish was fulfilled like a precious jewel.
I cherished you as a treasure; I never loathed the foulness of excrement, nor did I grow weary of the toil of nursing you.
Once you had reached maturity, I sent you away to pursue your studies. When you failed to return for even a short time, I would gaze longingly from my door.

Your letter insists that you must leave the household life, yet your father is deceased, your mother is old, your elder brother is destitute, and your younger brother is cold-stricken. On whom can I rely? You have the heart to abandon your own mother.
A mother has no heart that can abandon her child. Ever since you departed for another land, I have constantly shed tears of sorrow day and night.
Alas, alas! Since you have now vowed not to return home, I shall grant your wish;

I dare not hope for you to be like Wang Xiang, who lay upon the ice, or Ding Lan, who carved wood, but I only pray that you will be like the Venerable Maudgalyāyana, delivering me so that I may escape this deep sinking into suffering.
Ascending to the fruit of Buddhahood—had it not been for me, there would have been grounds for retribution in the unseen realm. You must take this to heart.
*The Ten Oxherding Songs of Chan Master Zhenxie Qingliao of Kuang’an on Liangshan:
Seeking the Ox*

It has never been lost from the beginning; why then seek it? It is because one turns one's back on awakening that estrangement arises, and by turning toward sensory objects that one ultimately loses it.
The home mountain grows ever more distant, and the forked paths suddenly diverge. Gain and loss blaze forth, and the beacon fires of right and wrong erupt.

In haste, they brush away the weeds to pursue their search; the waters are broad, the mountains distant, and the path grows ever deeper. Their strength is spent and their spirits exhausted, with no place to find it;
they hear only the evening cicadas singing among the maple trees.

Those who perceive traces rely on the scriptures to interpret their meaning; they examine the teachings to recognize the footprints [of the Buddha]. They clarify that the various vessels are but a single metal and realize that the myriad things are themselves.
When right and wrong are not distinguished, how can the true and the false be differentiated? Until one has entered this gate, such provisional understanding is merely "perceiving traces."
Traces abound by the waterside and beneath the forest trees; can you not see them through the fragrant grasses and the open fence?
Even in the deepest recesses of the remote mountains, how could he hide his nostrils from the vast heavens?

Seeing the ox, one enters through sound; seeing the place, one encounters the source. In each and every engagement of the six sense-faculties, there is no discrepancy; in every movement and function, it is manifest head-on.
It is like the taste of salt in water or the presence of blueing agent in dye; even before you raise your eyebrows, it is not some other thing.
The oriole calls out note after note upon the branch; The sun is warm, the breeze gentle, and the willows by the bank are green. There is no place here to hide or evade;
