These towering, formidable features are difficult even for a painter to capture.

I have found the ox that was buried long ago in the outskirts; today I have encountered it. Because the environment is so sublime, it is difficult to pursue; yet, longing for the fragrant thickets, my attachment does not cease.
My stubborn heart still harbors vigor, and my wild nature persists. If I wish to attain pure harmony, I must apply the whip and the lash.
Exhausting all supernatural powers, one may reach its source; yet it is difficult to remove even with a strong heart and robust strength.
Only at times does one briefly reach the high plateau, only to enter again and dwell deep within the clouds and mist.
When tending cattle, as soon as a thought arises before, the subsequent thought follows it. Through awareness, it becomes true; through deluded sentiment, it becomes false.
It exists not only in the external object, but arises solely from the mind. The nose-rope pulls firmly, allowing no room for deliberation.
The whip is never far from one's person at all times; for fear that it might wander off into the dust.
When herded together until they are pure and harmonious, though bound by halter and chain, they follow people of their own accord.

Riding the ox, the clash of arms has already ceased; gain and loss are likewise non-existent. Singing the village songs of the woodcutters and blowing the wild flutes of children, he rests his body across the ox while his gaze is fixed upon the clouds and the sky.
He cannot be called back, nor can he be caught or confined.
Riding the ox, I proceed leisurely as I wish to return home; the flute’s notes, slightly off-key, accompany the fading evening glow.
With every stroke and every breath, there is boundless meaning—what need is there for those who understand to puff their lips and grind their teeth?

The Dharma of forgetting the ox is the non-dual Dharma. Let the ox serve as the thesis; it is like the distinct names "fish" and "hare," which reveal the differences between their crouching and their tracks.
Like gold extracted from ore, like the moon emerging from clouds, a single beam of cold light shines beyond the kalpa of Bhīṣmagarjita.

Having already mounted the ox, one has reached the mountain of one's home; both ox and man are empty, and all is at ease. When the red sun has reached three *gān* [of its height], one is still dreaming;
the whip and tether lie idly within the thatched hall.
When man and ox are not seen, ordinary sentiments fall away and the holy intent is entirely empty. Where there is a Buddha, one need not linger;

where there is no Buddha, one must swiftly pass through. Not clinging to either extreme, it is difficult for a thousand sages to perceive. The hundred birds holding flowers—what a scene of shameless confusion!
Whips and ropes, people and oxen—all belong to emptiness. The azure sky is vast and boundless; truly difficult to penetrate. Upon the red furnace, how can snow be tolerated?
Only upon reaching this point can one harmonize with the ancestral source.

Returning to the root and restoring the source, one is originally pure and does not admit even a speck of dust. Observing the flourishing and decay of conditioned forms, one dwells in the stillness and silence of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is not like illusory transformations; how could it depend upon cultivation or maintenance? With waters clear and mountains green, one sits and observes success and failure.

To return to the root and revert to the source already requires great effort; how much better it is to be directly like one who is blind and deaf. Within the hermitage, one sees nothing of what lies before it;
the water flows on boundlessly, and the flowers are naturally red.
Entering the marketplace, he extends his hand;
the thatched gate stands alone closed. The thousand sages do not know him as he buries his own brilliance and neglects the tracks left by former worthies.
Carrying his gourd-bowl into the market and leaning on his staff as he returns home, he transforms wine shops and fish stalls, leading them all to Buddhahood.
Baring his chest and barefoot, he enters the marketplace; smearing dust and ash, his cheeks are full of smiles.
Without needing the true secret instructions of the immortals, he causes withered wood to burst forth into bloom.

It was only upon obtaining Master Tanyou’s *Diagram of the Six Oxen* that I first received instruction from my spiritual mentor and immediately gave rise to faith. Once this faith had sprouted, it became the eternal foundation for the Way;
thus, there is a single white dot atop the head of each ox.

A single thought of faith is the foundation; it is the cause for entering the Way throughout a thousand lifetimes. I pity myself for being deluded regarding the nature of awakening, becoming defiled by dust and grime wherever I go.
Wild grasses turn green from time to time; mad flowers bloom anew day after day. Yearning for home, I have no means to reach it; I can only feel my tears soaking my kerchief.
Once faith has sprouted, one polishes and refines it moment by moment until, suddenly, illumination dawns. A joy arises in the mind;
this is the very first entry point, which is why the head is entirely white.
Inquiring after this ox: Why is it so late in realizing its error? Having abandoned its home for many kalpas, it has pursued delusion for so long a time.
Moment by moment, return to thoughtlessness; thought after thought, sever the object of thought. From this point, the entryway begins; step by step, one realizes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Having already attained illumination, one gradually undergoes refinement through cultivation; wisdom becomes clear and pure, yet not yet entirely unified.
With half the body turned white, one observes the herds for many autumns and springs, becoming a cow of the open field that has left the fragrant grass behind to roam near the Snowy Mountains.

Although right mindfulness has returned to oneness, perverse thoughts still flow in confusion. When one is suddenly liberated and both mind and its traces are exhausted, the six sense bases can no longer contain it.
There are no further deluded thoughts; there is only the single true mind—pure, serene, and profoundly still, with the entire body becoming luminously clear.
The six sense bases cannot encompass it; the *udumbara* flower blooms within the fire. Utterly free from attachment, it is luminously pure and devoid of even a speck of dust.
Ropes and cords are rendered useless; where are the man and the ox? Far beyond the void of kalpas, neither Buddhas nor patriarchs can fathom it.
Mind and phenomena are both forgotten; man and ox are both obliterated. Forever transcending the realm of forms, there remains only the emptiness of emptiness.
This is called the Great Gate of Liberation, the life-vein of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

The news of man and ox is exhausted; the ancient path has lost its connoisseurs. The mists roll away and a thousand crags fall silent; moss grows thick upon the three narrow paths. The mind is empty and possesses nothing;
feelings are spent and do not belong to the present. Where is the old fisherman holding his line? The Panxi Stream is locked in green shade.
At the point where the life-faculty is severed, one passes away and returns to life again, receiving a body according to one's kind and performing acts as the occasion demands;
it is only the person of old that changes, not the place of one’s former conduct.
Exquisite and ultimate, yet again reaching through and beyond; returning once more to the midst of the six realms. In every mote of dust lies the Buddha-work; in every place resides the family style.
Like white jade distinct from the mud, like refined gold encountered within the fire. Wandering freely upon the path of no interval, drifting like a tumbleweed according to one's kind.
The Moon Cave’s Instruction for Novices (Chan Master Qing):
Listen, you novices, to my admonitions: "The high is founded upon the low; the vast arises from the minute. Throughout antiquity and the present, the sages and saints..."

There is nothing that does not proceed from this. Among the Confucian masters there are many such examples; among the followers of Śākyamuni, they are even more numerous. I shall not cite them at length here, but will briefly mention two or three.

Even the supreme sovereigns of the Yu and Xia dynasties once underwent trials; could it be otherwise for the Two Ancestors, who still served with diligent toil? It is because their single thought was rooted in the Truth.

The fruit of a thousand lifetimes [is gained through this]. If one takes it indiscriminately, nothing will ever be accomplished; regardless of whether one alters their outward form, it only serves to increase black karma.
You, both young and old, until now have each been singularly sincere and practiced in reality; you have trodden the path of truth without following the current.

Dwelling in the world yet remaining in a pure state, you have conceived the mind that finds such an encounter difficult to meet. Upon seeing the Buddha and meeting the Sangha, you have been diligent and respectful. If you can thus reflect upon yourselves with self-reproach, you may truly be called "measures" (丈).
When meeting with a donor, one should first perform a respectful bow. When encountering fellow practitioners wearing their robes, do not fail to offer a greeting.

At evening and morning, let the fire and incense be maintained without ever flagging. During meals and breakfast porridge, maintain a constant sense of shame and mindfulness. Whether on duty in the hall or serving in the quarters, one should diligently sweep and wipe without indolence.
One should attend to the master’s every movement and ensure that one’s deportment remains exemplary. This is the essential requirement for both speech and silence.

The Way. Those of the lower grade should cease their inquiries [into worldly affairs]. One must thoroughly master the *palm-leaf* scriptures (*pātra-patra*) and remain broadly learned in the ancient classics.

Only when one has some knowledge of the past and present can one truly understand how to act as a human being. If one is like a mute sheep, what benefit is there in leaving the household life? Before the Tathāgata attained the fruit of Buddhahood, he was proficient in both civil and military arts;

when Yongjia (Wangxi) first became a teacher of men, he possessed both the school of practice and the school of doctrine. To emulate the countenance [of the sages] and to follow the tracks of the great steeds—this is the aspiration of Ziyun.
He said: "Recite the *broom*, recite the *rushes*. The World-Honored One Śākyamuni was without error. Each of you must exert yourselves; do not indulge in idle negligence.
Set your resolve firm and lofty so that you do not fall back into the realm of the ordinary. Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Set your resolve like a high mountain; cultivate virtue like a deep ocean.
Such bitter words are intended for you to become true human beings, to repay the immense kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, and to deliver sentient beings from their immeasurable suffering."
Day after day it was thus; he felt no shame before his own heart. The verse says:
Carrying grain and weeding grass, he displayed a noble model; To carry on the lineage, one must return to those of fierce resolve. In a single thought, the three periods of time are severed;
Only the Old Man of Zaohu was willing to accept this direct transmission.
Inscription for the Abbot’s Quarters of Chan Master Xuedou Mingjue:
To transmit and uphold the ancestral lamp and to succeed to the Buddha’s longevity is no small task.

One should emulate the predecessors, maintaining solemnity in one’s deportment and honoring the dignity of one’s presence. Subdue anger and restrain desire; regulate the breath and nourish the mind. Let not fame or profit stir the emotions.
Do not allow gain or loss to create a division within your mind. Do not follow the fluctuations of the world’s rise and fall. Do not pursue the judgments of others as to right and wrong.

Let both black and white be held within your breast; do not manifest joy or anger upon your countenance. Rejoice in the joys of others as if they were your own; grieve over the sorrows of others as if they were your own.
Be tolerant toward the masses and honor the worthy. Overcome yourself and return to ritual propriety (*li*); do not lose what you have attained because of a minor lapse.

Do not turn your back on public opinion because of what you have long been fond of; do not abandon those you have long held in low regard because of their faults. Do not take pride in your own abilities, nor rely upon your power.
Do not seek to protect your own shortcomings, nor conceal the virtues of others. When beholding virtue, do not forget your own person; when in a position of honor, do not forget your humble origins.

Furthermore, the purpose of learning is fundamentally to cultivate one’s nature—how could one be resentful that others do not understand it? The Way prizes the preservation of the whole person—do not begrudge yourself for the sake of worldly affairs.

If people admire righteousness, it is only natural that they should be extended with the remnants of such virtue. You must certainly instruct me with sincere heart regarding the rules of conduct, drawing extensively from various scriptures to reveal the profound essence.
One must not be parted for even a moment from the garment of patience within the chamber of compassion; the precious jewels of the Great Vehicle should be sought even in moments of haste.
Thus, whether moving or resting, one must maintain constancy; one must be cautious of suspicion and avoid being treated with contempt by others. Heaven...
One must not be deceived. Regarding the coming and going of the multitude, there is neither pursuit nor rejection. Regarding the slander or praise of others, there is neither anger nor greed.

Internally, there is nothing to feel ashamed of; externally, there is nothing to worry about. Even if one’s reputation overflows with praise and material gains are abundant, one should fear the causes and effects of the four realms of existence, and be diligent in the mutual practice of the Three Jewels.
Since birth and death have not yet been transcended, the suffering of karma is difficult to escape. Only when one attains this state...

Aspire! Reflect deeply on how to benefit and rectify yourself. This body is like a walking latrine; worldly gain is called a "soft thief. A hundred years are not long, and there is no peace within the three realms.

It is a pity that even a moment of time is wasted; you should seek liberation. The various patriarchs of antiquity set forth noble examples: some carried their staffs for a lifetime and ate only earth;
Danxia wore nothing but a single cloth robe; Zhaozhou had green ash covering his head; and this Master [Huangbo] wove grass for his clothing.

Whether it be the felt mat, or deep meditation practiced for a long time, or declining an imperial summons, in general, moderation ensures few errors; extravagance invites censure. Humility brings luster;
withdrawal leaves one free from reproach. As our distance from the Sage grows ever greater, the practice of the Way becomes increasingly difficult.
Observe the times to advance or retreat, and do not bring shame upon yourself.
The Tripitaka Master Yijing cautioned those reading the scriptures:
Between the Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Tang dynasties, eminent monks sought the Dharma and departed from Chang’an; of those who left, hundreds went, but scarcely ten returned.
How could later generations know the hardships of their predecessors? On the Snowy Peaks, the rugged terrain chilled to the very bone; at the River of Sand, the surging waves scraped the skin raw.
My hair stands on end with cold. People today do not understand the provenance of the scriptures; they often treat them with casual indifference.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty inscribed this at the Gate of the White Horse Monastery (the place where the scriptures were burned):
The path is desolate, overgrown with long green moss. Each time I ascend these steps, I linger in hesitation. In vain was the Blue Ox said to have passed through the Pass of the Box.
Depart! The white horse personally came from India; to determine right from wrong, one relies on the fierce flames. To distinguish the true from the false, a high platform was built.
Even the eastern wind understands the desolation; it has blown away the ashes of the Way of the Gods from those years.

Dongshan has stilled the world’s censure; he seeks neither fame nor profit, nor does he seek honor. He flows along with the natural course, carefree, passing through this life. When the three-inch breath ceases, who is the master?
After a hundred years, behind one's back, names are called in vain. When garments are torn, they are patched layer upon layer; when provisions run low, they are gathered as needed.
Returning to the camp: how long can a single illusory body last? For the sake of such trivial matters, one’s ignorance grows ever longer.
[The following] summarizes the Five Houses and Seven Schools, encompassing the Linji lineage.
Nanyue, Mazu, Baizhang, and Yun; Linji, Xinghua, Nanquan, Shoushan, and Fenyang; Ciming, Nanhua, Kai, Yi, and Xu;
Xin, Chushi, Qingyuan, Wendeng, and Xingshan.
The Baizhang lineage gave rise to the Muzhou and Yangshan schools; Xiangyan and Yangshan personally inherited the transmission. Qing of Nanata and Bajiao continued the tradition;
yet their descendants have not been seen to carry on their legacy.
In the Yunmen school, Qingxi received the virtue of Tianlong; Xuefeng, Yanyuan, and Xianglin Yuan followed. Beita and Xuedou transmitted it to Tianyi;
from these two lineages, the school became greatly manifest.
In the Caodong school, Qingxi Zushen of Yaoshan and Yundong Zuying were prominent; Tongan Daopi and Daoyi followed.
Liangshan Guan obtained the Dharma from Dayang Hongzhi, while Touzi Yiqing and Furong Daokai walked alone as peerless masters.
From the lineage of Fayan, Xuansha Bei branched out from Xuefeng; Dizang was even more honored than Fayan. Guoshi Shao transmitted it to Shou and Jin.
As for the Buddha-dharma, there is only New Ra (Silla). (One must know this in detail; one must seek the chart of the lineages.)

Entering the eight overflowing gates of noble liberation, they pay homage to the Buddha and revere his virtues; they mindfully recollect the Buddha and respond to his grace; they uphold the precepts and practice the Buddha’s conduct; they study the sutras to clarify the Buddha’s principles.
Sitting in meditation, one reaches the realm of the Buddha; engaging in Zen, one unites with the Buddha’s mind; attaining awakening, one realizes the Buddha-way;

preaching the Dharma, one fulfills the Buddha’s vows. On the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not a single speck of dust is accepted; within the gate of Buddha-activity, not a single dharma is abandoned.

Yet these eight matters are like the four cardinal and four intermediate directions—none may be lacking. From the sages of the past to the sages of the present, the principle is one and the same. The Six Paramitas...
The *pāramitās* must also be practiced concurrently. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Those who cling to emptiness remain stuck in one corner.
To claim that 'no reliance on words' applies to oneself may still be a personal delusion, but to slander the Buddha’s scriptures is a grave obstacle of sin; how can one not be cautious?"
The Letter of Chen Xianliang (also published in the *Jingyan Baoxun*).
Chen Guiqian, the Judicial Intendant, replied to the letter from True Minister Zhen Dexiu, saying: "I have received your inquiry concerning matters of the Chan school.

Looking up, I see your magnanimity and delight in the good. Considering my own shallowness and meagerness, how could I be worthy of such an honor? Nevertheless, I venture to respond with my limited perspective..."
I have seen Chen’s submission regarding whether or not one should contemplate the *huatou*. From my perspective, there has never been a fixed doctrine on this matter.
If one can achieve the state of non-arising in a single thought-moment, one’s entire being is the Buddha; where else would a *huatou* exist?

It is only because of the habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes that we turn our backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, such that in a single instant thoughts arise and perish moment by moment, much like a young monkey picking up chestnuts.

The Buddhas and Patriarchs, having no choice, provisionally established skillful means, causing one to chew upon a "head-word" (hua-tou) that has no flavor, such that the conscious intellect has no way to function.
This is like exchanging honeyed fruit for a bitter gourd; it is intended to wash away your karmic consciousness and possesses no ultimate reality.
It is also like the weapons of a state, employed only when there is no other recourse. Yet, students of the present day [instead] focus on the head-word...

To force interpretations upon the head [of the teaching] is a grave error; some even go so far as to provide detailed explanations for each phrase as if they were their primary task—this is to stray further and further from the truth.
Master Linji sat for twenty years, wearing out seven meditation cushions, simply watching for the "donkey business" to depart before the "horse business" could arrive.
It was because of rolling up the curtain that he attained great enlightenment. As it is said: "The eighty-four thousand locks and bolts are all dispelled by a single key."

The key is opened; how could it depend on many words? Your instruction says that by reciting the Buddha’s words, maintaining the Buddha’s mind, and practicing the Buddha’s deeds, one will surely attain realization after a long time.

While practicing in this manner certainly does not fail to make one a worthy person of this age, in the Chan school, one must further see through to the very essence of one's own original ground and its natural radiance before reaching the ultimate goal.

Although this matter is inherently present within every person, it is merely shrouded by adventitious delusive thoughts. If one does not apply oneself with diligent refinement, it will never become clear and pure.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "It is like refining gold ore; the gold does not exist inherently before the refining.
Although it is gold from the very beginning, it is ultimately through refining that it is perfected. This is precisely what is meant. Furthermore, your letter suggests that if the Way were not...
Regarding words and letters: why did the Buddhas and Patriarchs leave behind so many sutras and treatises in the world?
The sutras are the Buddha’s words; Chan is the Buddha’s mind. From the beginning, there has been no contradiction between them.

However, worldly people pursue words and follow phrases, drowning themselves in the net of teachings, unaware that they possess their own segment of radiant, great matter. Therefore, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he did not establish [reliance on] words.
"Words and letters directly point to the human mind; seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood. This is called the 'separate transmission outside the teachings.
It does not mean that there is some other principle apart from the teachings; it simply requires that one clearly realize this mind and not become attached to the forms of the teachings.

If you now merely recite the words of the Buddha without bringing them back to yourself, it is like someone counting another's treasures—of which you yourself have not even half a cent's worth. Furthermore:

It is like a pearl wrapped in tattered cloth: upon leaving the door, it leaks away once more. Even if one obtains a slight taste within it, this is still the view of attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Regarding the matter of one's fundamental nature, it is said that although gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract.
One must thoroughly sweep away everything until it is completely purified; only then will there be a slight degree of resonance with the truth. Although I have not previously studied...
Regarding the Tripitaka, I have become somewhat proficient in reciting such sutras as the Avatamsaka, the Śūraṅgama, the Awakening of Faith, and the Vimalakīrti.
Furthermore, over several decades, I have enjoyed and contemplated works such as the various records of the elders in the *Chuan deng lu* and Master Shou’s *Zongjing lu*.
During this time, I have been so absorbed within these "houses" that I have had no leisure to study the sutras and śāstras. Although the Laṅkāvatāra is indeed a work of realization...

The *Moxin zong* (Essentials for Polishing the Mind) is also difficult to read due to its phrasing and punctuation, and I have never investigated it deeply. However, one must understand that we all possess a sincere mind;
it is not merely a matter of deceiving oneself with worldly conventions to provide material for idle conversation. Let us briefly verify this through daily experience:
although one may be free from gross impurities and coarse transgressions, can one truly penetrate and illuminate all circumstances—whether wholesome or unwholesome, favorable or adverse?
Is it not subject to being shifted or replaced by others? Is it exactly the same whether waking from a dream during sleep at night?

Are there no terrors or inversions? Can you maintain mastery even when afflicted by illness? If there are still objects present before one's eyes, then one cannot avoid inversions even in dreams and sleep.
Since dreams and sleep are inverted, one will certainly be unable to maintain mastery when ill. Once one is ill...
If one cannot attain mastery, then at the very brink of birth and death, one will certainly lack autonomy. As the saying goes:

"Just as a person drinking water knows its coldness or warmth for themselves," you, Gentleman of the Palace for the Reception of Guests, while in the midst of the peak of fame and achievement, have cultivated purity and diminished desire to devote yourself to this Way;
this may truly be called a lotus flower amidst the flames. An ancient said: "This is the business of a great man; it is not [the work of] a general..."
This is what one who possesses the [true] marks is capable of doing. It is further said: "One simply wishes to stand atop the highest peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor;
one further desires to exhaustively penetrate and reach far away, until arriving at the stage where there is no doubt. Your instruction states that there is no place to begin;
yet this very lack of a place to begin is precisely the point where power is gained. As stated in your previous letter, whether in stillness or in bustle, it is all the same.
Focus with single-minded attention. What is the principle here? After a long time of such mastery, there will naturally be no distinction between stillness and bustle.
Should thoughts instead become chaotic and scattered, arising and ceasing without cease, then take up a koan and confront them head-on.
Then the mind of arising and ceasing will naturally and suddenly come to rest; illumination and the one who illuminates will simultaneously enter quiescence.
This is precisely "arriving home. I have also studied this, yet I have not yet reached it. For now, I have disclosed my thoughts to this extent; there is no need for further instruction.
Fearing that there might be points where Confucianism and Buddhism do not coincide, people will surely find this most strange.

One day, when the Attendant Censor and Gentleman finds his mind’s eye opened and enlightened, he too will surely laugh heartily and revile them (as the Circuit Intendant met with the great masters such as Yue-lin and Tie-bian).
Lord Wen Zheng urges Chan Master Yuanwu on his travels:
"When observing water, do not observe a small, filthy pond; the fish and turtles in a filthy pond are base. When climbing a mountain, do not climb a low, rolling hill;
the vegetation on a low, rolling hill is sparse. Observe water by looking directly at the vast blue ocean; climb a mountain by ascending straight to Mount Tai."

On the mountain peak, what is gained is no small matter; what is seen is lofty. Though you exhaust all your efforts, it will not be in vain. Fortunately, there is a place for selecting Buddhas in the South;
you should go there to exhaustively investigate the wondrous principle. In years to come, having become a vessel of the Way, you shall straighten the collapsing纲 (the social order).

Do not fail the ambition of a man who has left the home life. Great Man! Cease your deliberations. How could you sacrifice your life’s purpose for the sake of empty fame? Let us harmonize in joy at this time.
There is little awareness of the passing years; time only darkly adds to one’s age. Chengdu, moreover, is a land of flourishing splendor—a mere den of flowers and wine.
But you, my teacher, are by nature a renunciant; how could you allow yourself to be buried among such vulgarities?
You, my teacher, fortunately possess the ambition of a rainbow; why do you hesitate in the mire? Have you not seen the fish that swallow ships?
Do not conceal your flowing brilliance. How could a tree thick enough to be embraced by both arms grow in the Red Mound?

When the Great Peng spreads its wings for ninety thousand li, how can it be compared to the sand-swallowing gulls flying along the spring shore? Why not urge on the thousand-li steed at once, rather than imitating the jiao-liao bird that clings to a single branch?
Even if one could expound upon a thousand sutras and treatises, it would still fall into the second level of the Chan school’s pedagogical devices. White clouds have long cherished the high terrace;
shrouded by evening mists and morning fog, they do not open for even a moment. Yet, to comfort the hopes of the common people for drenching rain, he casually emerges from the mountains as before.
Furthermore, have you not seen that there is jade on Mount Kun known as *qióngyáo*? When its auspicious time has not yet arrived, it dwells among the weeds and brambles. At such a time...
If at that time one had not remained in Jingchu, how could the price of the "linked cities" have been so much higher?

Regarding the Elder Master Wuguan’s *Exhortation to the Elder An*, this poor monk has often perused the Tripitaka teachings and carefully examined the Buddha’s intent; he finds that the Buddha did not permit bhikṣus to sit and receive food for which they have performed no labor.
They give rise to a mind of indolence and conceive the view of a self. Whenever it is morning, the Buddha and his disciples take their bowls to beg for food;
they do not discriminate between the noble and the lowly, nor do they harbor thoughts of superiority or inferiority, so that those who obtain merit may all share it equally.

That which is later called "permanent property" (sanghika) was originally established for the sake of aged or infirm bhikṣus who are unable to go begging; it is not for the use of those who are young and strong.
They obtained [alms] and ate them. This remained the case even during the era of the True Dharma following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

Since the age of the Semblance Dharma, however, the practice of begging for alms has not been discontinued in the Chan monasteries of the Central Kingdom; yet, they merely appoint those deemed capable to perform it, and the gains and offerings thus acquired are pooled to support the *caitya* (the monastery) so as to provide for the broad assembly of monks.
Consequently, the rule of daily wandering for alms has been abandoned. Now, I have heard that the abbots of several monasteries...
Failing to recognize cause and effect, you show no respect for this old monk; you turn your back on the Buddha’s intent and weaken the Dharma-gate.
If you do not remain in the monastery, where will this old man go? Do you not reflect further upon this: for whose sake were the permanent assets of the monastery originally established?

What state of mind should you cultivate to accord with the Buddha’s mind? What practice should you cultivate to accord with the Buddha’s conduct? In the past, when the Buddha was alive, there were times he did not attend invitations.
He remained in his private quarters at the monastery, touring the monks' cells one by one to visit the elderly and the infirm, inquiring after each of them and attending to their every need.
He further exhorted the bhikṣus to show mutual respect, to act with skillful means, and to eliminate anger and resentment;
this was the model for a Master who governs the great assembly. Yet nowadays, those in authority freely expend the monastery's permanent assets to provide for themselves.

Regarding their mouths and bodies, they form alliances with the powerful and influential, yet they continue to exclude the elderly and the infirm. They conceal the property of the Sangha as their own private possession;
of the Buddha’s mind and the Buddha’s practice, there is not a single trace. How tragic, how tragic! An ancient worthy said: "The elderly monk is the banner of the mountain gate.
Yet in the Zen groves of today, among a hundred monks, there is not one who is old. Even when old, they—
I submit this. I have come to know all the more that longevity offers no benefit; it is even worse than an early death.

I pray that from this day forward, each of you shall follow the Buddha’s words to perpetuate the ancestral seat and provide comfort to the elderly and the infirm. Regarding the assets of the permanent residence (saṃghārāma), whether they exist or not, provide for them as appropriate.
Do not allow ignorant persons to monopolize authority and act with negligence, thereby inviting the retribution of a short lifespan in future lives. You must examine this matter most earnestly.
The Master Dharma’s Verse on True Nature:
When the Dharma came from the West, he did not establish written words.
He sat in silence at Shaolin for nine years, until alone Shen Guang comprehended the essential meaning.
Having already attained resonance with those of superior faculties, he still took pity on those of middling and inferior capacities;
thus, he forcefully composed twenty characters, which he called the "Verses on True Nature.
By reading them repeatedly from beginning to end, he produced forty stanzas, each verse...
There is a profound intent here. It is my hope that future descendants may, by following the finger, see the moon.
Should there be a person who, before the character for "nature" has even taken form, attains a deep realization, its brilliance will manifest of itself.
"It is not obtained from elsewhere. This would surely provoke laughter at the old barbarian with missing teeth; he truly deserves a severe blow from my staff!
When the devas and humans pay homage to a withered bone, Maitreya accepts it and says, "You were I in a previous life;
today my celestial eye has opened. My jade robes arrive as soon as I think of them, and my precious food comes naturally."
I thank you for your past diligent toil, which has brought me such joy today. As the flowers are scattered, I prostrate once more; let no one in the human world harbor doubt or suspicion.

This stinking skin-bag is the cause for hungry ghosts to whip their corpses; from kalpa to kalpa, they are in a frantic rush, knowing only how to crave pleasure and refusing to turn their light inward even for a moment.
White karma is but a tiny fraction; the years in the Yellow Springs are long. One must truly lash oneself with a heavy whip; this regret is ultimately difficult to forget.
The śramaṇa destroys the two views—shame on you, deluded child!
Why do you not observe yourself? To whip a corpse is a true perversion; to prostrate before bones is self-deception.
Good and evil are created by the mind; Buddhas and demons are seen with fixed eyes. Tread upon and overturn the ocean of afflictions, and birth and death will no longer concern you.
End of the "Verses of the Various Patriarchs of the Chan School," Part II (Conclusion).
